We're able to prove that under specific conditions, the difference in test accuracy between real- and quantized-weighted models is solely a consequence of the former being an approximation of the latter. These findings are further validated through the analysis of various quantization methods, as well as the integration of regularization techniques.

Quantum systems possessing geometric duals exhibit a more restrictive set of entropy inequalities than general quantum systems do. The set of admissible entropies derived using the Ryu-Takayanagi formula forms the Holographic Entropy Cone. This stricter set of inequalities is violated once quantum corrections are introduced through the Quantum Extremal Surface prescription. The structure of the QES formula allows for a detailed analysis of the interplay between quantum contributions from bulk entropies and the HEC inequalities. This paper begins exploring this problem by establishing a connection between bulk entropy constraints and boundary entropy inequalities. Specifically, it is demonstrated that bulk entropies adhering to the HEC lead to corresponding adherence of the boundary entropies to the HEC, as well. Additionally, it is shown that bulk entropies conforming to monogamy of mutual information (MMI) lead to corresponding adherence of the boundary entropies to MMI.

We examine a broad category of solvable lattice models derived from the foundational knowledge of conformal field theory.
These models are generated using any conformal field theory.
We analyze specific lattice models tied to affine algebras identified by Jimbo et al., for algebras ABCD and Kuniba et al., for G2.
We develop a universal formula for the crossing multipliers of these models and find that these are also reflected in the characteristically specialized characters of the respective models.
Based on this discovery, we propose that the crossing multipliers in this comprehensive group of solvable interaction round the face lattice models are represented by the conformal field theory they originate from.
Using this conclusion, we explore the local state probabilities within these models and show they conform to the branching rule under regime III conditions.

Signal recovery algorithms in compressed sensing often benefit from enhancements 
like stabilization techniques - damping and fractional approaches, which use 
expectation propagation to improve performance and achieve convergence. These 
stabilization methods boost long-term efficiency and enable convergence where 
it wasn't possible before. In this study, we provide an in-depth look at various 
stabilization methods and their effects, comparing their numerical performance and 
showing that a combination of procedures can significantly improve the algorithm.

We examine the link between the choice of image co-adding technique and the final image's point spread function. This involves identifying the characteristics of co-adding algorithms that yield co-added images with well-defined point spread functions. Our investigation centers on the following points:

  1. A clear illustration shows how linear co-adding techniques can generate images without well-defined point spread functions even with straightforward scenarios and weight functions.
  2. A more rigorous analysis reveals that linear co-adding algorithms have well-defined point spread functions in two specific situations: when all input images share the same point spread function, or when weights used to co-add images are not influenced by the signal intensity.
  3. Two viable nonlinear co-adding approaches are identified that can produce images with clearly defined point spread functions even when individual input images have distinct point spread functions.
  4. A practical example highlights the potential issue of losing signal information when applying a nonlinear approach to achieve this result.
  Ultimately, the choice of image co-adding algorithm should be guided by a thorough consideration of the nature of the signal, the characteristics of the point spread function, and the specific requirements of the application in question.

Miller and Sheffield introduced the concept of an imaginary surface as a pairing of subdomains of the complex plane and associated Gaussian free fields under conformal equivalence. Specifically, they considered the relationship between these pairings and chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution. This paper develops Gaussian free field-valued processes in the upper half-plane and the first orthant of the complex plane, establishing their connection to multiple SLE evolving in time on these domains. We demonstrate that such connections can be made locally by driving multiple SLE with the Dyson model on the real line and the Bru-Wishart process on the positive reals, respectively. Ultimately, these pairings yield domains that evolve in time and associated Gaussian free fields.

In this research, we address the Cauchy problem for the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations in multi-dimensional space with smooth periodic initial conditions and obtain analytical estimates of the solution's maximum norm, tied to the initial conditions' maximum norm.

The verification problem for quantum computation is crucial and challenging, where a quantum server attempts to convince a less computationally powerful classical client that a quantum circuit has produced a specific output. The fastest known protocol for verifying classical results in quantum computation has a time complexity of O(poly(κ)|C|^3), but recent advancements have led to a new, more efficient protocol. By developing new techniques, the complexity has been significantly improved to O(poly(κ)|C|), which is a substantial breakthrough. Additionally, the developed protocol utilizes secure quantum random oracles and the existence of noisy trapdoor claw-free functions. Furthermore, the study introduces a new, parallel classical channel protocol for remote state preparation, enabling efficient preparation of independently random states in specific forms within constant rounds, while also achieving faster execution time compared to previous approaches.

Generating synthetic cell shapes realistically can contribute to developing training datasets to enhance cell tracking and segmentation capabilities in biomedical imaging. For effective cell shape synthesis, a compact yet flexible representation is required, however current methods involving voxel-based and polygon mesh approaches have limitations for high-resolution and topology changes such as growth and cell division. Our proposal utilizes level sets of signed distance functions to model cell shapes, which can represent complex shapes and their changes efficiently. By applying this representation to single cells and symbiotic cells consisting of two, we demonstrate the synthesis of realistic cell shapes and their evolution, which could be developed into a training dataset for improved cell tracking and segmentation. These models facilitate the exploration of generative convolutional networks (GCNs) and their potential to learn a compact representation of cell shapes, which can significantly reduce computational complexity and memory requirements. Our research also marks the first application of deep learning on biologically significant 3D shapes with dynamic topologies.

Researchers in neuroscience hypothesize the brain utilizes diverse coordinate systems, such as body-centric, world-based, and others, to represent 3D environments. Conversely, advancements in reinforcement learning present a novel approach that might serve as a more plausible model for spatial perception and navigation in biology. Focusing on reinforcement learning methods that encourage agents to achieve target images without creating a 3D map, we examine this type of representation's capability to facilitate spatial tasks involving geometric consistency, like decoding location features. To demonstrate this, we design a hand-crafted representation ensuring high geometric consistency, and show that retaining information on persisting visual features during camera movement can improve performance in these tasks. Our findings provide a significant stimulus for neuroscientists to explore non-Cartesian spatial representations as an alternative to cognitive mapping.

To evaluate the efficiency of event-chain Monte Carlo algorithms for complex simulations, specifically in two-dimensional models of hard-disk dipoles tethered together, researchers assess their suitability for future use in molecular water models. They analyze the rotational motion of these dipoles through measurements of their polarization's autocorrelation times. Four distinct event-driven algorithms are examined: straight, reflective, forward, and Newtonian ECMC, all differing in their updating methods at specific times. These non-reversible methods exhibit considerable performance gains over traditional local Metropolis algorithms. Additionally, there are notable speed disparities among the ECMC variations, with the Newtonian variant showing exceptional potential in overcoming the dynamic stagnation often encountered in 3D dipolar models with electrostatic interactions.

The challenge of Sound Event Localization and Detection involves pinpointing the presence of multiple overlapping sounds, accurately categorizing their types, and estimating their source locations. Recently, neural networks have emerged as the leading solution for this problem, with Convolutional Recurrent Neural Networks being a prominent architecture used in such applications. A novel system submitted to the 2020 Challenge for Detection and Classification of Acoustic Scenes and Events uses a specific type of Convolutional Recurrent Neural Network with rectangular filters, optimized for recognizing distinct sound features. By employing data augmentation through channel rotation and reflection in the First Order Ambisonic domain, the training dataset was expanded, allowing for more robust performance and improved Accuracy in locating sound sources. Evaluation results demonstrate that this approach surpasses baseline results, significantly reducing Error Rates and increasing F-scores for location-aware detection.

In traditional communication systems, signal interference is generally seen as unwanted noise that distorts transmitted signals, but a new perspective has emerged where multiple transmissions occur simultaneously and potentially benefit from one another. Various wireless applications have taken advantage of this principle, as evidenced by non-orthogonal multiple access and other methods such as joint source-channel coding, computational codes, and federated learning, which were initially influenced by techniques like the natural order binary fingerprint. The simultaneous approach has numerous advantages, as seen in the source coding domain, where better results can be achieved, or in the channel coding domain, where longer codes can be replicated. Furthermore, simultaneous transmissions have the potential to shape the future of computing, with areas such as distributed artificial intelligence and machine learning leading to more efficient processing. The authors of this article are promoting the simultaneous transmission paradigm as a unifying theme across communication disciplines, encouraging further exploration and innovation inspired by this idea.

Time-frequency analysis heavily relies on spectrograms, being a crucial component derived from the short time Fourier transform (STFT). Recent years have witnessed significant advancements in spectrogram denoising, achieved through deep learning-based methods. Nevertheless, these successes have been grounded in empirical evidence, rather than theoretical soundness. The underlying challenge lies in the intricately structured data set generated by the STFT, known as Gaussian analytic functions (GAFs). This research aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of the spectrogram, and subsequently the spectrogram denoising problem, through which valuable insights into the denoising process can be gleaned. Our findings reveal that the spectrogram's sequential nature necessitates a denoising approach tailored to the individual spectrogams, rather than the entire data set. We have formulated spectrogram denoising as an ill-posed problem due to the spectrogams' inherently chaotic structure. By developing a new framework that leverages the specrgoams' unique properties, and cites examples such as the Brownian compainement model, our denoising approach is grounded in the underlying analytics of the spectrogram. Our denoising algorithm's efficacy is validated through empirical comaparisons with state-of-the-art deep learning-based methods. Moreover, the spectrogram's intricate structure has been found to render conventional probabilistic denoising techniques ineffective.

We present a novel universal method for detecting multiple types of dynamic behavior,
including stable and traveling chimera states using a dynamically adjusted measure of
coherence. This method automatically identifies and differentiates between synchronized
clusters, traveling wave patterns, chimera states, and asynchronous states. Additionally,
it is capable of determining the number of clusters present in cluster synchronization
situations. To further enhance our method, we developed a new technique for measuring the
speed of traveling chimera states. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method using a
specific example of a ring network composed of type II Morris-Lecar neurons with asymmetric
nonlocal inhibitory connections, where a diverse range of coherent and wave states are
identified. Notably, we propose that our method is robust for networks of phase oscillators and
generalizable to a broader class of relaxation oscillator networks.

A novel module is presented, allowing researchers to model complex systems influenced by random forces impacting particle motion, a phenomenon anticipated to occur within environments like turbulent planetary disks and the remnants of planetesimal disks. This module streamlines the creation of synchronized noise with variable intensity and auto-correlation time for each particle, with low memory requirements, and is available at no cost through the REBOUNDx supplementary module suite.

Key aspects of quantum science include precise measurement and feedback mechanisms, offering wide-ranging benefits from advanced quantum technology to the conversion of information into work within quantum thermodynamics. Mathematical tools used to model and analyze feedback control systems are essential for understanding these processes. This paper provides a comprehensive examination of the quantum feedback control literature, comparing quantum estimation theory and feedback control models. It also highlights notable experiments, assessing their practical value and assessing the viability of quantum- enhanced precision for specific measurement objectives. Crucially, quantum feedback control has potential real-world applications and can contribute to the advancement of quantum technology.

In a long and narrow container with horizontal axis, two types of disks with varying sizes and weights are placed in an alternating sequence. This container is sealed by movable pistons which ensure all the disks come into contact with one of the container's walls when in a jammed state, resulting from a combination of external forces such as moderate pressure, gravity, and random vibrations. By dividing the disk arrangement into segments and constructing species of particles with statistically interacting states, exact calculations for jammed configurations have been obtained. These calculations have been further extended to include artificial additions of 'frustrated particles'. The exact jammed configurations have been found to be in perfect agreement with simulation results. The concept of entropic pressure, extracted from the model, may offer potential alternatives to chemical pressure in the design of molecular motors.

Research into El Ni\~no's two main flavors - East Pacific and Central Pacific types - has become a significant focus in climate research. Recent studies that combined climate indices in various ways have found intriguing results, but it remains unclear how these are linked to precipitation patterns. This study uses a novel approach, involving statistical analysis of a large climate dataset, to investigate the characteristics of East and Central Pacific El Ni\~no events. Our research reveals that these events exhibit distinct profiles in a climate index, affecting global precipitation patterns differently, and tend to occur at different times of the year. This is further confirmed by an evaluation of climate model simulations. Our study also discovers that these events display non-steady state behavior, with varying intensities over the course of a year. This research could lead to a greater grasp of the dynamics behind these two types of El Ni\~no events.

Evidence suggesting the demographic characteristics of massive black holes is accumulating, spanning a broad spectrum of galaxy types, from large clusters to tiny dwarf galaxies. Despite this, the original paths of massive black holes remain shrouded in uncertainty. We've discovered a potentially significant indicator of massive black hole formation in dwarf galaxies, which could help reveal how these celestial bodies came into being. The presence of a seamless mass range of massive black holes within these galaxies, as observed in a study by a team from the University of California, Santa Barbara, may be interpreted as an sign of 'black hole fragmentation' - a phenomenon in which massive black holes are created through the collapse of dense cloud formations. This process is thought to be an alternative to the established'merger pathway' in larger galaxies, where massive black holes emerge from the integration of smaller black holes over time. The findings from our analysis suggest that massive black holes in dwarf galaxies could have originated from a unique pathway, resulting in an uneven mass distribution among these celestial bodies. The potential implications of our discovery need to be further investigated, and could affect our comprehension of massive black hole evolution if confirmed.

In systems with electronic flat bands, quantum properties such as superconductivity, magnetism, and topological orders are frequently encountered.  Although the existence of flat bands is established in certain structures with geometric frustration like the kagome lattice, flat-band driven correlation effects are uncommon in such systems with multiple atomic orbitals.  In the study presented here, negative magnetoresistance and indicators of ferromagnetic fluctuations are found in a model kagome metal CoSn featuring a flat band at the Fermi level.  It was observed that the material's magnetoresistance can be influenced by tuning the Fermi level to modulate electronic interactions.  By using computational tools and experimental data, it is determined that a previously unseen flat-band driven correlation effect exists within the system, enabling potential new pathways to achieve unconventional superconductivity and topological materials in metals exhibiting geometric frustration.

Understanding how genomic elements affect specific traits through genome-wide association studies remains complex due to the sheer number of available genomic elements where associations can occur. We conducted new studies to define subcategories of genomic elements that are most associated with specific traits. These subcategories, specifically transcription factor binding sites and areas sensitive to certain enzymes, can be studied in relevant cell types to infer trait information without needing fine-grained resolution. We confirmed the accuracy of predictions using data from QTL analysis in relevant cell types, demonstrating that these genomic elements can accurately forecast the effects of specific genetic variations. Additionally, we confirmed that our model's predictions are compatible with the principles of evolutionary genetics, and that the associations between specific genetic variations and their effects are relatively conserved across different populations.

This study identifies and classifies 2-designs that satisfy specific conditions and have specific automorphism properties. A non-trivial 2-design's automorphism group can either be an instance of the previously documented examples described in this research or a specific subgroup within a larger group of automorphisms that corresponds to a geometric linear transformation involving a prime number.

This study examines electronic correlation within confined hydrogen, helium and lithium ions in their base states using entropy measures. Different wavefunctions are used to better account for inter-electronic interactions. The resulting entropy values show sensitivity to these interactions. In situations of extremely tight confinement, Coulomb effects are minimized and models treating particles as independent or non-interacting pairs in an impenetrable sphere are increasingly applicable. Energy estimates derived from these models align well with existing literature values.

The velocity distribution pattern of distant binary star systems can be an effective means of determining how gravity behaves at low acceleration rates, typically found on the outskirts of galaxies. To explore the possibility of using this test, the binary star system HD 147971, which sits about 11.7 kiloparsecs from Earth, was studied using data from SPECTRUM-10. The measurement of its velocity of 87.2 km/s was found to be in alignment with 200 km/s/y predictions made by other researchers. The analysis also uncovered evidence suggesting that the star's motion may be part of a wider structure comprising several parsecs.

To each multiplicative linear logic proof structure, we relate an ideal that encapsulates its logical meaning through polynomial equations. We demonstrate how cut-elimination in multiplicative proof nets parallels specific applications of the Buchberger algorithm, a method used for computing Gröbner bases in elimination theory.

A sophisticated time series analysis tool called cross-correlation analysis is used in this study to explore the interconnected behaviors of time series, with a focus on financial markets. A novel prediction method for determining the future synchronization state of two related time series has been developed. Cross-recurrence plots are applied as a non-linear approach to measure the coupling between the time domain of two series, thus establishing their synchronization status. A deep learning strategy is employed to address the task of predicting synchronization states, utilizing dynamic sampling of cross-recurrence plots as key features. Experimental results from multiple stocks, including significant S&P 100 constituents, have been gathered to test the efficacy of this method. Findings indicate that synchronizing predictions for time series pairs can be challenging, yet achieveable with substantial accuracy for certain stock pairs.

THz radiation enables the precise stimulation of vibrational frequencies in molecules and crystals, leading to the introduction of inertial influences on electrons. By drawing a comparison to classical mechanics, where circular motion generates Coriolis and centrifugal forces, analogous effects arise, specifically spin-rotation coupling, centrifugal field coupling, and the interplay of these forces with the spin-orbit and the redshift of energy levels. These effects can persist for a few picoseconds following the initial stimulation, and potentially amplifying their magnitude could make this approach a promising means of controlling localized quantum states and chemical reaction barriers via vibration.

Current click-through rate (CTR) prediction models are largely dependent on recent user browsing history and tend to underperform on new ads, unseen by the user previously. To address this, we propose a unified framework, named DipSum, integrating deep learning and robust information retrieval methods to boost new ad prediction. By partitioning the user and ad sets in a manner sensitive to both user browsing history and ad content, DipSum effectively reduces the complexity of the problem. We employ nested clustering technology to divide the data into manageable segments, and then leverage information retrieval to shortlist potential candidates from separate clusters based on similarity. Meanwhile, a dual deep learning model works in tandem, fine-tuning candidate selections at a micro-level. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that DipSum significantly raises the accuracy of new ad predictions. Notably, our approach achieves a remarkable 15% and 8% enhancement in absolute values for new ads and traditional ads, respectively.

Traditionally, business process management concentrated on organized, task-based processes, but the rise in importance of knowledge-intensive processes has led to an increasing need for semi-structured process management. Current approaches to such processes often rely on workflow engines, but these often require significant technical knowledge and are not adaptable to processes that rely heavily on knowledge, such as those in professional services. To address this, we present a new approach, Business Knowledge within Process Management (BKP), which allows for the separation of process management into two distinct layers: an executive layer and an operational layer. The executive layer focuses on high-level process management, while the operational layer tackles the intricate, local tasks. BKP introduces a new data model to facilitate the definition of business rules and objectives, which are enforced through BKP engines to ensure perfect compliance. To support BKP, we have developed a toolset, including a designer and an interpreter, to demonstrate the efficacy of our approach.

Wildfires disrupting solar energy operations due to atmospheric aerosols pose significant economic impacts. Monitoring solar energy production's impact requires precise aerosol property measurements, including optical depth, refractive index, and size distribution. Employing data from the MODIS satellite, this research develops a rapid method to obtain these parameters using a combined approach of simplified aerosol property retrieval algorithms. The fast aerosol property retrieval algorithm determines optical depth and angular distribution of solar radiation with high accuracy, while a modified single-scattering model predicts the other parameters by incorporating predefined particle shapes. Evaluating this approach in multiple regions affected by wildfires shows good to excellent accuracy when compared to in-situ and co-located ground-based data. The calculated aerosol properties are then used to assess the impact of wildfires on solar energy production.

Protecting users of location-based services with significant privacy requirements is extremely difficult when multiple locations are shared within a short time frame due to the significant relationships anticipated between these locations. Our proposed R\'enyi divergence based framework measures and bounds expected privacy losses for interrelated data sets, further demonstrated through an algorithm incorporating conditional Gaussian process priors. This framework illustrates the challenges in safeguarding dependent data and provides a strategic approach to maintaining sensitive location data privacy within a specified boundary.

Research has shown that combining resting-state functional MRI data from multiple sites can potentially introduce systematic biases in connectivity measures. In this study, we investigated how site-to-site effects impact our ability to detect individual and group differences, and assess the effects of multisite studies on our statistical power. Using simulated data and two statistical tests, we evaluated the effects of site variability on our ability to detect changes in two groups. Our results show that multisite studies generally demonstrates equivalent or improved statistical power in detecting abnormalities, but detecting cross-group effects is less effective. To minimize adverse effects of site variability, we recommend incorporating site-specific terms into our models. Furthermore, our simulation data suggest that increasing the number of subjects per site can also mitigate this issue.

Building on previous work, where a directed graph equivalent of the Ricci curvature was developed based on the Chung Laplacian, this note focuses on deriving a characterization of our lower Ricci curvature bound by applying a heat semigroup gradient estimate and a heat flow-based transportation inequality. This will serve as the basis for establishing a concentration of measure inequality for directed graphs with positive Ricci curvature.

Recent advances in NLP for code-mixed texts have gained considerable attention, 
mainly driven by the widespread use of social media across different cultures.
A crucial step in NLP for such texts is developing a suitable word representation.
However, creating effective word embeddings for code-mixed languages is challenging 
due to issues like non-standard spelling, missing or alternative language options.
Additionally, most existing methods and datasets focus on bilingual settings, which 
is not compatible with languages used by larger online communities, like Hindi.
To address these problems, we introduce a new model called ${\text{L2X}}$ that 
pre-trains word embeddings for any language using a large, independently-collected 
dataset, independently of other languages used in the word's context.
We evaluate our approach by developing word embeddings for eight Indian languages 
using a massive dataset of publicly-available Wikipedia articles, and demonstrate 
the efficacy of these embeddings in improving the performance of NLP tasks.

Using a combination of density functional calculations and the linearized Migdal-Eliashberg equations with the functional derivative approach, we analyzed how the density of states affects the behavior of H3S as a function of pressure between 162 and 250 GPa. Our results show that accounting for the variable density of states significantly improves the match with experimental data for the critical temperature. Additionally, we found that considering two key components - the positive electron-phonon interaction and the negative electron-electron interaction - yields a predictable trend in the isotope effect coefficient as a function of pressure. However, incorporating the variable density of states enhances our understanding of both interactions and improves agreement with experiments, particularly at high pressures, suggesting the importance of its van Hove singularities in superconducting H3S compounds.

Fisher developed the Fundamental Theorem of Natural Selection using the concepts of average excess and average effect, where he initially defined these ideas somewhat abstractly. However, some experts believe that reframing his theories using statistical methods such as covariance and regression would clarify these concepts, both are part of classical statistical techniques. We propose an interpretation where Fisher's average excess and average effect are intended to represent a fundamental distinction between statistical correlation and causality, and according to this understanding, the average effect specifically measures the weighted outcomes of a physical change in the genes of a homologous pair. We show that this apparent conflict can be resolved if specific relationships are maintained between gene frequencies and residual non-additive components, and also discuss the idea that maintaining causality as a Fisherian concept may offer a new approach to understanding the direction of effects in biological systems.

This paper will present our approach to optimizing bipedal robot walking assisted by thrusters using a closed-loop feedback system. By assuming that supervisory controllers are properly set, we will concentrate on refining joint trajectories to meet specific performance requirements. To achieve this, we will create a mediator filter that combines performance metrics and then applies them to an error-correcting filter to ensure accurate trajectory implementation. To optimize this approach, we will use the adversarial decomposition technique and ensure the stability of this optimization point through a singular perturbation analysis. Finally, we will test this strategy on two distinct datasets involving bipedal robots with and without thrusters, and the results will demonstrate significant enhancements in performance as well as robustness to disturbances.

This research proposes a visual relocalization technique based on 3D surfel mapping with optimized clustering. A pre-processed map of 3D surfels is created from prior knowledge or training data. An efficient clustering method is developed to optimize map construction time. A novel surfel point representation is introduced for accurate online feature extraction and descriptor calculation. A single wide baseline stereo image is used to derive 3D surfel points and an optimal subset of learning points is selected to refine the map. A point correspondence strategy is employed to maintain consistency between the map and incoming images. New observations are matched to the pre-computed set of learning points to update the map. This process is repeated to update the map incrementally. A direct association strategy is employed to connect the map with the local observation space for visual relocalization. A single iteration of the EKF slip algorithm is used to correct the pose. Our method demonstrates the efficacy of visual relocalization with 3D surfel mapping, especially for situations involving occlusions, low-resolution imagery, limited memory, and monocular systems.

Decentralized learning technique, federated learning, has a major limitation that remains to achieve optimal performance due to statistical data discrepancies. Overcoming this issue, researchers have focused on personalizing machine learning models, which typically rely on having complete datasets, an unrealistic scenario given data labeling complexities. When models receive limited labeling, they experience reduced adaptability to local distributions and, subsequently, suffer performance degradation. Addressing this issue, we propose an innovative approach where under-resourced clients collaborate with data-related clients, dubbed 'helper agents', for informed labeling. We then develop a trustworthiness-based data association metric to ensure that the helper's labels enhance the local training. Moreover, we devise an efficient protocol to optimize interactions between helper and resource-constrained clients. Experiments confirm our approach offers enhanced performance with stable convergence in complex scenarios, outperforming baseline methods.

Simulations of second-long black hole-neutron star mergers in numerical relativity are conducted to obtain a comprehensive picture of the inspiral, merger, and post-merger stages.  The analysis across various initial and computational configurations reveals universally similar qualitative evolution.  The inspiral behavior is marked by equilibration following the initial oscillations induced by the neutron star's antitrapping effect. The onset of the post-merger phase is characterized by the emission of a gravitational wave and the formation of a massive accretion disk accompanied by a spinning neutron star.  The subsequent thermal evolution leads to a supernova-level explosion with considerable ejecta mass, largely determined by the neutron star's angular momentum.  The massive accretion disk and hot, initial state enable the system to emit a bright magnetic and thermal luminosity in the early seconds, detectable by observational satellites such as NVST and ZTF.  The subsequent thermal evolution leads to a supernova-level explosion with considerable ejecta mass, largely determined by the neutron star's angular momentum.  The duration and intensity of the emission vary depending on the neutron star's angular momentum.  The contrast between neutron stars of low- and high-angular momentum leads to distinct binary evolution.  The possibility of a binary neutron star system resulting from a black hole-neutron star merger cannot be ruled out, given the likelihood of a secondary merger within a timescale of hundreds of years.

A novel variation of the Kawazumi-Zhang invariant, specifically $\varphi(C)$,
for compact Riemann surfaces $C$ of genus $g \geq 1$ is presented, exploring
its connections to the first Mumford-Morita-Miller class $e_1 = \kappa_1$ on the
moduli space and its relation to the traditional Kawazumi-Zhang invariant.

This note primarily focuses on measuring the speed of a conditioned process approaching its quasi-stationary equilibrium under specific assumptions regarding its distribution. In reverse, we establish that a conditioned process achieving a quasi-stationary equilibrium in a certain subset reaches its equilibrium within the same subset at a rate comparable to the overall escape rate of the process. Furthermore, we illustrate a scenario where a process's equilibrium is reached solely within a specified subset. Additionally, we establish a relation between a process's largest eigenvalue and its escape rate, which turns out to be precise for geometric Markov processes. In a separate section, we examine the convergence of a process to its quasi-stationary equilibrium under specific distribution assumptions and, more broadly, the process's evolution within various subgroups. Finally, we investigate the speed of a process approaching equilibrium within a specific subset and, more broadly, the process's behavior within various subgroups.

This research explores the optical interaction between a dimer of dielectric nanoparticles near a graphene layer. By applying a precise electromagnetic model, we computed the optical force acting on each particle and derived equations to assess the influence of graphene's surface plasmons. Our findings demonstrate that the excitation of graphene's surface plasmons can produce numerous stable positions with interparticle distances much shorter than the photon wavelength. Additionally, we found that these positions can be dynamically manipulated by adjusting the graphene's chemical potential. Both perpendicular and angled light incidence have been taken into account in the study.

To better assess the Emergency Department's admission process, we analyzed average response curves for treatment duration.  Extending the time for treatment evaluation is an effective strategy for achieving a balanced admissions rate.  By modeling the admissions process, we obtained a solution curve based on the arithmetic mean, which can be effectively applied to address admissions overload.  While previous studies relied on specific assumptions about the underlying process, our method utilizes observed data to estimate key process variables without making those assumptions.  Implementing our approach, the Emergency Department was able to achieve an optimal admissions rate of 28.895 patients per hour, which is close to the actual rate of 29 patients per hour.

In cooperative systems with multiple agents, coordination enables tasks to be performed that would be beyond the capabilities of any single agent. We investigate the concept of coordination through strategic decision-making by focusing on a scenario where agents select between two tasks of varying difficulty that are randomly distributed and partially known. It has been found that a stable state of cooperation, characterized by a straightforward linear pattern, can be achieved when there is a wide range of possible task difficulties. Furthermore, it was discovered that the most advantageous action for each agent in response to an approachable strategy profile can be complex and nonlinear when the distribution of task difficulties is not uniform. A computational method has been established to calculate a cooperative equilibrium through learning within the set of linear policy options.

Research has examined the correlations of charges in particle interactions within Pb-Pb collisions, specifically looking at whether evidence of the Chiral Magnetic Effect (CME) exists in the collision data collected at 2.76 and 5.02 TeV. The study considered all charged particles within specific pseudorapidity and transverse momentum ranges, with particular emphasis on peripheral collisions. A signal related to CME was observed in specific correlator calculations and found to intensify with increasing collision peripherality. Calculations accounting for effects of background that are rooted in heavy-ion collision data, but vary based on specific assumptions, can partially explain the observed signal. The study, however, did not rule out the possibility that CME contributes to the observed effects, with the signal strength potentially outlying statistical fluctuations by up to 2 standard deviations.

The surge in online fundraising (or "crowdfunding") research focuses on understanding the crowd dynamics that predict the success of crowdfunded projects. Differing from prior studies that concentrated on project characteristics, our analysis takes a more holistic approach and is less dependent on the specific crowdfunding platforms being used. By combining various research methods, we explored the impact of features describing crowd behavior on project success. Through a multi-platform investigation of fundraising in online markets, our findings reveal the common crowd dynamics that significantly influence project funding. The research shows that what happens to other buyers can be just as important as the features of the product being offered in determining project success. By uncovering common patterns in crowd behavior that occur across similar online markets, the research contributes to a more general understanding of crowd dynamics and highlights the potential for applications in predicting project outcomes.

Machine learning (ML) based detection of network attacks has shown effectiveness when tailored to a single organisation, but combining data from multiple sources is challenging due to data format inconsistencies and privacy concerns. To address this issue, this paper introduces a collaborative federated learning framework, allowing multiple organisations to co-create and train a robust ML-based intrusion detection system without compromising their data's privacy. A key feature of the proposed framework is the ability to detect new attacks beyond established ones, demonstrated through detailed evaluations using the KDDCup'99 and UCI malware datasets.

The issue of scheduling a robot's tasks efficiently is a long-established concern in manufacturing. Solutions have commonly drawn on a variant of the classic Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP), with a focus on achieving the quickest or most time-efficient task sequence. However, these methods have tended to rely on precomputed data and been suitable for simulation but too slow for actual execution. Furthermore, they have used inaccurate estimates of the time each task would take to complete, assuming all tasks can be undertaken by the robot without interference. Our innovative approach involves using a graph that reflects the real-time costs of the tasks and is constantly updated as new data becomes available, all while ensuring the optimal sequence can be recalculated quickly enough for the robot to act promptly. Our experiments, involving several widely-used test environments, have shown that our model can be processed in a matter of milliseconds, outperforming other methods.

The performance of the interface between semiconductors and barriers is a crucial factor in producing consistent, high-quality quantum dots essential for reliable quantum information processing. This research investigates the characteristics of undoped Si substrates by measuring SiMOSFET Hall bars, thereby evaluating the quality of fully fabricated CMOS devices. A notable mobility level of 17,500 cm^2/Vs was achieved with oxide thickness below 10 nm, showcasing a superior interface ideal for use in qubit-based technologies. Additionally, the study explores the impact of different gate materials on mobility and identifies the underlying principles to guide future optimizations of quantum computing hardware.

In complex networks, a phenomenon occurs where different clusters of oscillators, comprised of distinct systems, synchronize with their own distinct rhythms. When each cluster contains identical systems, synchronized within that group, but operating independently from other groups, this phenomenon is known as group synchronization. Typically, strict conditions must be met to achieve synchronization, but research has revealed that slight discrepancies in parameters or connections do not necessarily preclude it. Through advanced analysis, it is now possible to identify stable conditions for synchronized rhythms, including robust time-series data. We demonstrate the concept of group synchronization in a system of simple nonlinear oscillators, arranged in intricate network configurations, where seemingly disparate groups synchronized despite existing in a diverse environment of symmetrical forms.

Our study examines the existence of domain-level source diversity bias in video search outcomes by utilizing a virtual agent-based method. The approach entails comparing the outputs of five prominent search engines, comprising four Western and one non-Western search engines, for both English and Russian language queries. The research reveals significant variations in source diversity according to language, with search engines returning a broader range of video platforms for Russian language searches. Conversely, Western search engines tend to exhibit bias towards a limited subset of video hosting platforms for English language queries. Furthermore, we identify that the likelihood of using a particular video platform is linked to the type of content and the platform's estimated traffic, although the order of platform preferences differs significantly across the examined search engines.

To gain insight into supersymmetric monodromy defects in the critical Wess-Zumino model, researchers utilize analytical bootstrapping techniques, beginning with a comprehensive analysis of the model's two-point interplay without the influence of such defects. These methods are applied to a specific type of defect exhibiting a ${\rm SU}(N)\times {\rm SU}(M)$ symmetry, resulting in the theoretical calculation of the model's free energy in the presence of such a defect. These findings demonstrate that the energy of this system can be expressed as a sum of spectral series. Furthermore, the study shows that the model's spectral series can be computed up to any desired spectral index. These theoretical predictions are compared favorably to simulations conducted in related systems. Ultimately, the findings suggest that the use of such a defect in the Wess-Zino model may induce a non-trivial phase transition, an phenomenon that warrants further investigation.

We prove that there is exactly one elliptic curve, up to uniqueness, defined over a cubic Galois field extension of rational numbers with a point on the curve having an order of 13 that is rational in the extension and that curve is not defined by the rational numbers.

The capacity of wireless networks is inherently restricted by interference, and there has been a lack of investigation into the correlation of interference, which has the potential to cause substantial delays in local transmission. This study addresses the query of whether randomizing the Medium Access Control (MAC) layer, using protocols like frequency-hopping multiple access and ALOHA, can mitigate the adverse effects of interference correlation. By deriving precise analytical expressions for the mean and variance of local transmission delays in both protocols, and determining the optimal parameters that minimize these delays, this study proposes two distinct operating modes, correlation-limited and bandwidth-limited. Ultimately, the results demonstrate that, depending on the network scenario, both protocols have the capacity to minimize the adverse impact of interference correlation on local transmission delays.

Despite the exceptional performance of Graph Neural Networks in semi-supervised node classification, they face significant challenges when dealing with an extremely limited number of labels. The semi-supervised pseudo-labeling technique attempted to address this issue, but it has ultimately proven to be inadequate. The pseudo-labels produced by this method are often inaccurate, confusing the model and distracting it from the main classification task. To overcome this limitation, we have developed an informative pseudo-labeling framework for GNNs, which selects and assigns labels to pseudo-inputs more effectively. The framework comprises two modules: an informative selector, which chooses relevant pseudo-inputs that are informative for the model to improve its classification skills, and an optimized k-nearest neighbor classifier, which produces more accurate labels based on these selected pseudo-inputs. The framework can be integrated with any GNN model and is adaptable to various graph datasets. Experimental results have demonstrated that it significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art pseudo-labeling approaches by an average of 8.44% in terms of the training label count required to achieve comparable performance.

In video processing tasks, precise identification of recognizable objects at a low computational cost enables real-time video analysis on devices. We present PatchNet, a highly efficient neural network approach for tracking objects across adjacent frames in videos. Unlike traditional pixel-based learning, our method leverages patch-wise correlation features. This results in not only reduced computational requirements but also improved performance by selectively focusing on relevant areas between frames. Through the incorporation of a proposed dual constraint loss function, the network is guided to selectively learn features from patch correlations rather than the overall image. Ultimately, this leads to enhanced accuracy in distinguishing identifiable objects and simplified training of the model. We applied the PatchNet framework in monitoring the movement of individual cells within large cell populations and accurately detected cell migrations across different frames with high precision. Additionally, the incorporated occlusion estimation feature enabled the model to accurately determine which areas of the image were obstructed by other cells during the process. This information was utilized to correct the calculation of the flow of each cell, which sometimes resulted in errors due to partial visibility. As a result, the combination of the dual loss function and the dynamic constraint on the optical flow of cells led to increased robustness of the model in handling partially visible cells and improved the overall precision of the flow of cells.

We examine the one-dimensional discrete-time asymmetric exclusion process with periodic boundaries, using parallel updating rules. Based on a modified random walk approach, we derive a family of probability distributions for various time intervals, leading to a determinant representation. By combining this result with a method of coalescence of exclusion processes, we determine a formula for a semi-group that governs the exclusion process, expressed as a sum involving the derived probability distributions. This formulation yields a determinant representation for the exclusion process' probability distribution at various times, particularly for finite-range interacting processes. Additionally, we explore a method for reflecting some particles at specific locations on the exclusion process, introducing an equivalent stochastic process. By extending our previous methods, we investigate the fundamental hydrodynamic limits of the exclusion process, including the macroscopic behavior, for a large system size. This involves verifying the macroscopic conservation equation, with potentially non-linear interactions, under specific conditions.

A new method of efficient mobile data transmission is proposed by integrating simultaneous wireless information and power transfer technology with network slicing in 5G mobile data systems. An optimization model was created to find the optimal allocation of resources to data subchannels by minimizing power consumption while ensuring that a minimum amount of information and energy is transferred to user equipment. An algorithm based on the Majorization-Cauchy method was developed to solve this optimization problem efficiently and tested under different scenarios. The results show that this integrated approach leads to significant power savings and increased information transfer rates in 5G mobile data systems.

In Fermi gases with low concentrations of magnetic properties, a particular phenomenon occurs at specific points beyond the applicability of second-order approximations in mathematical modeling. To address this issue, researchers revisited third-order approximations for systems with multiple magnetic components and developed expressions incorporating both gas concentration and magnetic alignment parameters. Unlike similar models at the second-order level, a critical point exists within this new framework, leading to a phase transition that matches experimental data on a particular system involving two types of magnetic properties. Furthermore, equations describing fifth-order approximations for systems with single magnetic components also show a phase transition, although its impact is only visible at extremely low concentration levels, well below current experimental capabilities.

We present and analyze a plan for-experimentally implementing a precise quantum simulation of the Srinivas-Birula photon-jamming effect. The simulation involves a mechanical oscillator integrated into a parallel RLC circuit, connected to a coherent laser source via a high-Q microwave resonator. By precisely tuning the oscillator's frequency to that of the resonator's, we can effectively model a massless, mass-dominated wave equation. The plan involves two parallel experiments to achieve this: the first utilizes the inherent motion of the oscillator as a source of jammed photons, while the second involves modulating the jamming effect using an external electric current. The jamming effect is quantified by measuring the average number of jammed photons in the resonator and comparing it to the corresponding quantum fluctuations in the oscillator's position. We present a detailed analytical model of the setup, which includes the analysis of its non-classical characteristics and discusses the realistic implementation of the plan in a real-world setting.

Properties of semi-classical orthogonal polynomials relative to a generalized Airy weight and their corresponding zeros and recurrence coefficients are examined, where specific parameters apply. The study extends to a symmetrized form of this weight known as the generalized sextic Freud weight, resulting in a parallel investigation of the associated polynomials' properties.

This study investigates the controlled flight of a single rotor agent within a confined 2D space near a wall using the Thermal Noise Actuation method. The aim is to generate diverse movement directions, including horizontal, vertical, and diagonal trajectories, by managing a system subject to unpredictable thermal forces. A computational model, based on the Euler equations, simulates the agent's rotation and translation, incorporating a control strategy that adjusts a single parameter to produce the desired flight paths. A comprehensive analysis of the model's stability and sensitivity is conducted, and it is demonstrated that this simple approach can successfully replicate a range of movements in the presence of unpredictable thermal forces, achieving stability in steady-state conditions.

This article further explores and develops the concept of chiral aspects in 2dcft within the pAQFT framework, building upon a previously published study.  It specifically investigates how these aspects relate to a massless scalar field in globally hyperbolic 2-dimensional spacetimes.  The study identifies subalgebras that contain either chiral or anti-chiral observables, constructing these explicitly and showing they are embedded in the full theory's algebra.  It also establishes that the construction of these subalgebras is Cauchy surface-independent and yields a well-defined covariant theory on the space of null geodesics.

Laparoscopic surgery has limitations due to a narrow field of view. Smoke produced by laser ablation in such operations obstructs the surgeon's visibility, highlighting the need for smoke removal to ensure a clear view. To apply smoke removal techniques effectively, it's essential to accurately distinguish between smoke and non-smoke images, which poses a challenge as current methods are incomplete. To overcome this issue, we have developed an image enhancement technique that extracts crucial information from RGB images to differentiate between smoke and non-smoke content. Leveraging a weighted least squares optimization framework, we employ statistical features derived from bivariate histograms and specific image characteristics to create a distinctive feature space. By utilizing a support vector machine classifier, we achieve a 0.91 AUC score with our proposed method, surpassing the 0.65 AUC score achieved with the baseline approach.

This research focuses on creating resilient Gaussian-entangled gates for trapped ions using an optical crane, capable of moving individual ions within a string of ions. By combining the crane's laser pulse with a dc laser field, we develop a method to implement a precise ion swap without compromising entanglement across the chain. We outline a plan to incorporate this method into a broader quantum computation strategy, which we expect will contribute significantly to the development of frequency-resistant quantum gates.

Using advanced computer simulations of atoms in motion, we've found that titanium in barium titanate maintains an unexpected position within its molecular structure even when it's not polarized. This finding challenges the common assumption used to model this phase. To address this discrepancy, we performed a thorough analysis of the symmetries at play and created a series of more accurate, detailed models that capture the underlying structure of the material. From these, we identified the smallest models that are stable and consistent with experimental data; two of these models can also be applied to similar materials. These discoveries open up possibilities for using computational modeling to design more effective materials. Additionally, we've determined that certain characteristics in barium titanate, such as the movement of certain atoms and the vibration of the molecular structure, can be controlled through changes to the volume of the material, and further that these changes are influenced by the presence of certain other atoms.

Multivariate data that change over space or time can often be analyzed with a statistical model known as multivariate Gaussian processes (GP). Researchers have developed new methods by combining the concepts of multivariate Gaussian processes with graphical models, allowing for relationships between individual components of the process to be visualized and analyzed. Two specific approaches, functional Gaussian graphical models and graphical GPs, provide different frameworks for understanding these relationships, with the latter being equivalent to a special type of the former. A new method is proposed that combines the analytical benefits of these models with the flexibility of functional data analysis, using a approach that is both easier to interpret and more general than existing methods. The idea is to represent relationships between individual components of the process as edges in a graph, with the strengths of those relationships being modeled using a multivariate Gaussian distribution. The model is then simplified into a more tractable form that can be estimated using existing methods, with the effectiveness of the approach being validated through simulation studies and real-world data analysis.

Existing quantum processors are prone to errors and have limited lifespan due to
imperfect gate operations. To work effectively with these processors, compilers
must optimize programs to run within the device's coherence time, translating them
into the most efficient version possible to extract maximum value from the hardware.
We have developed new, deterministic methods to efficiently compile repetitive quantum
circuits within a short period of time. Specifically, these patterns are found in
circuits that use the variational quantum eigensolver to study molecular systems and
RyRz heuristic approach to wave function. We've demonstrated that our pattern-based
compilation approach, combined with an efficient program swapping strategy, results in
optimized programs that use fewer than 300 gates, compared to an unoptimized version
exceeding 30,000 gates. These compiled programs achieve a 97% deduction in the number
of gates and 99% reduction in the length of the program without affecting its
performance.

A recent approach to optimizing techniques employs value-of-information stochastic approximation, which repeatedly samples and analytically solves sub-problems to investigate unexplored actions in a decision-making environment. This process is supported by a theoretical foundation, which demonstrates that the algorithm remains near optimal in the vicinity of the equilibrium and exits the exploration phase once the sample distribution's spectral characteristics converge to the stationary distribution of the M/M/1 queue. However, the spectral convergence rate is complex, making its analysis difficult. Instead, the theory is approximated by using two simplified expressions, one based on the standard model of random matrices and the other on the model of deformed GUE, both of which offer precise bounds for the spectral distance from which the optimization complexity is derived.

Recent breakthroughs in producing two-dimensional materials with specific patterns of layered structures have paved the way for achieving unique states known as excitonic insulators, in which certain inherent electronic characteristics spontaneously emerge within the layers. A novel concept has been introduced where an intralayer particle (formed through light exposure) interacts with particles that can leave the excitonic state to form interlayer charged entities called polarons. Utilizing complex computational models, our study begins with calculating the strength of bonds between particles composed of those from different and the same layers, crucial in the understanding of charged entities' behavior. To model excitements within the primary state, we rely on a specific theory describing paired entities and, for analyzing interactions with optical stimuli, adopt a simplified representation of these interactions to predict optical behaviors. Predicted features match known patterns in this type of scenario, indicating that by targeting specific layers with light, researchers might be able to control the flow of charges between them and, through proper manipulation, induce desired states in the materials.

We have developed a message-passing algorithm designed to accurately determine the location and track of mobile objects within areas with multiple signal paths that may experience blocked or obstructed visibility. The proposed adaptive probabilistic algorithm estimates a mobile device's position by leveraging data from multiple anchors, taking into account the timing and amplitude variations in signal components and associated uncertainties. Utilizing an adaptable noise model, the algorithm enables accurate estimation of the agent's position, even without precise knowledge of the surrounding environment. The algorithm dynamically adjusts its operation in real-time according to changes in signal strength and the likelihood of direct line-of-sight visibility with each anchor. Numerical testing demonstrates that the algorithm remains effective in areas with intense signal interference and temporary obstructions.

Measurements of joint polarization states for $W$ and $Z$ bosons in $W^{\pm}Z$ production processes have been reported. These measurements were derived from $139$ fb$^{-1}$ worth of data from proton-proton collisions at a $13$ TeV center-of-mass energy, obtained with the ATLAS detector at CERN's Large Hadron Collider. Events resulting from the decay of these bosons into electrons and muons were examined, and occurrences of simultaneously polarised $W$ and $Z$ bosons were looked for across a range of kinematic thresholds. The distribution of electron and muon transverse momentum, and the occurrence of same-sign $W$ and $Z$ bosons, were analysed to quantify longitudinal and transverse polarisations of individual and joint boson occurrences. The measurement of joint longitudinal polarisation in $W^{\pm}Z$ production processes for the first time, revealed a preference for simultaneously polarised $W$ and $Z$ bosons within a shared reference frame, with occurrences of fully transversely polarised joint boson pairs across specific kinematic thresholds, reaching a statistically significant value of $3.3$ standard deviations above background expectations. The occurrence of jointly longitudinally polarised vector bosons within specific kinematic thresholds was also measured, reaching a statistically significant value of $3.9$ standard deviations above background expectations, with occurrences of fully longitudinally polarised joint boson pairs across a

Research into the Cotton tensor has picked up speed in recent years, leading to a comprehensive review of its foundational and theoretical aspects. The article delves into the Cotton tensor's intriguing properties and its significant connections to the conformally flat space hypothesis within Einstein's theory of gravity. It also explores the Cotton tensor's role in extended gravity theories and the conformally flat space model, covering key advancements in the field.

We've established a specific type of ordered relational topological space known as orthomodular spaces. Our method for creating these spaces involves combining a particular kind of frame, introduced by Hartonas, with a topology in a manner similar to the approach taken by Goldblatt and then extended by Bimbó, in relation to the representation theory of ortholattices. The orthomodular lattices and their corresponding homomorphisms can be shown to have a dual equivalence to the orthomodular spaces and their respective continuous morphisms.

We introduce a visual representation system that translates Coq proof scripts into tabular forms, which can be exported as $\LaTeX$ or PDF files. Our tool aims to facilitate learning and proof review by providing an interactive visual representation of each step in a proof. Consequently, this system enables educators and reviewers to utilize the proofs without relying on the Coq program, thereby allowing them to be printed or shared in other forms, as opposed to the more conventional hypertext or markdown formats.

We demonstrate that the fourth moment of holomorphic Hecke cusp forms is limited under the assumption of the Riemann Hypothesis for a specific degree 8 L-function. This is achieved by leveraging Watson's formula, which allows us to recast our investigation as a tractable problem related to L-functions, ultimately facilitating the application of Soundararajan and Harper's methods to derive our result.

In interior point methods (IPMs), where an iterative method is employed to solve a linear equation system, speeding up convergence often involves developing optimal preconditioners for the linear solver. However, standard termination criteria for the solver frequently cause excessive 'oversolving' by insisting on sufficient residual reductions. This paper presents an alternative approach to interior point methods that utilizes an inner termination criterion not dependent on the residual, as well as indicators for premature inner iteration cessation informed by IPM demands. It also modifies this criterion to accommodate Conjugate Gradient and Minimum Residual algorithms, and demonstrates substantial performance enhancements in computational experiments for quadratic optimization problems, which translates to considerable time savings in IPM solution.

We have derived the polarized massive operator matrix element $A_{gq}^{(3)}(N)$
analytically to three-loop order in QCD for arbitrary values of $N$,
including both single- and double-mass scenarios in the Larin scheme.
Furthermore, the result serves as a crucial transition function for the variable
flavor number scheme at $O(\alpha_s^3)$ and is also expressed in momentum
space for convenient use.

Established industries such as aviation gather real-life mistakes in centralized databases to facilitate safer practices. Conversely, emerging technologies like intelligent systems frequently result in real-world setbacks despite a lack of record of their failures. Intelligent System Incident Reports is a collaborative effort aiming to prevent and mitigate intelligent system failures by documenting real-life incidents. This paper shows how to transform daily experiences into actionable research by sharing instances of intelligent system incidents that the author has encountered. It is hoped that these incident reports will aid in preventing similar incidents and advancing intelligent system research.

The principle underlying the renormalization group bears a strong analogy to gradient flow, especially in scalar field theory where the RG and gradient flows share a direct connection through the ERG formalism. To generalize this connection in gauge theories while maintaining physical gauge degrees of freedom, we introduce a new ERG equation based on a maximally symmetric gauge condition. Our approach is applied to the example of SU(N) Yang-Mills theory, and we examine its application to the calculation of the anomalous dimension of the Casimir operator in the fundamental representation of SU(N).

Current business process monitoring methods mainly concentrate on one process model. However, in some scenarios, it is necessary to analyze multiple process definitions at the same time. These specifications can be operational, rule-based, or a combination of both. For example, in the medical field, a treatment guideline might not cover all co-factors a patient can have and therefore supplementary restrictions might need to be considered. Sometimes, these constraints may conflict with existing guidelines, requiring either the guidelines or the constraints to be violated. To address this issue, we suggest a solution to monitor hybrid process definitions expressed through a combination of (data-aware) Petri nets and temporal logic rules. During the process execution, the monitoring system can handle conflicting specifications by possibly violating some of them, and can even provide recommendations for the next course of action based on a violation cost model that minimizes the total cost of violations.

Quipper, a domain-specific language, enables the description of quantum circuits by embedding in Haskell, resulting in a highly functional and practical language. Yet, its embedded nature in Haskell hinders the development of a formal semantics and restricts the type system. The absence of linear types in Haskell makes it simple to write non-linear quantum circuit protocols. The Proto-Quipper family addresses this limitation by incorporating linear types, a must-have for reliable quantum protocol design. This family includes PQ-1, a type-safe quantum protocol design language with predictable high-level properties, and higher-level variants, such as Proto-Quipper, which adds functional programming principles and provides efficient tools for designing and verifying quantum protocols. We demonstrate the effectiveness of these approaches by implementing the SOS protocol, a well-known quantum steering experiment, and verifying its predictions and outcomes.

In this study, we have modelled a two-dimensional percolation model using random matrices with occupation probability p. Our findings reveal that the behavior of the model is dominated by the two largest eigenvalues. While the second eigenvalue lies on the periphery of a semicircular distribution, influenced by the parameter p, the first eigenvalue is characterised by a distinct, isolated Gaussian distribution, leading to a diverse set of critical behaviors and finite-size effects. Our computational analysis of various metrics, such as the trace of the matrix to the power of k, reveals a transition in behavior from a normal distribution for k=1 to a diverse, non-regular pattern for k>1 at the critical p value. Our findings are further validated through the computational determination of critical exponents. Our study demonstrates that the behavior of this two-dimensional percolation model is equivalent to that of the two-dimensional Ising model, with a diverse set of critical exponents. However, in higher-dimensional models, the influence of extreme eigenvalues is diminished, resulting in a more regular behavior and fewer critical phenomena.

We suggest creating bosonic pairs using laser-controlled dipoles that undergo rapid growth in entanglement via virtual photon exchange, resulting in the spontaneous emergence of optical Bosenova events. To exploit this phenomenon, we propose implementing a detection method that recognizes Bosenova events based on fluctuations in the optical transmission of the dipole pair. Additionally, we examine the interplay between this new detection approach and the collapse of quantum entanglement in the context of open quantum systems.

Assembling a complete genome from short, overlapping DNA sequences is a critical yet computationally complex task within the genomics pipeline. Due to the rapidly expanding genomic dataset, high-performance and scalable approaches are essential for managing the increased computational demands. A novel, parallel algorithm is proposed, using a graph representation and sparse matrices to generate continuous, overlapping DNA sequences within a chromosomal region. By applying graph abstraction, sequences with no linear connection are grouped and eliminated, then the genome is partitioned to repeat occurring regions. A comprehensive strategy is implemented to guarantee the accurate assembly of all sequences within a genome, which significantly boosts algorithm efficiency. Through thorough evaluation of its performance, this proposed method is found to meet the demands of current genomic data, while its potential to adapt to future datasets makes it a promising tool for genome assembly and rearrangement applications.

A modified logistic equation, previously known as the Riccati equation, has been studied for its potential to model oscillating patterns in ecological systems. By introducing a parameter in the context of a nonlinear differential equation, it can help explain frequent observations of oscillations in predator-prey models in ecological studies. Like many nonlinear equations, it can be solved another way - as a first-integral or harmonic oscillator equation, depending on the approach chosen, which highlights the versatility of mathematical tools in physics.

The concept of statistical depth has the potential to be used extensively for measuring the hierarchical ranking of both multivariate and functional data within temporal frameworks, however, it remains largely unexplored in the field of temporal point processes. Recent research has developed a point process depth by incorporating a weighted product of two terms - one representing the depth of process magnitude, and the other describing the temporal occurrence of events given that magnitude. The second component is challenging due to the inability to divide events into distinct, discrete groups as the true realization time is unknown. To address this issue, the authors propose a novel method of comparing the relative rankings of two temporal point processes, focusing on events' onset order rather on their occurrence times directly. The approach is applied in simulation studies and ultimately demonstrated through real-world data analysis of two elections-related datasets.

Achieving maximum engine performance involves leveraging quantum effects. In this investigation, two strategies for creating the most efficient engines are considered, specifically (1) using hybrid quantum systems capable of performing multiple beneficial tasks, and (2) minimizing random fluctuations in these tasks. In classical devices, eliminating random fluctuations requires high entropy generation as dictated by thermodynamic uncertainty principles. Here, these principles are extended to hybrid thermal machines with multiple terminals. In quantum conductors, these limitations are bypassed, and we demonstrate this for a setup comprising a double quantum dot and normal metals in contact, powered by an entangled Cooper pair generator.

Researchers employed a precise laser spectroscopy method on three isotopes of germanium at the ISOLDE-CERN facility to study their hyperfine properties. The study involved a state |1;1> in germanium, which exhibits unique characteristics allowing researchers to make precise measurements of the nucleus's quadrupole moment. The data collected on these moments led to updated values for the nucleus's magnetic and quadrupole properties. The study also provided insights into the signs of these properties and confirmed existing data, or made precise corrections.

Researchers have introduced an innovative technique for accurately measuring the masses of extremely short-lived, unusual atomic isotopes over a wide range of frequencies. This method utilizes the principle of isochronous mass spectrometry, combining real-time ion velocity and trajectory analysis at the Lanzhou CSRe particle storage facility. Dubbed Bρ-defined isochronous mass spectrometry, or Bρ-IMS, this technique enhances precision and sensitivity, paving the way for new mass measurements. Specifically, in a single test setting, precise mass readings were obtained for $^{46}$Cr, $^{49}$Cr, $^{50}$Cr, $^{52}$Fe, $^{54}$Fe, and $^{55}$Ni with exceptionally low margins of error. This breakthrough technique will serve as a crucial tool for evaluating the variation in the neutron charge radius and understanding the underlying physics of the relativistic mean field theory.

This tutorial notebook exemplifies a novel technique for generating Boltzmann distributions of lattice field theories through normalizing flows, a subset of machine learning models. The underlying concepts presented in papers arXiv:1904.12072, arXiv:2002.02428, and arXiv:2003.06413 are summarized, accompanied by a detailed, concrete implementation of this approach.
