The tutorial showcases its application in a lattice scalar field theory and U(1) gauge theory contexts, which particularly incorporates gauge symmetries into its flow-based method for the latter. The tutorial's interactive format is best experienced with the associated Jupyter notebook, which we highly recommend utilizing.

We aim to enhance the accuracy of structured text recognition by incorporating predefined formats defined through regular expressions, thereby facilitating the identification of specific patterns. Our method, involving a Weighted Finite-State Transducer model, boosts recognition accuracy on targeted formats, with minimal losses in other instances. A key parameter governs the intensity of the formatting influence. The proposed technique finds applications in text analysis, particularly when dealing with formatted documents, domain-specific lexicons, or known formats like driver's license numbers and medicinal prescription terminology. We evaluate the effectiveness of this approach on a range of structured text datasets and examine its implications on overall recognition performance.

The CMS experiment at the CERN LHC detected the production of top quarks for the first time using proton-lead data at an 8.16 TeV nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy. Top quark production was identified in events featuring one isolated electron or muon and four or more jets, from a data set totaling 174 inverse nanobarns of luminosity. The measured signal exceeded the five-standard-deviation threshold expected for a background-only hypothesis, and the cross-sectional measurement for top quark production in proton-lead collisions was found to be 45 nanobarns with an 8-nanobarn uncertainty, consistent with theoretical predictions from quantum chromodynamics.

This study focuses on key elements in cross-domain text-to-SQL parsing, specifically schema linking and value filling. To enhance encoding abilities, a column selection auxiliary task is proposed, leveraging explicit targets for relevance matching. Additionally, two value filling approaches are presented to bridge the gap between current zero-shot parsers and practical applications, considering many real-world datasets often lack training grounds due to their atomic nature. The first approach combines existing value filling parsers with a post-processing step adapted from entity linking, while the second employs a conditional generative model to directly generate atomic values. The proposed architecture, called VetWin, is a unified framework that tackles both schema linking and value filling. Experiment results indicate that VetWin surpasses state-of-the-art baselines in terms of accuracy. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/AlibabaResearch/Timing/tree/master/VetWin.

The ongoing LoTSS survey is conducting a thorough observation of the Northern sky to better understand how the large-scale structure of the Universe changes and develops. Although only 1% of the sky is covered in the LoTSS DR1 data release, analysis reveals anomalies in the measured redshifts of galaxies. These discrepancies raise potential issues with modelling the observed redshifts and therefore accurate measuring of galaxy clustering. To address these concerns, the loTSS_DR1 data will be reanalysed with a more advanced modelling approach that includes how galaxy distributions vary in density and the way galaxies emit light. Additionally, the statistical methods used to analyse the data will be revised to improve modelling and a more realistic model of the galaxy redshifts will be introduced. Further observations are needed to confirm whether the observed anomalies are due to a genuine effect and to understand how the large-scale structure of the Universe is changing over time.

The High-Dimensional Rank Lasso (HDR Lasso) model offers a computationally efficient solution to handle complex data analysis. Introduced as a parameter-free and robust approach to handle data contamination. The HDR Lasso can be solved in a computationally efficient manner using an iterative algorithm. The statistical reliability of the HDR Lasso has been re-evaluated by considering key variables influencing its performance. The outcomes indicate that the assumed incoherence and coherence conditions are not essential to ensure the HDR Lasso's effectiveness. The findings show that the HDR Lasso can still provide reliable results even in scenarios where these conditions are met. The critical factors influencing the HDR Lasso's performance involve the problem's rank, data redundancy, and the lasso lambda-minor constraint. The findings indicate that the HDR Lasso can be susceptible to feature selection errors when the problem's rank is low and data is highly redundant. Conversely, the HDR Lasso provides accurate feature selection results for low-relevance data or high-rank problems. The discoveries have practical implications for the use of HDR Lasso in various applications and raise questions about the utility of parameter-free approaches in the context of high-dimensional statistical models.

Identifying whether an optimal solution is localized or universal is particularly challenging in complex optimization problems. This work addresses that challenge by demonstrating the existence of a single, optimal, and universal method for achieving the lowest possible rate of entropy production in fast and sluggish driving processes. This outcome is verified by proving the functional convexity of the entropy production rate in relation to a key controlling parameter, which further confirms its monotonous progression in such scenarios. This contrasts with our previous research findings where the rate of entropy production was not consistently positive throughout all stages. Our analysis demonstrates that an analytical technique previously employed is, in fact, effective in determining the optimal solution, which is subsequently verified by comparing it with the results from an exhaustive search approach.

Over the past decade, significant advancements in artificial intelligence have positioned it as a key tool for addressing environmental issues, primarily considered benign. However, our review of the literature reveals a previously unacknowledged truth: the development and use of AI can also have various adverse environmental impacts. These effects stem from several factors, such as the environmental toll of the physical infrastructure needed to support AI systems (e.g., data centers), the inherent limitations of AI models (e.g., lack of generalizability), and the emphasis on technical AI excellence over environmental sustainability in the AI community. This review aims to promote greater awareness of these ecological limitations and spark a conversation about incorporating sustainability principles throughout the entire AI lifecycle. By doing so, we aim to help researchers adopt more environmentally responsible methods and approaches in AI.

This paper investigates and classifies various prescriptive process monitoring methods, which identify potential issues during business processes and provide interventions to prevent problems at the point of execution. The systematic review encompasses a comprehensive analysis of the current approaches in the field. To better understand these methods, a conceptual framework has been developed to evaluate prescriptive process monitoring techniques based on performance targets, metrics used to assess performance, intervention types, employed modeling techniques, utilized data, and predefined rules for intervention. The findings of the SLR highlight gaps and possible research avenues that could further improve the effectiveness and versatility of prescriptive process monitoring methods, emphasizing the necessity for method validation in practical scenarios, extension of intervention types beyond temporal and financial aspects, and design of more comprehensive intervention policies that take into account causation and subsequent consequences.

This study introduces an error control strategy for a Boussinesq model with adaptive coefficients, where temperature-dependent properties of heat transfer and fluid viscosity are taken into account. The coupled system is formulated using a mixed finite element method combined with a Galerkin method with test functions weighted by error indicators. The solution approach is generalized from existing models with constant coefficients to accommodate temperature-dependent properties, and the new indicators are formulated to reflect the effect of temperature on these properties. The implementation is demonstrated using benchmark problems, and the results show the effectiveness of the proposed method in identifying critical regions and ensuring global and local convergence of the solution.

Polynomial-time reduction methods, referred to as kernelization algorithms, decrease instance size to a small fixed value, especially useful for combinatorial problems. These algorithms have become crucial for studying problem complexity and deriving lower bounds via lower bounds for parameterized complexity. Researchers have made significant progress in this area, but it's important to note that "hard" problems may become significantly smaller after reduction, which raises the possibility of other difficult instances remaining untouched. To address this, researchers have introduced more stringent requirements, such as hardness parameters and hardness densities, to measure the strength of kernelization algorithms. A stronger algorithm should yield smaller kernels for more "hard" problems, as indicated by these metrics. In this work, researchers introduce and explore new notions of hardness parameters and kernelization strength for parity functions and Boolean satisfiability problems, examining the limitations of current kernelization algorithms and their relations to problem hardness metrics.

This study explores how opinions are shaped and social connections evolve in a complex system, governed by a delicate balance between friendly and hostile relationships. We have developed a model that captures how individuals with limited confidence in their judgments form opinions based on their personal relationships. We considered scenarios with one and two distinct aspects of opinions, and found that our framework consistently leads to the separation of agents into two distinct groups, characterized by distinct opinion sets. Depending on the level of trust, these groups either develop uniform views or multiple distinct perspectives within each group emerge. In the case of opinions based on a single dimension, the two groups have opposing views, forming a 'left' and 'right' category. In scenarios with multiple dimensions, the two groups are separated by a dividing line in opinion space. We have applied our model to the study of politics, and our results are consistent with theories suggesting the polarization of political views within a two-dimensional system. We have also extended our model to relate to the field of medicine, and have used it to investigate the effects of varying levels of trust on the development of distinct groups within a population of individuals with differing levels of risk tolerance.

We've investigated a newly constructed series of asymptotically flat, electrically charged black holes that form scalar "hair" when their charge increases at a fixed mass. Inside the event horizon, these black holes resemble a holographic superconducting material, exhibiting similar behavior in their scalar fields and culminating in a singularity that heavily depends on the black holes' parameters when the instability first arises. Additionally, we present a general theory in an appendix stating that certain types of stationary black holes with scalar "hair" cannot possess Cauchy horizons.

Different genes exhibiting similar activation patterns may show distinct mRNA expression levels at different time points due to variations in transcription duration, RNA breakdown speed, and processing rates. The impact of RNA splicing on delaying mRNA production cannot be ignored. We developed a model combining transcription dynamics and RNA accumulation to estimate the rates of transcription, RNA production lag, and RNA breakdown using sequencing data from multiple time points. The model blends a mechanistic approach with a flexible statistical method, incorporating uncertainty into the calculations through Bayesian estimation. We applied this model to ER-alpha activated cells from a breast cancer line, analyzing transcription using ChIP-Seq data and mature RNA quantities from RNA-Seq data. The results show that a considerable number of genes exhibit a prolonged period between transcription completion and mature RNA availability. Furthermore, genes exhibiting longer delays are typically shorter and are associated with retained introns in pre-mRNA data, suggesting significant production delays attributed to splicing events.

Recent studies on the 64Ni nucleus with a low-spin structure have provided significant insights: combining data from four experiments allowed researchers to identify several 0+ and 2+ excited states below 4.5 MeV, and characterize their properties. Using a Monte Carlo shell model, scientists were able to explain the findings and uncover a surprisingly intricate and stable structure of 64Ni, which features a large number of clusters and excited states. Moreover, researchers discovered that the ground state of 64Ni contains a high number of 44Ti and 56Fe clusters, and that these clusters play a crucial role in the formation of its low-spin excited states.

Chiral SU(N) gauge theories, consisting of Weyl fermions and additional fermions, are examined to analyze their dynamics. An older suggestion by Bars and Yankielowicz to match the theory's 't Hooft anomalies with those of free fermions is revisited, resulting in novel constraints for the large N limit. Furthermore, SU(N) theories with an additional Weyl fermion are studied, yielding an anomaly matching condition that can be satisfied by a confining chiral gauge theory, resulting in a spectrum of mesons and a matched 't Hooft anomaly.

A linear complementary pair of group codes $(C, D)$ is formed when the direct sum of $C$ and $D$ results in the entire group algebra $R[G]$, given a finite principal ideal ring $R$ and a finite group $G$. We identify a required and confirming criterion for pairs of group codes $(C, D)$ in group algebra $R[G]$ to be a linear complementary pair, subsequently proving the equivalence in terms of permutations between codes $C$ and the dual code $D^{\perp}$.

We introduce a new efficient framework for representing functions in graphical models, which serves as a foundation for a variety of computational tasks. Our concise model uses a machine learning-friendly deterministic finite state automaton to encode any function, and we demonstrate its advantages in several applications such as graph clustering, variable selection in semi-supervised learning, and constraint-based reasoning. Our approach leads to a novel semi-supervised learning scheme called $K$-way label propagation, which resolves a label merging issue and provides exact results, comparable to graph clustering techniques. Additionally, we show that variable selection can be framed as efficient world-wide propagation by leveraging our new framework. Our method enables the exact computation of variable support through the detection of equal equivalence classes in the graph's partition, and can be extended to handle continuous variables. We also introduce a new scoring function called scoreBP, which reflects the impact of label propagation decisions on the graph's original probability distribution, and uses our framework to efficiently calculate scores for all possible subsets of variables. To validate our framework, we apply it to graph clustering and variable selection problems, and show improved runtime and accuracy compared to existing methods. Our scoreBP and selection of variables can be extended to handle hard constraints by efficiently calculating the equivalence classes of variables involved in the constraints through the detection of equivalence classes.

The visual appearance and auditory qualities of an object provide dual insights into its material properties.  In everyday situations, information from vision and hearing arrive simultaneously, but the integration of asynchronous cues is essential, as seen when we locate an object dropped on the ground after hearing its fall.  In this paper, we explore the integration of visual and auditory object representations, focusing on an object's 3D pose in a complex scene.  A novel approach, Real-time Integrated Audio-Visual Object Localization (RAO), is developed using a end-to-end trainable deep network that leverages both object representations.  RAO is based on a simple yet robust hypothesis-driven architecture that generates an object's 6DoF pose from camera and microphone input.  In our experiments, RAO successfully predicts an object's 3D pose in response to auditory cues, either by predicting the object's pose at the time of its detection or forecasting its pose from sound.  This work marks the first instance of deep learning being used to integrate asynchronous visual and auditory object representations for localization purposes.

When subjected to high stresses, the vast majority of dense mixtures undergo a sudden and extreme thickening, characterized by a transition from fluid-like behavior to rigidity. Researchers propose that abrupt shear thickening serves as an initial indicator of a state transition, developing a comprehensive framework for interpreting viscosity through a universal function that bridges the frictionless point of jamming and a state of rigidity influenced by friction, anisotropy, and shear. Studies involving cornstarch in glycerol and silica spheres in glycerol found that for these two systems, viscosity can be condensed into a singular, stress- and volume-dependent curve, implying that these arrays with irregular particle configurations and those with more ordered structures both exhibit similar transition behavior, however the order at which the transition occurs differs in these scenarios. Additionally, simulations of disks under different interparticle forces and randomly shaped particles in glycerol also demonstrated that for these two systems, viscosity can be condensed into a singular, stress- and volume-dependent curve, implying that these arrays with irregular particle configurations and those with more ordered structures both exhibit similar transition behavior, however the order at which the transition occurs differs in these scenarios.

This research focuses on modeling a power shortage in Ghana as a Markov process to implement an optimal pricing policy within a theoretical framework. Based on real consumption data from the Ghana Grid Company Limited for 2020, we developed a two-state Markov model, categorizing days into high and low electricity consumption periods. The model revealed that the probability of staying in the low consumption phase lasts approximately two and a half days. To address pricing, we employed a control theory approach to determine the optimal pricing schedule, which maximizes utility under constrained individual electricity needs. Furthermore, this pricing model was adapted to account for the costs involved in increasing generation capacity to meet rising electricity demands.

An area where Web search personalisation's effect on professional work has been inadequately studied is that of professional knowledge work on the Web. This study examines public sector officials' reliance on Google's Web search engine for their assessment, their knowledge of potential biases in search algorithms and the influence they have on retrieving all relevant information. The study's results show that a substantial number of the participants are unaware of potential biases in search algorithms and the possible strategies to prevent them from overlooking essential information. Notably, our data reveal that as much as 20% of the necessary information may go undetected due to the influence of Web search personalisation. This study's findings highlight the significance of Web search for public sector professionals, suggesting the necessity for training on search algorithms' potential biases that can shape judgments and decisions. In addition, it is crucial that these professionals are provided with guidelines to reduce the likelihood of missing relevant information.

Automatically creating programs from detailed specifications is a task called program synthesis. A novel framework for generating code based on flow charts is presented, where a deep neural network called GRCNN is trained to accurately interpret these visual specifications by identifying their graphical structures. By being trained end-to-end, GRCNN is capable of simultaneously predicting both the recognition of visual features and the synthesis of code. This framework's results reveal that GRCNN achieves exceptional accuracy in recognizing visual features, and also produces high-quality code. Specifically, our system can successfully translate over 80% of flow charts into working Java code. Moreover, enhancements to the framework enable it to handle ambiguous and incomplete specifications by producing suitable code modifications, resulting in even better quality outputs.

This text explores multiple reduction techniques that facilitate the connection of Earth's climate models of varying complexity, emphasizing approaches that enable thorough reduction. It distills key mathematical concepts behind each method while showcasing several benchmark climate modeling examples for illustrative purposes.

The groundbreaking discovery of gravitational waves emanating from a binary neutron star merger in August 2017 paved the way for a new era in multimessenger astronomy. Kilonovae, produced by the expelled material from neutron star collisions, present an attractive opportunity for optical and near-infrared follow-up observations following the detection of GWs. The observation of the kilonova from GW 1780817 revealed crucial evidence for the astrophysical site of heavy element formation via the rapid neutron capture process or r-process. Given that properties of the emission are heavily influenced by the opacities of the expelled material, recent calls for action have led to the development of accurate theoretical models, incorporating cutting-edge computational techniques and data for diverse r-process elemental sets. This chapter presents an overview of kilonova theory and the significance of precise theoretical models in optical and near-infrared follow-up observations following GW detections. Additionally, it discusses the potential for advancements in theoretical models through the use of machine learning and probabilistic forecasting.

Radiation oncologists' goal is to target tumors accurately while shielding surrounding vital organs, specifically the stomach and intestines, from x-ray beams. The incorporation of MR-Linac systems allows real-time tumor positioning, enabling precise radiation dosage adjustments based on shifting cell populations. The manual process of identifying these organs and calibrating X-ray beams can be lengthy, extending treatment times up to one hour a day, making automated techniques with deep learning essential. A recent paper explores the use of deep learning-based automation to streamline this complex task and provide faster access to treatment for a greater number of patients.

Compositional data analysis is a technique commonly used to investigate complex datasets with a constant sum. The pcoproxy package offers a versatile tool for visualizing and understanding these datasets through principal components. This tutorial serves as a comprehensive guide, showcasing the capabilities of pcoproxy by utilizing a dataset of sediment samples. The tutorial covers how to create a compositional data object, perform principal component analysis, and customize visualizations to obtain detailed insights.

The exoplanet sample from CORALIE/HARPS (Mayor et al., 2011), which was discovered through Doppler radial velocity measurements, does not demonstrate the anticipated 'desert' at high masses (10-$100 M_\odot) with close orbital radii (<=3 AU), as predicted by the runaway gas accretion theory. Notably, similar findings have emerged from the MOA gravitational microlensing survey, which did not detect the 'desert' effect for planets in slightly longer-period orbits with lower-mass host stars (Suzuki et al., 2018). These studies collectively suggest that runaway accretion is unlikely a major factor in shaping the mass distribution of exoplanets.

Artificial intelligence models, powered by artificial attention, can regulate their awareness within a limited scope to resolve problems.  A new method develops within this framework by creating a competition for attention within a computational model of the environment, where the likelihood of an agent perceiving an item is increased if that item is important to the agent's objectives.  The model, called the Partially Observable Bandit Attention (POBA) structure, incorporates a simple yet effective mechanism for attention span by employing a Poisson process, thereby enabling agents to manage their awareness and solve complex problems.  In theoretical analyses, the model's performance is compared to a comprehensive benchmark system.  In practical evaluations, the model outperforms alternative systems, especially in scenarios where agents encounter large amounts of data or where there is uncertainty about the state of the environment.

Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) can efficiently solve complex problems that demand memory, allowing for the adjustment of local inattention via parameter adjustment, although this comes at the cost of increased computational and memory costs. Local inattention can also create "skip paths" where hidden states between connected nodes bypass each other during information flow. A novel class of locality-aware RNNs, termed Locally-Attentive Recurrent Neural Networks (LARNNs), is being developed. In this study, the researchers are exploring an alternative type of LARNN, termed Locality-Masked RNNs (LM-RNNs), where relative distances between nodes in the graph are used to create a localized, trainable attention mask that diminishes hidden state interactions. This type of LARNN shows promising results on various benchmark problems as it facilitates reduced latency, lower memory requirements, and accelerated training times, ultimately making it more efficient and data-efficient compared to fully-connected RNNs.

We categorize nilpotent algebras by dimension with a focus on their commutative, commutative nilpotent and anticommutative properties. Our findings reveal the irreducibility of corresponding geometric spaces, allowing us to accurately calculate their dimensions and establish general families of algebras associated with each space. Additionally, our research highlights the relationship between anticommutative algebras and the split bicomplex numbers.

Active galactic nuclei with exceptionally powerful radio signals are among the brightest known celestial sources, spanning across a wide range of wavelengths. These powerful jets from supermassive black holes can significantly influence both the black hole's growth and its surroundings in the vast expanse of space. In the radio spectrum, these jets can be observed on various scales, but their X-ray and gamma-ray emissions are predicted to be concentrated on smaller scales, typically under 10 parsecs. Recent findings by the Chandra X-ray telescope have revealed the presence of kiloparsec-scale jets, which has sparked a debate about jet dynamics. This study aims to understand the underlying mechanics of these large-scale jets by examining the characteristics of 11 jets spanning over 10 kiloparsecs, identified through a comprehensive analysis of radio and X-ray data. By comparing the properties of these jets, such as their speed, geometry, and connections to their central black holes, we aim to shed light on the potential mechanisms that drive these massive spectral extensions.

We perform a covariant expansion of the Einstein-Hilbert action in powers of
$1/c^2$, considering a generic spacetime foliation defined by a set of
coordinate functions. We achieve a precise matching with the standard
semi-invariant action employed in $1+1$ AdS/CFT correspondence, up to a
misidentification of the light speed. To rectify this, we propose a
redefinition of the Lorentz metric, thereby introducing a 'physical'
metric that maintains invariance under the Lorentz group. We then apply
this expansion to derive Maxwell and Dirac equations in the light-cone
 gauge, yielding a semi-implicit formulation that could be suitable for
numerical computations in holographic superconductors. Additionally, we
obtain an expanded energy-momentum tensor, providing an alternative
to the Bogush-skoblanov method for computing stress tensor in
condensate problems.

This study presents an enhanced approach to 3D image features that incorporates invariance to discrete symmetry by considering inversions of spatial axes and image boundaries.  The proposed descriptor includes a binary feature that distinguishes between the inside and outside of an image region, facilitating more precise characterization of image properties near boundaries.  In contrast to earlier methods, the novel approach can withstand any combination of scale and rotation distortions without compromising its accuracy.  Research indicates that the newly developed descriptor contains distinctive, computationally efficient image attributes that are capable of distinguishing between dissimilar 3D shapes with high reliability.  Further investigation demonstrates that the attribute is particularly resistant to variations in pose and light intensity.  In particular, the novel approach for computing symmetry enables more robust computation of image properties, ultimately contributing to more robust 3D shape recognition.  Specifically, it was found that the newly developed descriptor yields lower error rates for shape classification and object identification.

We've analyzed the data from a unique binary star system, SDSS J082239.54+304857.19, using our ZTF telescope, and revealed it has a substantial temperature difference between its two components. During our observations, we detected a notable eclipse of about 1 day that allowed us to determine the binary's orbit. Additionally, we identified two earlier, deeper eclipses with differing periods, indicating that this star system is a type of non-interacting binary with irregularly shaped orbits. Our analysis of the binary's z-band light curves using the EBASY tool revealed that its components have temperatures of around 2800K and 6100K. We estimate that the cooler star is about 3.4 times larger than the hotter one. With further observations, we aim to clarify the binary's irregular orbit and better understand its temperature disparities.

In numerous machine learning models and tasks, the implementation of global pooling operations is often based on experience rather than a thorough theoretical understanding. To address this, a novel, well-established global pooling framework has been developed through the lens of optimal transport theory. The research reveals that most current global pooling methods are essentially specialized solutions to an unbalanced optimal transport problem. By revealing the connection between global pooling and optimal transport, the study provides valuable insights that enable the design of new global pooling layers with adjustable dropout and residual structures. The proposed framework is exemplified by the implementation of a new global averaging layer, which significantly enhances the performance of one-dimensional convolutional neural networks for classification tasks.

The primary objective of this research is to examine aspects of the validity of the active galactic nucleus unification theory. Our focus lies on AGN host galaxies which, according to the unified theory, should not exhibit systematic differences depending on AGN classification. We used the SDSS catalogue up to a redshift of 0.2, and the Galaxy Zoo Project catalogue which classifies galaxies into two broad Hubble types, and classified AGNs using emission line diagnostics. Our findings reveal that elliptical galaxies have a significantly higher fraction of Type 1 Seyfert nuclei compared to other AGN types, and the transition from Seyfert 1 to LINER, Type 2 Seyfert, and composite nuclei corresponds to a rise in spiral host galaxies. These findings contradict the unified model, suggesting that there's an interaction between the black hole and its galactic environment. Our research also discovered that spiral host galaxies with Type 1 Seyfert nuclei have more extended nuclear emission, and the host galaxies of LINER and composite AGNs have distinct Hubble types. These outcomes imply that there's a cause-and-effect relationship between the black hole activity and its host galaxy.

This paper delves into a comprehensive analysis of general rotational surfaces in the 4-dimensional Euclidean space, focusing on flat general rotation surfaces characterized by a 1-type Gauss map. Additionally, it's established that a non-planar, flat general rotation surface with this distinct Gauss map is a Lie group if and only if it's a Clifford torus.

Deep neural network training for semantic segmentation requires considerable effort,
so many researchers opt for pre-training their model on a different task before
further refining it using a smaller annotated dataset. Top-notch approaches
traditionally rely on image classification for pre-training, but this method has
already become overly standard. We examine an alternative that could provide
even stronger foundations: leveraging 3D data from unseen video feeds. Our
method involves two primary components. Firstly, we develop a way to extract and
unify depth information from unlabeled videos, which enables the representation
learned to capture rich three-dimensional contextual information. Secondly, we
apply this depth-based representation to the typical semantic segmentation task
and show that this approach surpasses conventional methods that only utilize single
frames. To achieve this, we created the DeepVideo3D dataset, comprising video
footages with corresponding 3D objects, and conducted an extensive, frame-by-frame
evaluation of different unsupervised depth estimation techniques, followed by a
comparison with semantic segmentation state-of-the-art methods. Our results in
semantics-from-depth experiments demonstrate that fusing multiple frame estimates
significantly enhances performance and that integrating depth information surpasses
classification-based pre-training. Nonetheless, we discovered that simply
incorporating depth might not always yield better results than using a purely
classification-based representation. Thus, we performed an in-depth analysis of
our results to better understand the underlying mechanisms.

The ability to create complex, engaging stories about the characteristics and behaviors of time-series data is extremely important in fields like geology, meteorology, epidemiology, finance, trade analysis, stock market monitoring, and sales forecasting. Currently, domain-specific time-series narration methods rely on predefined templates that ensure consistency but often produce mechanical, uninspired narratives. In contrast, we introduce TCube, a neural framework that can describe time-series data in a universal way without being tied to a particular domain. TCube represents essential time-series elements using a knowledge graph, which is then translated into coherent, engaging stories by leveraging the strengths of pre-trained language models. Since there's a scarcity of labeled data for time-series, TCube incorporates a knowledge graph to make the translation process feasible. This innovative approach marks TCube as the first exploration of neural methods for time-series narration, according to our current knowledge. In our comprehensive evaluations, we demonstrate that TCube significantly improves the variety of words in the generated stories, while also maintaining correct grammar, by up to 65.38%. Furthermore, an expert review of 21 professionals showed that 76.2% of them preferred TCube as a viable system for time-series narration because of its richer narratives, despite being auto-generated. TCube's open-source code and supporting materials are publicly available for verification and potential use.

The ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has achieved precise measurements in two areas, namely neutral B meson mixing and CP violation, as well as in rare electroweak processes occurring in suppressed B-meson decays. This study concentrates on recent findings from the ATLAS collaboration, encompassing evaluations of rare occurrences like $B^0_s \to \mu^+\mu^-$ and $B^0 \to \mu^+\mu^-$ decays and the determination of CP-violating processes in $B^0_s \to J/\psi\phi$.
On a Cayley tree, we analyze the Ising model and find novel periodic measures that are linked to index-2 normal subgroups within its group representation.

This study explores the well-posedness of global solutions, dependence on initial data, and potential loss of regularity in strictly hyperbolic equations with certain properties. These equations feature coefficients that experience moderate blow-up as sublogarithmic growth, represented by the function $|\ln t|^\gamma$ where $0 < \gamma < 1$. By applying a specific metric on the phase space, we can categorize these equations and examine their coefficients, which have polynomial bounds in x, x-derivatives, and a certain degree of singularity in t, specifically $t^{-\gamma}$. We leverage a pseudodifferential operator with a variable metric symbol to establish the desired connections, and show that the operator is an isomorphism in a specific Sobolev space when its symbol meets specified criteria, having a positive index and a nonvanishing determinant on a certain phase space region. By linking this operator with our equations, we can state the existence, uniqueness, and potential loss of regularity of the solutions, which are defined in a limited period and not globally. We also provide an isotropy result, illustrating that the equations' coefficients are invariant under a specific transformation, which has the effect of replacing the loss of regularity condition with a statement about the operator's singularity in t.

This research introduces a novel application of the Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural network to tackle the challenging task of Japanese word segmentation. Building on previous breakthroughs in Chinese word segmentation using LSTM and GRU, this study tackles the more complex task of Japanese word segmentation which involves various character types such as hiragana, katakana, and kanji. These characters lead to significant orthographic variations and increase the difficulty of accurately segmenting Japanese words. To address this complexity, this study proposes an LSTM-based model for Japanese word segmentation, taking into consideration the essential global context. Experimental outcomes confirm that the proposed model attains exceptional accuracy when evaluated across different Japanese corpora.

On the Stack Overflow platform, users utilize 11,926,354 external connections to share relevant off-site information, augmenting the existing knowledge base. This collaborative effort involves repeated link sharing activities, where 82.5% of all links are external and 57.0% consist of frequently shared resources. To streamline users' knowledge management, this study delves into the characteristics of these shared links to identify common patterns in external resources that are repeatedly disseminated. Our research focuses on Stack Overflow, where our team collected 1,792,398 posts containing 11,926,354 links, including 4,622,398 external connections. Our analysis reveals that users primarily leverage a limited set of links, shared up to 20 times, which are extracted from popular repositories, including GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, and other well-known knowledge-sharing platforms. This study aims to understand how users collaborate by sharing external resources, thereby contributing to the accumulation of Stack Overflow's extensive knowledge base.

Galactic rotation curves show a range of varying inner slopes. Observations suggest a potential relationship between a galaxy's brightness and its central dark matter, indicating the need for a more comprehensive explanation. This study investigates various theoretical models that account for galaxy diversity. A model based on Self-Interacting Dark Matter is contrasted with a distribution function-based Cold Dark Matter model, both of which are applied to two galaxies with distinct rotation curves. A new model parameter, representing the ratio of cross-section to mass, is introduced and varied to fit the observed rotation curves. Contrasting the models' responses to baryonic feedback and their dependence on halo concentration is also explored.

Although climate change is widely accepted, meaningful conversations about it are scarce,
resulting in slow implementation of the necessary societal changes to mitigate its effects.
To enhance climate communication and promote individual actions, we are developing a system
that leverages climate information tailored to each person's values. To achieve this goal, we
need a comprehensive dataset that maps climate causes to their corresponding effects in
terms of their impact on the environment. After examining existing climate taxonomy datasets,
we observed a gap in current research and a need for a more extensive, fine-grained, and
evolving dataset to support climate communication. To address this, we have created a new
dataset that combines multiple existing taxonomies, and incorporates natural language
processing to generate additional nodes and relationships. Our dataset consists of 4811
nodes and 12041 relationships, constructed by analyzing 1121 academic papers and categorizing
them into a 13-level hierarchical structure. By utilizing this dataset, we aim to assist researchers
in understanding climate concept evolution and improving effective climate communication.

Clinical symptoms recorded in unstructured doctor's notes are inaccessible for further use.
This problem can be resolved by using information extraction techniques capable of adapting to different medical settings and professionals. 
In this research, we address the issue of extracting symptoms by using pre-trained and fine-tuned models, trained on diverse patient data, medical institutions, and specialties. 
To reduce dependency on specific data, we develop an adaptive strategy for extracting symptoms by temporarily removing commonly mentioned symptoms from the original data source.
Also, our approach pre-trains the language model using relevant but unmarked text for enhanced data representation. 
By using this strategy, we significantly improve the extraction of symptoms from original data and achieve better performance when comparing multiple model architectures.

Deep reinforcement learning stands out as a promising AI paradigm for instructing machines via environmental interaction and adaptive learning from their errors. Despite initial expectations, however, its successful application in the automotive industry remains elusive. Following in the footsteps of notable achievements by Google DeepMind in mastering Atari games and Go, we have developed a comprehensive framework for autonomous driving through deep reinforcement learning, given its relevance due to autonomous driving's inherent complexities and environmental dependencies. In particular, autonomous driving poses significant challenges as a supervised learning problem due to dynamic interactions with pedestrians, vehicles, and road conditions. To overcome these obstacles, our framework leverages the integration of simulated environments and the utilization of sensory data for model training and validation. Additionally, we have conducted an in-depth analysis of the effectiveness of diverse reinforcement learning algorithms and their correlation with extraction techniques. As a result, we have achieved a trained agent capable of navigating a virtual city and reaching a target goal in the face of detours and obstacles. Our work showcases the potential of deep reinforcement learning in tackling complex autonomous driving tasks.

In recent years, AI networks, specifically those based on artificial neural systems, have significantly outperformed competitors in a wide range of tasks including image recognition, sound analysis, and language interpretation. However, widespread use of such models was previously hindered due to their massive computational requirements for both initial training and operational deployment. Neuromorphic computing technology, which allows bio-realistic neural networks to operate at high speeds while minimizing energy consumption, has now become an appealing substitute. We present a proposal to utilize a Random Neural Network as a versatile classifying tool, which we then further refine into the Spiking Neural Network structure to leverage the advantages offered by Spiking Neural Networks over traditional Artificial Neural Networks in computational and time efficiency.

This research investigates the thermodynamic characteristics of spin-polarized strange quark matter under a strong magnetic field at finite temperature, applying the MIT bag model. Furthermore, we derived the equation of state for spin-polarized strange quark matter in the presence of a strong magnetic field, and subsequently, we examined the structure of spin-polarized strange quark stars across varying temperatures and magnetic fields.

A surge in personal device ownership offers an immense, yet largely underutilized resource of computational power, making it feasible to utilize it. To harness this potential, we developed Pando, a novel volunteer computing system based on declarative concurrent programming, and powered by JavaScript, WebRTC, and WebSockets. By employing a dynamic network of unreliable, volunteer-sourced personal devices and their browsers, Pando facilitates parallel execution of a function on multiple values, thus enhancing efficiency on compute-intensive applications like animation rendering and image processing. Furthermore, our approach's adaptability is demonstrated through Pando's deployment on various platforms, such as mobile devices, Linux servers, and embedded IoT devices, showcasing its effectiveness on a range of use cases including scientific visualization, machine learning, and deep learning.

A computational method for resolving nonlinear eigenvalue problems is presented, using an approximating function derived from the eigenvalues of a modified eigenproblem equation.  By utilizing a variable sampling process that focuses data collection on the areas most critical to solution resolution, this algorithm efficiently distributes resources. It then employs the collected information through a least squares optimization to produce accurate results.  A demonstration of this method's efficiency and effectiveness is shown by comparing its performance to other established methods.

We demonstrate the topological equivalence of all intermediate beta-transformations with a specific type of greedy beta-transformation that incorporates a hole at zero. By employing this equivalence, we obtain a detailed characterization of these transformations, yielding new insights and results in various areas, such as Krieger embeddings, survivor sets, Hausdorff dimensions, bifurcation sets, and badly approximable numbers. We show that certain classes of sets associated with these transformations possess unique properties, specifically that they are winning in Schmidt games and have the countable intersection property.

We've found that gauge theories with $SO(N_{c})$ as a gauge group and matter fields represented as vectors confine, resulting from monopole condensation and the quark bilinear breaking $SU(N_{F})$ chiral symmetry down to $SO(N_{F})$. Our findings derive from an ${\cal N}=1$ supersymmetric theory, specifically with anomaly-mediated supersymmetry breaking.

Machine learning models such as random forests and AdaBoost have proven effective across many fields but their high performance comes at the cost of clarity in understanding their predictions. Users are generally unable to discern how individual characteristics, or sets of characteristics, influence these models as their values change. In order to improve this understanding, a method called Disentangled Attribution Curves has been introduced to offer more transparent explanations for tree ensemble models through detailed (multi-dimensional) curves depicting feature importance at different variable values. By using this new approach, it is possible to boost the accuracy of regression models and maintain clarity in how their predictions are made, as demonstrated on real-world data and further validated in simulation studies where it was found to surpass alternative methods in recovering predictive models. Finally, a practical analysis using bike-sharing data highlights the utility of DAC in uncovering valuable new insights.

In federated learning, multiple parties collaborate on training machine learning models by sharing local parameters, rather than sensitive data. Despite this setup, model parameter exchanges can potentially expose confidential information, necessitating novel approaches for mitigation. Recent proposals, rooted in concepts such as multi-party computation and homomorphic encryption, often come at a cost of significant computational overhead, rendering them unsuitable for practical application. This work presents an alternative solution by harnessing the capabilities of Trusted Execution Environments to safeguard data and model interactions, allowing for the development of more efficient and realistic protocols for collaborative machine learning. A prototype implementation, centered around the Intel Software Guard Extensions architecture, demonstrates the feasibility of our approach for privacy enhancement in federated learning. This implementation achieves substantial performance improvements over existing solutions, marking a notable advancement in this area.

The embedded systems industry is massive and ubiquitous, as evidenced by its presence in most of the world's produced processors. Interactions between drivers and external components like sensors and actuators pose significant challenges to embedded software development, particularly during the testing phase. Factors such as environmental unpredictability, limited hardware availability, and costs often hinder effective testing. To address these issues, this research presents a novel testing framework that targets driver verification on microcontrollers. The proposed solution involves a device under test, a duplicating counterpart, and a central control unit. The control unit manages testing procedures while the device under test runs the code being tested and its counterpart simulates the interactions with external peripherals. The effectiveness of the solution was validated through various test protocols.

This paper introduces a method called Timeloops, which enables system call filtering for complex microservices applications by leveraging model checking and learning techniques. Unlike static analysis-based methods, Timeloops can handle dynamic system call patterns that emerge at runtime. By extracting system call templates from running services and constructing a Gorel model, Timeloops identifies valid system call sequences and generates BDDs to define allowed system calls for each process. As system templates evolve dynamically, Timeloops updates the Gorel model and refines the BDDs, ensuring system call consistency. We showcase Timeloops on seven real-world microservices applications and demonstrate its ability to block malicious system calls while permitting legitimate ones, even with template modifications.

Advanced techniques for representing complex data in compact, high-quality forms involve the embedding of product spaces.
We've identified a new challenge - linear classification in complex product space structures composed of different geometric configurations, like Euclidean, Riemannian, and spherical spaces.
To tackle this problem, we first demonstrate that linear classification models can effectively function within product spaces of various curvature structures, similar to Euclidean space-based models.
Furthermore, our analysis shows that models using a single vector can achieve this capability.
We've then developed and analyzed a new linear classification model for high-dimensional, manifold-based product spaces, including those with non-Euclidean structures.
Our model's efficiency was verified in low-dimensional (3D) spherical space experiments, where it significantly surpassed more complex deep learning approaches.

This introduction focuses on stochastic Model Predictive Control methods that account for uncertainty in constraints, illustrated through a linear system under unpredictable conditions. The corresponding Matlab code is also accessible online for reference purposes.

This paper bridges the gap between compressed sensing and statistical learning, leveraging sparsity and structure to minimize the computational burden of learning tasks. We focus on independent component analysis through a compressive lens, demonstrating that certain properties within the cumulant-based ICA model yield a compact set of solutions that can be effectively represented within the cumulant tensor space. Utilizing a property that ensures randomness and coherence, we establish the existence of a compressive ICA scheme and propose two novel algorithms, IPG and ASD, to realize the compressed order through experimental verification. The CICA algorithms are further integrated with the compressive ICA framework, allowing for the identification of the optimal sensing matrix via optimization. The success of CICA is validated across both synthetic and real-world datasets, and the proposed sensing matrices are found to consistently perform remarkably well.

To analyze the interplay of species competition and dispersal, an asymmetrical noisy voter model was developed for a regular lattice. The model allows one species to colonize nearest-neighbor sites, while another species can settle at any distance but is less successful in doing so. The model includes external noise, which can lead to random species swaps in the lattice. The combination of these dynamics results in various species competition outcomes, including the exclusion of one species, distinct population coexistence, or bistable coexistence dependent on the starting population ratio. The model shows that an abrupt transition occurs as immigration intensity surpasses a critical point, causing the irreversible decline of the species with shorter dispersal range due to a cusp catastrophe leading to half loop dynamics.
We prove that von Neumann algebras associated with compact regions within abelian quantum double models have infinite type $II$.

To enhance magnon-photon-phonon entanglement in cavity magnomechanics, we develop an approach incorporating a coherent feedback loop. Furthermore, our findings confirm that both the steady and dynamic states of this system exhibit genuine tripartite entanglement. We utilize the logarithmic negativity to quantify quantum correlations between individual subsystems, as well as genuine tripartite entanglement through a nonzero minimum residual contangle. We investigate experimentally feasible parameters that enable the generation of tripartite entanglement and demonstrate its significant enhancement with coherent feedback by adjusting the beam splitter's reflective parameter. Additionally, the proposed entanglement exhibits robustness against thermal effects, making our approach a valuable asset for applications in quantum information processing.

We've obtained one-loop triple-collinear splitting operators for color and spin spaces, applicable to all five scenarios: $q \to qq'\bar{q}'$, $q \to qq\bar{q}$, $q \to qgg$, $g \to gq\bar{q}$ and $g \to ggg$. The exact expressions are derived within dimensionless QCD and include the results of a specific integral up to its second-order expansion. Additionally, we've evaluated the associated splitting functions. Our results are crucial and necessary for developing subtraction and integration-by-parts techniques to solve one-loop triple-collinear cross-sections exactly. They'll also be useful for developing numerical tools, like triple-collinear color and numerical integrals, applicable to multi-jet production processes.

A formal proof for the Neron Desingularization, a multidimensional case algorithm, has been developed for one-dimensional local rings, building upon the foundational work of Neron, Raydan, and Vostrelov-Shen. Furthermore, the algorithm's convergence to the desired result is demonstrated through the accumulation of successive approximations.

Ancient sundials served as primary timekeepers before the invention of mechanical clocks, with the classical Islamic civilization utilizing the Sun's daily movement to determine prayer times, often relying on sundials for this purpose. This knowledge eventually spread to Indonesia through Islamic cultural influences. Indonesian sundials developed as a reflection of local advancements in astronomy, technology, art, and architecture, with historical examples warranting detailed documentation and study, though often overlooked in existing literature. To collect necessary spatial and temporal information on these sundials, a citizen science initiative could be implemented, addressing research inquiries while promoting science education among the general public. This concept has been proposed as a framework, referred to as the Suryakala-Nusantara program, to explore sundials through citizen science methods.

This research focuses on an integrated data and energy transmission network, which incorporates a D2D communication system. An energy harvesting D2D receiver (DR) is introduced to relay data from the base station to a mobile user (MU). An intelligent reflecting surface (IRS) is placed to optimize signal transmission between the base station and MU, and between the data transmitter and DR. We are looking to optimize the position of the IRS that maximizes the MU's data rate and energy harvested by the DR within a specific area, under constraints set by the availability of energy and maximum allowable reflection phases. A multi-stage problem is broken down into several sub-problems, including optimizing DR's location, scaling factor, and reflection coefficients. We use an iterative algorithm combining methods like maximum likelihood estimation, fractional order approximation, and alternating optimization to solve these sub-problems. The proposed method iteratively calculates the optimal values for each parameter, eventually converging to a solution. Simulation results show the method's effectiveness and reachability of the optimal solution.

The surge in telework needs has highlighted the potential benefits of fully
automating and controlling experiments remotely. This work presents the technical
advancements of creating a two-dimensional LDV measurement system using a single-
point LDV system via a remotely controllable and automated setup. The document's
aim is to expedite the development of similar setups for this kind of application,
which is highly versatile and can be applied to various scenarios including both
air-based acoustic signal-driven samples and mechanically induced samples.

The cardinalities of finite models for sentences with at least three variables and binary relations are studied in this research.  Specifically, we demonstrate that any such sentence, denoted as $\Phi$, has a corresponding sentence, denoted as $\Phi'$, utilizing the same number of variables and one symmetric binary relation, whose set of model cardinalities increases linearly with $\Phi$'s model cardinalities. Furthermore, we also establish the existence of an even more primitive class of such sentences: for any given $\Phi$, there is a sentence $\Psi$ with three variables and one binary relation whose model cardinalities are proportional to $\Phi$'s model cardinalities.  In contrast to previous results, in this research we do not require the relation to be symmetric for the second type of sentence.  However, we do know that for any given $\Phi$, if we can find a corresponding sentence $\Psi$ using only three variables and one binary relation, then there exists a sentence $\Psi'$ using the same number of variables and one symmetric binary relation whose model cardinalities increase linearly with $\Psi$'s model cardinalities.  An even more primitive class of such sentences exists: for any given $\Phi$, there is a sentence $\Phi_1$ with two variables and one binary relation whose set of model cardinalities increases linearly with $\Phi$'s model cardinalities.  In particular, we can construct such a sentence $\Phi_1$ for any given sentence using

The effectiveness of programmable electrostatic phase plates is subject to debate 
given their varying suitability for particular applications. Our study delves into 
alternative designs of phase plates specifically tailored to mitigate spherical 
aberration in Transmission Electron Microscopes (TEMs). Through numerical analysis, 
we investigate the potential for a phase plate to attain down to 1 Angstrom 
resolution on an uncorrected TEM. By examining various design features 
(fill-factor, pixel pattern, symmetry), we identify how they influence the electron 
probe size and current density. Our proposed designs exhibit probe sizes ($d_{50}$) 
as low as 0.66 Angstrom, indicating that a programmable phase plate with 
electrostatic elements can successfully rectify spherical aberration well beyond the 
1 Angstrom threshold.

Drawing inspiration from Feynman's and Deutsch's groundbreaking work, we introduce a theoretical framework that assesses computational capability across diverse physical platforms and complexity scales. This framework is utilized to analyze the fundamental principles of quantum computation. Furthermore, this study serves as a precursor to investigating more universal computation models by examining additional physical mechanisms exemplified throughout the paper.

This study focused on determining the general equation for calculating the potential positions of an $n$ step random walk in a $d$ dimensional space with a single unit step size, denoted as $|P_n^{d}|$. Our approach began by establishing a recursive relationship for the count formula: $|P_n^{d+1}| = |P_n^d| + 2\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} |P_k^d|$. We then presented two distinct methods to derive an explicit equation for $|P_n^{d}|$, involving the application of generating functions and Faulhaber's formula. Ultimately, our findings were presented in a matrix representation as our primary theorem.

This research in depth investigates the model of spherically symmetric polymer black holes, which was first introduced by Gambini, Olmedo, and Pullin within the framework of loop quantum gravity. We explored how in the GOP model the spacelike transition surface at the classical singularity replaces it. Utilizing transformations in the coordinates, the authors were able to extend the metric to the white hole region, and thereby transform the boundary conditions for perturbations into an inverse problem that is solved using the methods of Wronskians. The analysis that follows confirms that the model retains the characteristics of a quantum mechanical boundary, as the presence of spin-coefficients indicates. The analysis that follows confirms that the model retains the characteristics of a quantum mechanical boundary, as the presence of spin-coefficients indicates. Furthermore, the authors were able to compute the quasinormal modes of scalar, electromagnetic, and gravitational perturbations, and found that these modes are identical to those computed for the Schwarzschild-de Sitter spacetime.

We have derived a semi-analytical formula for the dynamic density-density correlation of massless Dirac electrons in doped graphene, which is applicable at finite temperatures. This finding is key to understanding the thermal screening of interactions among Dirac electrons and we leverage it to calculate the thermal capacity and compressibility of doped graphene. Notably, at very low temperatures, the thermal capacity displays a linear temperature dependence characteristic of normal Fermi liquids, with the coefficient controlled by the velocity of charge carriers in the material.

Continuous speech leads to consistent prosody patterns, yet current speech synthesis models often disregard context. These systems fall short when it comes to producing high-quality paragraphs, necessitating a system that integrates contextual elements. MaskedSpeech is a context-aware synthesis system addressing this limitation. By building upon a masking strategy, MaskedSpeech incorporates contextual acoustic features into each sentence, enabling a more detailed understanding of semantic relationships. Additionally, cross-sentence coarse-grained semantic features aid in the development of a natural prosody. Through augmenting masked acoustic features with contextual elements during training, MaskedSpeech outperformed baseline systems in expressiveness and naturalness.

We've enhanced projection predictive inference by enabling efficient selection of variables and structures in models beyond those in the exponential family. By projecting predictive variables into a latent space, we have created a new approach that maintains the original model's integrity while performing variable selection, ultimately resulting in improved predictive performance. This novel framework extends the original projection predictive methodology to a broader range of models and outperforms the original method in certain scenarios, while remaining comparable in others. We've rigorously tested our approach by evaluating its performance on various models, including the probit model, conditional Gaussian, and Gaussian Graphical Models, and have provided empirical evidence of its utility.

Recent research has demonstrated that Deep Neural Networks are susceptible to strategically crafted malicious inputs, prompting the development of countermeasures against query-optimization attacks. Our research diverges from previous studies by exploring the vulnerability of DNN models to Man-in-the-Middle attacks. From an attacker's standpoint, conventional adversarial attacks prove ineffective as they necessitate multiple interactions with the model prior to execution, whereas MitM attacks can launch without this limitation. Moreover, these attacks can only be applied to existing data sets, significantly diminishing the attacker's return on investment. To tackle this problem, we propose an efficient adversarial attack generation method, test its validity on DNN models, and evaluate its practical implications.

Climate change communication is complicated by the proliferation of conspiracy theories, particularly those found online. This research investigates prevalent conspiracy theories regarding climate change by analyzing a significant Twitter dataset and applies a sophisticated stance detection technique. Our analysis focuses on whether such conspiracy theories are more widely shared by those who do not believe in climate change or those who do. Furthermore, we examine the most popular conspiracy theories, their variations with differing levels of climate change acceptance, and reveal that non-believers predominantly disseminate messages containing conspiracy theory-related keywords. Notably, all conspiracy theories are not equally prevalent. Our findings also highlight their implications for effective climate change communication strategies.

A study focused on the production of dark matter in proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV has been carried out using the CMS experiment. Data samples amounting to 35.9 fb$^{-1}$ of collisions are analyzed under distinct phase-space constraints. Two models featuring complex scalar and pseudoscalar interactions are examined, yielding constraints on respective mediators and dark matter cross-sections, with masses below 1000 GeV. For example, this study places a limit of 7.9 $\times$ 10$^{-13}$ cm$^2$ on the cross-section for a 700 GeV pseudoscalar mediator producing dark matter. Additionally, this study explores signatures of monophoton production accompanied by missing energy, which results in novel limits on lepton-flavor non-uniform Z$^\prime$ boson interactions. Given its comprehensive data sets and theoretical interpretations, this study offers a crucial contribution to understanding dark matter and its possible mediators.

Given an n-exangulated category with specified properties, we establish that it satisfies Auslander-Reiten-Serre duality if and only if it possesses certain duality-based angles. We also determine a specific condition necessary for the presence of Serre duality. Assuming duality exists, we establish a one-to-one correspondence involving a bijection and specific category characteristics.

Building upon Kirkeboen et al.'s (2016) work that leverages multiple treatment instruments to identify a treatment effect in the context of multiple unordered treatments, this study reverses the paradigm by employing a single instrument that points to a range of potential outcomes. The proof is demonstrated through a real-world example, namely estimating the effect of attending a European Higher Education program on a student's chances of enrolling in a program, using data from Pytlak (2018).

To advance our understanding of matter's various forms, high-energy particle collisions with a wide variety of projectiles must be studied extensively.
Although scientists have utilized beams of numerous particles to make significant breakthroughs, creating and working with beams of antineutrons, specific hyperons and their counterparts has been notoriously challenging.
However, a recent high-tech research setup known as a super $J/\psi$ factory holds the potential to greatly improve access to these elusive particles. As a result, a huge number of $J/\psi$ decays occur annually, creating favorable conditions to accurately analyze these interactions using precision-tagging of co-produced particles. 
This state-of-the-art technology can facilitate groundbreaking studies of diverse targets and open doors for new particle physics, nuclear physics, and gravitational physics research, allowing scientists to better understand antineutrons, specific hyperons and their counterparts. 
This article serves as a comprehensive introduction to the possibilities presented by the super $J/\psi$ factory, exemplifying the benefits of this technology in studies of antineutrons, specific hyperons and their counterparts by presenting real research findings in the field.

Most of a multiple star system's final mass is accumulated during the first million years of its existence, particularly in the inner binary of a binary system within a larger triple arrangement. This critical period is often underrepresented in theoretical models of stellar evolution. Researchers have suggested that the distinctive characteristics of extreme multiple star systems could be the result of differential accumulation of matter from a third host system at an early stage. This hypothetical host system would need to be significantly more massive than the components of the inner binary, whose masses follow a uniform distribution. In contrast, earlier studies assumed that the host system's masses were randomly distributed. We have revised this standard in a simulation, replacing it with a realistic mass range that is based on the observed masses of multiple star systems and their characteristic arrangements. Our results indicate that the average mass of the inner binary in these systems is significantly affected, as the simulated masses fall below previous estimates in nearly 70% of cases. These findings also show that earlier simulations overestimated the rate at which the inner binary loses mass and undergoes mass gains. These discrepancies are attributed to the limited mass range in the prior simulation, as well as its assumption that the host system's masses were uniformly distributed. These results imply that the hypothetical differential accumulation scenario is even more prevalent than previously estimated, and may also be applicable to a wider variety of systems that are similar in mass.

This manuscript examines flat spacetimes with intrinsic properties, as viable models for understanding the universe on a cosmological scale. We find that such spacetimes naturally incorporate geometric patterns suitable for describing irregular, periodically-distributed matter within the universe. We also develop precise formulas allowing for accurate calculation of matter density from observed irregularties in the CMB for specific types of geometric patterns.

We're introducing a combined model for image segmentation and restoration that uses a versatile image representation, specifically designed for simple, interconnected image structures. This approach effectively tackles challenging cases by leveraging our multi-scale image representation, built upon repeated applications of a local image comparison, and leveraging our model's inherent property of generating interpretable, structurally consistent images. Notably, our model can be achieved through an intuitive optimization technique, starting from any given image and iteratively refining it within the relevant image domain. We're also introducing a segment-and-merge procedure that enables assigning specific features to distinct regions. We're evaluating our model on natural image restoration tasks, such as restoring images with occlusions, restoring images behind glass, and generating zoomed-in images, and finding that it significantly outperforms existing specialized models in these areas.

Active galactic nuclei (AGNs), containing accreting black holes at their center, allow for the investigation of black hole mass and spin through the analysis of electromagnetic spectra. This research uses the Spin-Modified Fundamental Plane of black hole activity, a non-linear model that links radio luminosity, optical or X-ray luminosity, black hole mass, and spin. Accounting for uncertainties in AGN emission processes and the effects of dust on optical luminosity measurements, we determine the minimum possible spins of seven supermassive black holes (SMBHs) with masses between $6.1 \times 10^{10} \rm{M_\odot}$ and $4.6 \times 10^{11} \rm{M_\odot}$. We find that five of these SMBHs have spins near maximal levels, potentially indicating a link between the growth of large-mass black holes and processes that place them near critical spin states. Additionally, we determine the likelihood of the remaining two SMBHs having spins near maximal levels, finding that one has a chance of 50% and the other has a chance of 12%. We discuss the implications of these results on the development of high-mass black holes.

Creating intelligent, neuroinspired systems poses a significant challenge due to its underlying hardware complexities. To overcome these challenges, a thorough comprehension of its fundamental building blocks is essential, coupled with the development of straightforward and user-friendly prototyping tools. To address this issue, an open-source emulator was designed, utilizing the Brian simulator and seamlessly integrating with existing workflows. This emulator successfully emulated error-free neural network behavior in software for individual neurons and networks of neurons connected in complex loops. Additionally, the emulator allowed for the analysis of how neural networks with noisy inputs and hidden neural states respond to various stimuli, leading to a deeper understanding of neural regulation mechanisms. Using this emulator, it was discovered that the internal neural state could be used to improve the identification of neural networks, potentially leading to new applications in the fields of computer vision and audio processing.

A solar type-I noise storm is created by particle beams accelerated from active regions experiencing significant changes in their magnetic field configurations. These storms exhibit significant intensity fluctuations in very short time frames and on very short wavelengths. The dynamic evolution of these storm sources remains largely unstudied due to a lack of high-resolution imaging data in metrewave frequencies. By analyzing data from the Murchison Widefield Array (MWA), this research identifies a new aspect of these storm sources associated with minor flares. It reveals the existence of two distinct modes of co-existence: rapid contraction and slow growth. These modes switch back and forth multiple times within a brief timeframe, and the rate of the switch is correlated with the strength of the flare. The implications of these findings could help improve our understanding of the physical processes governing flare-associated active region evolution.

A compact magneto-optical trap has been successfully developed, using a planar-integrated design that merges an optical grating chip and a magnetic coil chip. This novel setup minimizes the size and weight of the trap, requiring only a single laser beam to capture a population of approximately 10,000 cold rubidium atoms. The improved MOT architecture has potential applications in devices such as gravimeters, atomic clocks, and quantum memory systems, offering a reduction in volume, weight, and complexity.

The spherically symmetric merging of a kinetic cloud of particles onto a Schwarzschild black hole is investigated. Unlike earlier research, no assumption about the cloud's boundary or its treatment of particles is made. A series of conformal transformations is employed to the Dullin-MAthael-Sterbini metric, simplifying the problem and reducing the associated Einstein equations to a single, second-order differential equation. This equation is solved using a new approach, taking into account conservation of momentum. The merger process is discussed in terms of conserved currents. It is discovered that the mass accretion formula for non-rotating black holes can be derived. Specifically, the mass accretion rate is determined as $\dot{M} = (192\pi G)^{-1} \dot{\Phi}_{(1,0)}$ where $\dot{\Phi}_{(1,0)}$ is the time component of the energy-momentum tensor's stress tensor. Furthermore, a relationship between angular momentum in a gas cloud and mass accretion onto a black hole is established. It is found that the mass accretion rate is affected by rotational energy, and that the merger process results in a model trajectory consistent with the model of Dimonte et al.

The probability of (de-)excitation and photon emission is evaluated for a non-relativistic, moving atom interacting with a quantum electromagnetic field near a stationary, perfectly conducting plane.
