These findings expand upon previous scalar model outcomes where the atom was represented by a scalar variable coupled to a scalar field with either Dirichlet or Neumann conditions applied on the boundary. This assessment considers how spontaneous emission rates change when an initially excited atom is accelerated versus an atom at rest encountering a moving mirror.

A comprehensive study of massive star candidates within and surrounding the Rosette Nebula (NGC 2244) has been conducted using recent infrared images from the VISTA Telescopico Atacama (VISTA) survey. VISTA images covering over 2 square degrees have allowed us to identify over 300 massive star candidates across more than 2000 clusters and potential clusterless field regions within the Rosette Complex. Although a significant proportion (43%) of these candidate stars lie outside of the 25 most dense and well-known clusters within the field, our analysis shows that a substantial portion (around 30%) also reside within the nebula's central regions, particularly in and around the nebula's central ring where the candidate stars exhibit a strong spatial correlation with the observed dark clusters and velocities of the Rosette's filaments. Furthermore, a detailed examination of the distribution of massive star candidates in relation to the observed filaments shows that the candidate stars exhibit a strong spatial correlation with the observed filaments, suggesting that the clusterless massive star candidates may share a common origin with the observed filaments and therefore could be considered as 'nomadic' massive stars. Their supposed 'nomadic' nature implies that some massive stars can be found both within and outside of dense cluster environments, potentially shedding light on the processes involved in the dispersal of massive stars from their birth places.

Degraded handwritten document images can significantly hinder understanding, particularly in historical and official documents. The causes of degradation vary and lead to document images with multiple text lines in diverse script types and sizes. Despite these challenges, we develop an effective approach to improve severely degraded handwritten documents, even those with multiple text lines. Our method utilizes a combination of local image transformation techniques and a non-parametric restoration approach to create sharper, clearer text from the degraded images. The results of our algorithm are impressive, as evident from the substantial improvement in text clarity and the effective restoration of handwritten documents, especially the enhanced legibility of degraded text.

The growth of Global Mobility Partners Group requires effective management of information about its global member networks. Most of this information is initially stored as images of identification cards, often in hard-to-read formats, making them difficult to process manually. To simplify this process, an AI-based solution was developed, utilizing a combination of optical character recognition and deep learning techniques to extract and convert valuable information into easily accessible, readable text. By integrating this technology, the entire membership process is streamlined from start to finish, from initial identification card images to the final storage of member data in a secure database.

In vehicular communications, the complex and dispersive nature of channels makes reliable channel estimation vital for optimal system performance, yet the IEEE 802.11p standard's limited pilots lead to inadequate channel tracking. As a result, conventional IEEE 802.11p estimators experience significant performance decline, particularly in high-speed scenarios. To overcome these challenges, researchers have explored deep learning (DL) techniques for channel estimation in IEEE 802.11p. Nonetheless, these approaches either underperform in extremely high-speed situations or exhibit significant computational complexities. To resolve these issues, this paper introduces an innovative solution based on a long short-term memory (LSTM) model that surpasses the performance of its predecessor, SLSTM. The proposed solution incorporates side information into LSTM for side channel estimation, resulting in an enhanced channel estimator, S-LSTM. The evaluation reveals that S-LSTM boasts improved channel accuracy, reduced standard deviation, lower computational complexity, and superior generalization capabilities in high-speed scenarios compared to SLSTM. Furthermore, S-LSTM demonstrates superior performance even when side information is imperfect, showcasing robustness. Additionally, S-LSTM achieves comparable results to more complex DL architectures, such as convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and residual networks (RNs), while exhibiting lower computational complexity.

The task of automatically assigning colors to images without human involvement has garnered interest within the machine learning community for a limited time. Colorization is particularly challenging due to its inherently high degrees of freedom; when presented with an image, multiple plausible color combinations exist, and there may be no single definitive solution. Another related issue is Single Image Super Resolution, a task that involves converting low-resolution images into higher-resolution versions. This research targets a novel, automatic colorization approach, specializing in astronomical images and leveraging Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). We experiment with employing various models in the RGB and L*a*b color spaces, relying on transfer learning and pre-trained ResNet-18 architecture, due to the small size of the dataset available. Our approach successfully produces aesthetically pleasing, high-resolution, and colorized results for images lacking these characteristics. The performance of the proposed model is quantitatively assessed by measuring distance metrics, including L1 distance and L2 distance, and evaluating the generated images against the real data distribution using the Frechet inception distance (FID) metric.

We've developed a novel numerical scheme to efficiently calculate Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) weights without relying on tedious iterative processes. Based on the Universal Approximation Theorem, our proposed algorithm rapidly achieves low error rates in the regression and classification of intricate datasets, such as the Griewank function and the MNIST database for handwritten digits. Its mathematical formulation allows it to accurately approximate highly complex nonlinear functions with a minimal margin of error, and it also facilitates the solution of Partial Differential Equations. The approach works by determining the weights for each neuron in localized data subsets where a corresponding approximation matrix remains invertible, thereby rendering hyperparameter optimization unnecessary. As a direct consequence, this minimizes computational speed. With inherent overfitting prevention, our method provides reproducible results that are also easily interpretable. With respect to observations and features, our method's computational complexity lies in the P class and has a specific running time expressed in terms of these variables. Conversely, traditional ANN training algorithms fall into the NP-Complete class. Its exceptional generalization capability allows the method to achieve test-set errors comparable to or even lower than those on the training data.

The ECFA Early Career Researcher's panel started representing the interests of young researchers within the ECFA community in January 2021. Throughout its first two years of operation, the panel developed its organizational framework, cooperated with ECFA by offering input and insights, and introduced several projects focused on comprehending and addressing the varied needs of young researchers. This report outlines the details of the panel's formation and operations as well as its engagement with numerous activities during its first two years of operation.

Confining modes at the edge, known as line waves, can propagate on the boundary between two specially designed electromagnetic interfaces that maintain mirror symmetry properties.
Studies have previously examined line waves in theory and in practice, revealing their occurrence at both microwave and terahertz frequencies.
A new research explores the possibility of detecting line waves in the visible range of the electromagnetic spectrum by utilizing plasmonic waveguides and metasurfaces designed to maximize interaction with light.
By incorporating an array of optical resonators and high numerical resolution in 3D simulations, it is now possible to accurately study line waves in the visible spectrum range.
This work proposes a new method for detecting line waves, involving the analysis of the magnetic field component, identified through optical simulations of a specific structure consisting of a plasmonic waveguide and two interacting metasurfaces.
A comparison of both normal and dual polarization resonance scenarios shows that line waves can occur even when the metasurfaces do not mirror each other's magnetic field responses.
Additionally, this work involves the optical experimentation and demonstration of line waves in the visible spectrum range, involving the design of an integrated device consisting of a plasmonic waveguide and two specific gold nanostrands, arranged in a cross pattern with varying gap sizes.

One of the most effective approaches to building intelligent robotic systems is Learning from Demonstration (LfD), however research is still needed to overcome challenges such as multi-agent learning and prolonged autonomy.  A new architecture for multi-agent LfD is introduced which enables the creation of reliable and efficient robotic systems in complex and large-scale environments by leveraging advancements in Artificial Intelligence (AI) through the implementation of a Federated Learning (FL)-based collaborative learning environment involving both humans and robots. This novel approach addresses the traditional difficulties associated with multi-agent robotic systems and enables scalable robotic solutions by facilitating the integration of AI advancements. Furthermore, the implementation of a FL framework facilitates the exploration of new possibilities for robotic cooperation and enables the vision of collaborative robotic ecosystems to become a reality. This research has far-reaching implications for the development of robotic systems and can contribute to the creation of robust and complex robotic applications across a variety of domains, including AI-powered healthcare and secure multi-agent robotic environments.

A new bias-corrected estimator has been created for the mean absolute deviation of a median regression model, addressing the problem of irregularity that typically hinders conventional bias reduction.  To overcome this issue, a specific alternative strategy was developed and proven to work effectively in conjunction with a modified version of the traditional Le Cesse-Pinkham estimator.  The newly developed bias-reduced estimator is more efficient than its conventional counterpart and has lower asymptotic variance, making it up to 35% more efficient in certain extreme cases.  The established bias-corrected formula remains valid for datasets as small as n = 12 in linear models and n = 64 in non-linear models.  Theoretical estimates suggest that in practice, this alternative strategy can achieve asymptotic efficiency equivalent to that of the conventional method, with a minimum efficiency gain predicted to be around 80%.

The tasks of relation extraction and knowledge graph link prediction share a
common link in their objectives, allowing them to complement each other in the
process of predicting a subject-object relationship in a sentence. Specifically,
when a model identifies an object and its related subject, this relationship can
be utilized to forecast additional objects associated with the subject, which
in turn enables the detection of relevant object relationships. Conversely, when
a model predicts an object related to a subject, this relationship can be used
to forecast potential subjects, which in turn enables the detection of relevant
subject relationships. In our research, we utilized this connection by having
two specific tasks: relation extraction and knowledge graph link prediction, and
by having the model switch between these tasks repeatedly during the training
process, this approach allowed us to surpass current state-of-the-art results on
the MNLI, COPA, and WIKIPEDIA tasks.

The Analytical Exact Iteration Method has been employed to solve the N-dimensional Radial Schrödinger equation for complex-valued potentials, and further generalized to consider complex-valued masses in the Landau problem. Calculations of bound state energies were carried out for various dimensions (N up to 3), and results were verified by comparing the method's accuracy with existing approaches such as the Numerical Graphical Iteration, Complex Scaling and Complex Rotational methods. Owing to its algorithmic nature, this new method allows for the determination of energy spectra in systems exhibiting spatial anisotropy, and it has been utilized to investigate anisotropy's effect on quarkonium state dissociation temperatures.

Our study focused on the magnetic arrangements within the crystals of Tb3RuO7 and Nd3RuO7 using neutron-diffraction experiments. In Tb3RuO7, neighboring ruthenium atoms created a chain pattern, with some being ordered magnetically and others remaining randomly aligned. This unique combination resulted in an intermediate disordered state, with the two ruthenium types exhibiting similar yet distinct behaviors. In Nd3RuO7, the magnetic patterns were uniform and independent for the two ruthenium species, with both being ordered at temperatures below 17.5 K. We attribute the disordered state in Tb3RuO7 primarily to the magnetic frustrations, caused by the differing internal magnetic fields imposed by the ordered terbium atoms on the two ruthenium species, leading to distinct behaviors.

Multi-Layer Perceptrons are particularly effective at generating accurate
low-dimensional representations of data, such as images, shapes and light
fields. Despite advancements using periodic activations or positional
encodings, they have historically been tailored to a single type of data
and can suffer from compromised performance in new domains. To address this,
we introduce an innovative approach called Dual MLP, consisting of two separate
networks: a primary one optimized for specific data and a secondary one
generalizing well across multiple domains. By employing a learned positional
encoding, we enable flexible input representations, whether it's a 2D image,
a 3D shape or a volume of varying dimensions. Building upon a straightforward
training strategy, we demonstrate the benefits of Dual MLP by achieving
unprecedented results in new domains while retaining superior performance in
established ones. Notably, this achieves the first successful application of
MLPs to complex video representations.

Traditional methods of covariate-shift adaptation utilize unlabelled data for either determining importance weights or domain-invariant features. Then, a model is trained using only labelled data. We're examining a special instance of covariate shift that also enables learning from unlabelled data, effectively merging adaptation with semi-supervised learning techniques. By drawing on causality concepts, we propose a novel method that requires learning from both the causes and effects of a target variable. This leads to the development of a semi-generative model, $P(Y,X_E|X_C,\theta)$, which is shown to be resilient against domain shifts in causal features. Moreover, this model can employ causal information to produce labels for unlabeled data points, thereby resolving the initial domain shift. Experimental results validating the effectiveness of our proposed method are presented.

Despite its impressive task execution capabilities, the inner workings of deep learning systems remain shrouded in theoretical uncertainty. In our study, we establish a geometric model for deep learning architectures by identifying connections to pre-existing geometric frameworks in quantum computation and diffeomorphic template matching. Within this context, we map the geometric structures of convolutional neural networks, residual networks, recursive neural networks, recurrent neural networks, and the equilibrium propagation framework. Furthermore, this geometric framework enables us to explore the relationships between geometric structures and the performance of different neural networks, thereby guiding the design of deep learning architectures at an algorithmic level.

We consider the field extension $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{d},\zeta_3)/\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_3)$ where $\zeta_3$ is a primitive cube root of unity and $d$ is a positive cube-free integer. Our work examines the behavior of the chain of lattice minima in the cubic field $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{d})$ arising from the prime factorization of $d$ in relation to generators of ambiguous principal ideals. Specifically, we investigate the occurrence of generators of such ideals among the lattice minima and explain their impact on the principal factorization type of the cubic field and its associated field extension. We also provide the necessary conditions for a lattice minimum to be associated with a prime ideal in the ring of integers of $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{d})$.

A research strategy called "telling friends from foes" involves using substructure tagging to identify friendly jet configurations and exclude them from being considered backgrounds in analyses. Previous studies have explored ways to present jet configurations and teach classifiers to recognize these patterns. This work instead focuses on how to represent jet configuration information effectively. It introduces an approach that utilizes an expert network, a specialized neural network, to convert complex jet data into a lower-dimensional representation suitable for classification. By incorporating this representation into a downstream classifier, the study demonstrates that expert variables enhance the performance of deep neural networks in tagging techniques. Additionally, it identifies areas for improvement in current jet presentation methods and proposes alternative strategies.

For every positive integer r, a specific kind of Stirling number is used to count how many ways a set can be divided into a specified number of non-empty subsets, where each subset contains at least r elements. We're introducing a variation of these Stirling numbers, which represents their extreme forms, reducing to well-known cases when r equals one. This paper seeks to establish formulas linking these variations together.

Eighty sets of layer groups were examined, each consisting of four types: ordinary and double, as well as gray single and double. Layer group properties allowed for the efficient computation of relevant physical characteristics using symbolic methods, thanks to code such as POLSym. This involved an initial step of categorizing irreducible domains based on their action within the Brillouin zone and the topology of the torus. Additionally, band representations stemming from site symmetry groups were broken down into irreducible components. This theoretical data on layer group symmetry was then tabulated and made accessible online.

Momentum operators are explored in the context of intrinsically curved manifolds. It's established that for Killing vector fields representing these momentum operators, the manifolds are either flat or belong to specific categories: those with a compact structure and a constant sectional curvature of positive value, occurring in dimensions of 1, 3, or 7. Specific forms for these momentum operators and their associated Casimir element are studied, particularly for the three-dimensional sphere S^3. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the Lie algebra structure constants for S^3 relate proportionally to 2ℏ/i, leading to an investigation of the composition of multiple momentum operators, involving three operators in particular.

A sign problem encountered in Monte Carlo simulations beyond half-filling can be mitigated by transforming the integration path. However, this transformation introduces an additional computational cost associated with the Jacobian determinant in the Boltzmann weight, posing a significant barrier for large-scale simulations. Our proposed architecture, based on a novel application of complex-valued affine coupling layers in neural networks, efficiently circumvents this challenge by achieving linear scaling of the determinant cost. As a result, this method allows us to tackle intractably large systems plagued by a severe sign problem.

In a composite Higgs program incorporating an additional complex $S$ scalar field,
we deconstruct the mechanisms that generate the misalignment between the $H$ Higgs doublet and $S$ complex scalar fields, ultimately yielding a large hierarchy between their respective vacuum expectation values. When the composite sector is in a state near the top of the $S$ contour before symmetry breaking, both the Higgs doublet and the $S$ complex scalar contribute to the mass terms of the top and bottom quarks. As the composite sector moves down the $S$ contour, the large VEV ratio $\langle S \rangle \gg \langle H \rangle$ arises primarily from the composite sector, and the weakly interacting Standard Model fields including the top quark become embedded in a proximate $S$ contour, yielding a quasi-degenerate $T$ scalar heavy vector boson with mass around the $W$ mass. We explore the related phenomenology through both experimental signatures of additional scalar and vector states and precision tests of electroweak symmetry, particularly the impact of heavy vector boson $T$ on certain loop processes at LHC.

The use of Virtual-Physical Perceptual Manipulations, like redirected walking and haptics, extends VR interaction beyond conventional physical limitations by exploiting the boundaries of human perception, subtly guiding users' movements to enhance interactivity. This research examines the dangers of VPPM exploitation, beginning with a conceptual framework that confirms their existence and then applying speculative design to identify and mitigate threats. Findings focus on haptic VPPMs that manipulate users' sense of touch, introducing three potential areas where VPPM's true purpose could be disguised: when users are overwhelmed, when financial gains are involved, or when psychological manipulation is involved. By exploring these areas, we highlight how current VPPM applications could potentially cause harm and propose practical solutions that balance VPPM benefits with safety precautions and stricter governance to prevent exploitation.

To assess various approaches to expanding language coverage, we integrate German and Korean into BigScience's large-scale, 1.3 billion parameter multilingual language model, initially trained on 13 languages. Our study focuses on key factors influencing model adaptability for new languages and weighs the computational expense against potential performance gains.

Recent high-resolution observations using VLA and CARMA telescopes have unveiled previously unknown details in the formation of stars and planetary systems. Specifically, researchers have obtained precise data on mass accumulation among low-mass stars, including a binary system comprised of equal-mass siblings born from the same core. By examining CO isotopologic ratios, they determined that more massive cores tend to produce greater masses of binary systems. This finding could influence theoretical models on star, planet, and binary fragment formation. Furthermore, researchers have discovered that binary systems, including a previously known system and a newly discovered one, exhibit similar characteristics, including equal masses, similar ages, and orbital distances. Notably, all three systems share distinct features, including low X-ray fluxes and modest fluxes of mid-infrared light. By comparing these characteristics to those of extreme flux emitters, researchers have proposed that the former represent typical stellar formation, while the latter represent rare cases of enhanced mass accretion.

This research introduces the m-arcsinh Kernel ('m-ar-K') Fast Independent Component Analysis ('FastICA') approach ('m-ar-K-FastICA') for feature extraction, combining kernel-based dimensionality reduction with ICA to overcome the limitations of previous methods. Although the kernel trick offers a powerful way to tackle non-linearity, its effectiveness can be undermined by a lack of open-source and reproducible kernel implementations, especially in complex datasets. The proposed m-ar-K-FastICA approach uses a readily available and adaptable Python library that facilitates collaboration with scikit-learn, providing a more reliable solution for feature extraction even in data sets with high entropy levels and no need for data pre-whitening. Several classification experiments using datasets from the UCI dataset benchmark were conducted to evaluate the performance of the proposed method. The results show that the m-ar-K-FastICA method can successfully enable independent component analysis in data sets with high entropy levels, improving classification accuracy for two datasets and significantly reducing processing time from 8 hours to 12 minutes while maintaining classification accuracy.

This paper builds on existing research linking finite model theory to algebraic and propositional proof systems. It's proven that if a logic system can identify unique graphs in a specific category, then a related proof system can do so as well, and this implication has significant consequences for the complexity of that same proof system. These findings expand on previous studies and have strong implications for specific proof systems, such as polynomial calculus and related systems.

A subring collection in a ring $R$, that is associative, commutative nor unital, is considered correctly ordered if any finite group of non-zero elements from $R$ has a common subring with a minimal number that covers all elements from the group. This subring collection's covering number is then represented by the maximum size of all such subrings. Determinants of $2\times2$ matrices with entries from the integer ring define a ring which lacks commutative properties, a unital property and has a finite covering number. This collection's subrings are used to find all minimal elements which satisfy specific division properties with other elements, thereby providing a complete description of this ring's covering number. Additionally, a general description is given for the covering numbers of rings which lack commutative properties, a unital property and have a finite covering number. These numbers are directly related to the size of the ring and the characteristics of its ideal subrings. Finally, an example is given which shows that the covering number of an ideal subring may be infinite, yet the covering number of the ring itself is finite.

Social media platforms host an immense volume of content, encompassing a broad array of views on society. Despite the numerous opinions expressed, verifying their accuracy can be challenging due to their often unsubstantiated nature. To address this, we propose an innovative system designed to assess the truthfulness of social media posts by mimicking a fact-checking agency. Building on earlier studies, our approach incorporates a novel theme-based system, which segregates posts into clusters based on related topics. Each theme is then further analyzed to identify potential targets mentioned within the content. Using machine learning, we classify targets as claims or references, and subsequently evaluate the veracity of claims made in the posts. Our methodology leverages human-assisted annotation on two significant social media platforms, YouTube and Twitter, yielding an impressive 93.2% accuracy in detecting claims. Our experiments demonstrate that our system excels in language understanding and content association, showcasing the efficacy of human oversight in training.

Identifying trending topics and processing multiple social media data streams in real-time are crucial in building applications that track events like sports, elections, or natural disasters. We've developed a cloud-based architecture to cater to these demands by using Microsoft Azure services, combining Streaming Analytics and Machine Learning algorithms. This dedicated system captures social media data, performs data processing, and produces actionable results from multiple data streams.

New, high-precision data from the cosmic microwave background lensing measurements and tomographic galaxy surveys in the upcoming years will be crucial for constraining all types of gravitational nonlinearity. We introduce a weighted spectral method that effectively reduces data and estimates the power spectrum through a regularization technique, enabling the analysis of quadratic estimators near nonlinearity thresholds. We integrate a Gaussian prior into the estimator's variance to minimize bias, and from here, develop multiple regularization strategies. We outline an explicit Gaussian approximation and a Bayesian approach utilizing a Gaussian prior for the estimation error and then demonstrate the efficacy of these methods through simulations of a non-linear galaxy survey. We examine the efficacy of these methods in removing nonlinear artifacts and their impact on parameter estimation, including the case of non-linearly interacting dark energy models. We also introduce a weighted spectral method that estimates the power spectrum through a regularization technique, enabling the analysis of quadratic estimators near nonlinearity thresholds. We integrate a Gaussian prior into the estimator's variance to minimize bias, and from here, develop multiple regularization techniques. We outline an explicit Gaussian approximation and a Bayesian approach utilizing a Gaussian prior for the estimation error. We outline an explicit Gaussian approximation and a Bayesian approach utilizing a Gaussian prior for the estimation error. We examine the efficacy of these methods in removing nonlinear artifacts and their impact on parameter estimation, including the case of non-linearally interacting dark energy models.

By integrating Bayesian learning into adversarial training of deep neural networks, we developed a rigorous framework for training certifiable Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs). This approach combines constraint relaxation and modified cross-entropy loss to achieve robustness to potential attacks. The method, demonstrated through empirical tests on standard datasets, allows for training BNNs that are both accurate and certifiably secure on challenging datasets such as MNIST and CIFAR-10, further providing benefits in uncertainty calibration. This innovation facilitates the deployment of BNNs in applications requiring utmost reliability.

The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020 and caused a public health crisis while also disabling people's normal social interactions, forcing them to rely on online news for information but also increasing the spread of rumors through social media. To combat this, we developed a method to detect Chinese rumors starting in February 2020 using machine learning and introduced a new dataset containing 324 real-world rumors and over 19,800 accurately annotated instances collected from various news sources. Our proposed machine learning approach utilizing both traditional and deep learning algorithms achieved impressive results on this new data, with exceptional performance in predicting non-rumors but somewhat lower accuracy for identifying genuine rumors. We also explored other techniques such as rumor verification and tracking, outlining future research avenues and highlighting the particular challenge posed by the limited availability of public domain data for training and testing algorithmic solutions to the rapid dissemination of online rumors.

This study investigates the impact of hyperspectral pixel dimensionality reduction on classification tasks. Five methods (PCA, KPCA, ICA, AE, and DAE) are utilized to compress high-dimensional pixels down to 301 dimensions. The resulting pixels are used for classification, allowing a comprehensive assessment of each method's effectiveness based on classification accuracy, compression rates, and reconstruction errors. Our research employed the well-known NAIP dataset, utilizing 10 classes to classify pixels, and achieved a 100% compression rate for PCA, KPCA, and ICA, whereas AE and DAE reached 99% compression rates. Interestingly, our findings reveal that compression rates do not directly correlate with pixel classification accuracy; instead, PCA, KPCA, and ICA exhibited better performance (92% vs. 88%) and lower standard errors (0.04 vs. 0.08) compared to AE and DAE. Our study's findings provide valuable insights into the application of dimensionality reduction in hyperspectral pixel classification.

Neural networks are highly effective feature extractors but they pose significant challenges due to their large size. Understanding the parameters within various layers is complicated, resulting in the networks often being referred to as 'black boxes.' In contrast, simpler models are more interpretable but they are also much harder to find. Identifying and utilizing a sparse network that can be trained to replicate the same results is a viable option to improve network interpretability. According to the lottery ticket hypothesis, even large, dense neural networks harbor a smaller sparse sub-network that can be trained independently to achieve the same accuracy in the same amount of time. Our objective is to explore the existence of this trainable sub-network in the realm of natural language models, and we will accomplish this by examining and evaluating the most recent model compression techniques, such as quantization, knowledge distillation, and pruning.

A novel prediction method, referred to as ProCS, enables fast and precise calculation of crucial chemical shift indicators in proteins, thereby determining the spatial arrangements of proteins. ProCS is calibrated with the results of high-level quantum mechanical calculations, achieving remarkable agreement in predicting the amide proton chemical shifts of a small protein with a minimal error margin of 0.25 ppm (high correlation coefficient of 0.94). ProCS is now compatible with the PHAISTOS protein simulation program and used to determine the structural arrangements of a small protein, accurately reproducing the experimentally observed amide proton chemical shifts. ProCS is an innovative tool that enhances the predictive capabilities of protein structure prediction methods.

The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date. Despite this, research has largely overlooked the specific loss function implementation used to train a particular model, instead focusing on the inherent properties of the loss function. In contrast, our research sheds light on the impact of loss function variability within a fixed model on training and testing outcomes. We found that certain loss functions, including those not originally designed for classification, can achieve high accuracy on challenging datasets like CIFAR-100, often surpassing the results obtained with standard cross-entropy. Moreover, our results reveal that a loss function's performance is closely related to its ability to accurately predict class probabilities, rather than being a pre-requisite, as previously believed.

Describing the behaviors of complex systems comprised of strongly interacting elements requires concise expressions for their internal relationships. Ensuring the stability of these systems is the primary focus. Parquet theory is a set of equations designed to capture the essential correlations within such systems. A novel check on the validity of parquet theory involves comparing the distinct roles of direct and indirect interactions within a theoretical flux tube. At low frequencies, the model's response to an external stimulus is consistent with its approximation; however, at higher frequencies, the model is unable to accurately predict the strength of its internal interactions. Two potential modifications to improve the model are identified.

The process of exciton condensation leads to the spontaneous creation of electron-hole pairs and triggers a phase transition in a semimetal that forms an excitonic insulator by creating a gap at the Fermi surface. This theoretical concept has been around since the 1960s, but current approaches only offer approximate solutions to the problem. To gain a more in-depth understanding, a new method is introduced that utilizes the parity collective excitation functional to describe the excitonic insulator phase. By utilizing a parity-dependent mean-field approach, the excitonic insulator phase can be precisely calculated and the theoretical results agree with other methods in the weak-coupling limit. Additionally, this approach enables the calculation of dynamic responses, such as the current operator, which facilitates the identification of a semimetal-to-exciton insulator transition through spectroscopic means.

In the US, various safety organizations have adopted text-based systems for processing community members' incident reports, which necessitated a closer look at interactions between community members and dispatchers through these platforms. To investigate, researchers analyzed the system logs of LiveSafe, a community safety tool, combining quantitative and qualitative methods to identify patterns in the conversational flow. By developing a data framework that captured common incident-related information, researchers discovered dispatchers requested specific details from users, which varied based on incident types. Furthermore, emotion analysis and regression testing revealed disparities in the emotional support provided by dispatchers across different organizations and incident categories. Notably, dispatchers who showed emotional support received higher response rates and faster responses from users. These results have provided significant knowledge to practitioners and system designers, inspiring the development of AI-powered tools to enhance human service quality.

To analyze the impact of external magnetization on doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$ with spin-triplet nematic superconductivity, we computationally investigate magnetic field-dependent spin tunneling spectroscopy. Our study demonstrates that this technique is exceptionally sensitive to the inherent topology of the triplet nematic superconducting state. Additionally, we optimize tunneling symmetry and orientation to clearly distinguish between triplet and conventional singlet superconductivity. Our analysis further indicates that sufficient magnetic fields can induce a significant increase in tunneling current at certain bias voltages, providing a valuable means of measuring the superconducting order parameter in natively unconventional superconductors.

Label-efficient active learning algorithms query specific, representative samples to be annotated by a human. Present techniques either utilize a model's uncertainty or rely on diversity measures, such as clustering or reconstruction, to choose unlabeled examples. However, model uncertainty-based methods require precise models, and diversity-based methods can be costly to implement and may overlook key information. To address these issues, we introduce a new approach that combines the benefits of previous techniques with minimal added complexity. We consider both uncertainty and diversity when selecting examples to label, while also taking into account the annotation costs associated with each sample. This cost-aware strategy enables efficient resource allocation and accurate prediction results even with a flawed model. Experimental validation on text classification and image classification datasets demonstrates the effectiveness of our proposed method.

To study how music changed over time from the year 1960 to 2010, we measured the
variety of songs in the Million Song Dataset using several elements, including
melodic quality, texture, volume, and rhythmic patterns. By utilizing random
sampling of songs from both a broader dataset and a specific subset of
commercially successful tracks, we aimed to analyze the musical characteristics
found elsewhere in the dataset. The findings showed that commercially popular
songs released between 1960-2010 generally followed a consistent pattern of
increasing complexity in terms of melody, texture, and volume, despite some
fluctuations, whereas less commercially successful tracks exhibited more
unpredictable trends. The analysis also revealed that songs with higher sales
peaked at frequencies around 250 Hz, while less commercially successful tracks
peaked at lower frequencies and less consistent patterns overall. The study
confirmed previous research on music's evolving characteristics and identified
possible mechanisms by explaining the findings through musical preferences and
the role of successful artists.

A novel category of stochastic processes that incorporate reinforcement involves sequences of random events where each event may generate a new element in an existing group or create a new group. The decision to add an element to an existing group or start a new group is determined by a probability function governed by a multiparametric process. The distribution of group sizes is analyzed under two different scenarios: one where the process restarts from a beginning state after each iteration, and one where the process continues without resetting. The result shows that the probability of an element joining an existing group rather than creating a new group follows a multiparametric process, and the resulting group size distribution converges to a specific pattern, dependent on the original number of groups.

Prawitz identified a key feature of Gentzen's intuitionistic natural deduction as the inversion principle, typically paired in proof-theoretic literature with the recovery principle. This paper presents an alternative, by reformulating both principles into a single requirement, referred to as the harmony condition, within the context of the Computational Ludics framework. This new framework illuminates the underlying notions: that the inversion principle embodies containment, while the recovery principle serves as its converse. Additionally, this paper derives and demonstrates the equivalence of the harmony condition with two further conditions defined in the Computational Ludics framework.

A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via comparative evaluations, but their broader adoption is hindered by the expense and labor intensity of these comparisons. To overcome this limitation, we propose grouping multiple comparisons together and allowing human labelers to mark sub-regions of a condensed state space representation, thereby efficiently leveraging human time. Through data visualization techniques, we create an interactive interface for users to label these regions, thereby effectively enhancing the learning agents' performance. Our approach demonstrates a notable improvement in labeling productivity and quality for users, thereby holding promise for optimizing reward learning.

We show that a topological space's Smyth powerspace is core-compact if and only if the original space has local compactness. Consequently, this implies the Smyth powerspace does not uniformly preserve core-compact properties.

We're investigating singular vorticities in ideal two-dimensional fluids with specific properties derived from point vortices and vortex sheets. These characteristics are embodied in "pointed vortex loops," allowing us to concentrate on their corresponding orbits under area-preserving diffeomorphisms on the 2D plane. The results show that a specific subgroup within these diffeomorphisms preserves the shape of the vortex loop itself, indicating the configuration space of the vortex loop is divided into finitely many distinct components. Additionally, we identify the subgroups that act transitively on the vortex loop configuration space and determine the topological structures of the corresponding diffeomorphic classes, revealing either a torus, a sphere, or a product of these two manifolds as the configuration space in the various components.

The Average Treatment Effect (ATE) is a causal parameter that can be estimated in two steps, initially modeling treatment and outcome to incorporate potential non-linearities, followed by combining the predictions in a specified manner. Notably, the All Pay Inverse Probability Weighting method, though efficient, requires knowledge of the best predictor for the treatment to function properly. We propose an efficient and simple alternative, sharing key characteristics with AIPW: being consistent, having zero expected value, and being applicable in both simple and complex models. This new estimator can also be interpreted as a form of reverse engineering AIPW and offers potential avenues for further enhancement. Our method, named nAIPW, uses the predicted treatment and outcome means from the initial models to form an estimate that is comparable to AIPW. The key difference lies in how the expected outcomes are modeled, with nAIPW utilizing models that are orthogonal to a linear trend, as opposed to AIPW, which requires knowledge of the best predictor for the treatment. The efficiency of nAIPW is confirmed by theoretical evidence that shows its variance is less than or equal to AIPW's variance under specific conditions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of nAIPW through numerical simulations and introduce a possible improvement, named MA2, that uses the residuals from the initial models to form an estimate that is both efficient and easier to compute.

The role of $\tau$ is taking center stage in the current research into lepton flavor universality violations in B-physics, warranting greater theoretical attention in the coming years. Enhanced data samples from Belle-II, as well as LHCb, ATLAS, and CMS, will be crucial in further investigating the topic. Additionally, insights from $\tau$ decays into itself might provide clues to new physics, with the advent of more precise measurements from future $\tau$ charm factories and the LEPS TRITON facility. This presentation will summarize our current understanding and highlight the potential for future advancements in the field.

A tabletop-sized rotating annulus setup has been extensively studied to mimic the general circulation of mid-latitude atmospheric circulation. The device effectively replicates two crucial factors contributing to cyclogenesis, namely the influence of rotation and temperature variations, in a simple yet comprehensive arrangement. The laboratory model enables researchers to control and analyze the formation of baroclinic waves through adjustments in temperature gradients and rotational rates, thereby creating distinctive wave patterns at the free surface of the rotating liquid. These experiments were conducted alongside numerical simulations of the incompressible rotating shallow-water equations, leading to a deeper understanding of the model's behavior and the development of stable, long-lasting waves that could not be replicated in atmospheric models.

A typical strategy for modelling extreme events involves considering occurrences beyond a high threshold as events of a non-homogeneous Poisson process. While this method has the advantage of using threshold-independent extreme value parameters, it comes with the challenge of parameter interdependence, making estimation more complicated. We introduce a novel approach to estimating the parameters of the Poisson process in a Bayesian framework, by transforming them using a tuning parameter'm'. This study develops a technique for selecting the optimal'm' value, which results in the simplest model possible, by applying a version of the weakly informative prior distribution approach. We also develop methods to test the goodness of our model based on the smallest possible Fisher-Snedecor distribution values. A simulation of known parameters and real data using the daily maximum rainfall of Paris as an example show the effectiveness of our approach.

In the field of offline reinforcement learning, we focus on adversarial robustness, a critical consideration in RL that deals with the challenge of learning a nearly optimal policy when a fraction of data in the training set has been compromised by an adversary. Our study begins by examining a worst-case scenario involving the linear Markov decision process and finding that even with the adversary only modifying the reward in each data tuple, a certain threshold of optimality gap cannot be avoided. Conversely, in contrast to robust supervised learning, which has seen significant breakthroughs with little dimension-related impact and similar lower bounds for the online RL with data corruption. Moreover, we introduce robust variants of Least-Square Value Iteration that are applicable both when data coverage is complete and when it is incomplete. These robust LSVO variants show promising performance, but in instances of data incompleteness, we require prior knowledge of epsilon for the bonus of pessimism to function. Unexpectedly, we discovered that the adaptability to the value of epsilon when its value is not previously known does not necessarily lead to a higher threshold of optimality gap, which indicates there is still more to be discovered in this area.

This study demonstrates a logarithmic convexity linked to observability at a specific point in time for a one-dimensional heat equation under dynamic boundary conditions, leading to impulse approximate controllability in similar scenarios with dynamic boundaries. Additionally, we provide a detailed estimate for the cost of impulse control. Our research includes a step-by-step procedure for finding the impulsive control of minimal L^2-norm and supports these findings with numerical tests to verify the efficiency of the developed algorithm.

A consensus has not been established on the definition and optimal detection methods for out-of-distribution examples despite general agreement on their importance. We identified distinct behaviors of two major detection methods - model calibration and density estimation - in response to background and semantic shifts in data, which were found across various language understanding datasets. In our evaluation, density estimation outperformed model calibration in background shift scenarios but struggled with semantic shifts, with both approaches underperforming when confronted with challenge data, underscoring a need for clearer definitions in method comparison.

In recent years, various artificial molecular motors utilizing electric currents have been explored, and like Brownian machines, they generate directional rotation from random tunneling events. Despite their potential to drive molecular machines of the future, their theoretical modeling is understudied. Here, we create a mathematical model for simulating these systems and verify its validity by applying it to a renowned molecular motor, where the model accurately reproduces existing experimental findings. Furthermore, we utilize our model to extract hard-to-determine microscopic properties and examine the influence of electric currents. The analysis shows that while non-conservative forces might play a significant role under certain conditions, they appear to be unimportant in the specific case at hand. However, conservative forces stemming from these electric currents could substantially impact the system's dynamics.

Building on a 2014 framework, researchers introduced various interpretations of transducer behavior, including origins, paths, and runs, which offered distinct decidability outcomes for two equivalence problems related to transducers. In contrast, another interpretation, referred to as the'reach' semantics, yielded the same classification of decidability as traditional transducer equivalence. This notion, however, lacks clear implications for two equivalent transducer types. In this research, we introduce an enhanced'reach' semantics that accounts for entire sequences generated by transducers. Similar to the original'reach' semantics, this enhanced version results in the same classification of decidability for two equivalence problems related to transducers. However, we also demonstrate that this enhanced semantics does not imply the same conclusions as the original'reach' semantics. Additionally, we explore how to approximate origins based on path information and establish a connection to the computational complexity of two related problems.

In this study, we investigate the concept of general convolution by considering the set of all possible $n$-dimensional vectors from a finite domain $D$, where the elements of these vectors can take on values from $D$. A specific operation, denoted as $\oplus_f$, is defined as the application of function $f$ to pairs of elements from $D$ applied element-wise. This enables us to define a new convolution, known as the $f$-Convolution, for two functions $g$ and $h$, each mapping $n$-dimensional vectors from $D$ to integers between $-M$ and $M$. By applying $\oplus_f$ to pairs of $n$-dimensional vectors, $g \otimes_f h$ can be calculated, resulting in a function that maps $n$-dimensional vectors from $D$ to integers between $-M^2$ and $M^2$. A naive approach for computing the $f$-Convolution would involve exhaustive enumeration, requiring roughly $\mathrm{poly}(|D|^n, M)$ time. This study presents a new algorithm that computes the $f$-Convolution in roughly $\mathrm{poly}(|D|, M, \mathrm{polylog}(n))$ time. By leveraging this improved algorithm, we are able to strengthen prior results for the #Sum problem, a known challenge in the field, thereby establishing a new #Sum

The discovery of T-dwarf GJ 229B in 1995 offered initial insight into its composition, yet a detailed analysis with current spectroscopic methods has been lacking, especially concerning its atmospheric features, which display unusual properties and the treatment of methane's strong absorption effects has been suboptimal. To resolve this, we employed the utilization of a sum-of-Gaussians approach to model methane's absorption and employed a Bayesian analysis to determine the atmospheric parameters of GJ 229A, taking into consideration the systematic uncertainties associated with the instrument and the standard assumption of no systematic bias. This analysis revealed a best-fit solution of $T_{\mathrm{eff}}$ = 913$\pm$68 K and $M_{\mathrm{mass}}$ = 31.83$\pm$3.10 $M_J$. When comparing our findings to earlier studies using outdated models, we noticed that GJ 229B's mass was previously overestimated by a margin of about 40\% and our analysis resulted in a final best-fit solution of $M_{\mathrm{mass}}$ = 66.8$\pm$3.3 $M_J$. This new analysis presents the most accurate constraints on GJ 229B's mass to date.

To search for the potential existence of the unique $0^{--}$ state, we created a systematic approach to designing tetraquark operators. In the process, we found that $0^{+-}$ tetraquark operators without derivatives are not possible. Due to the distinct Lorentz structure of the $0^{--}$ currents, it is prevented from incorporating gluon operators into its operators. A series of explicit calculations in quark level were carried out, utilizing a four-quinquilinear structure to group the hadronic $0^{--}$ currents. These were then computed at the level of hadrons, resulting in the decay process $\rho \to \pi \pi$ as an example. A notable observation was made that the exotic $0^{+-}$ state, assuming it exists below 2 GeV, would likely be difficult to find.

A crucial goal of the LHCb experiment is to establish the $C\!P$-violating phase $\phi_{s}$ and decay width difference $\Delta\Gamma_{s}$ caused by $\bar{b}\to\bar{c}c\bar{s}$ decays. The precise prediction of $\phi_{s}$ within the Standard Model makes it a favorable means for detecting signs of new physics. The experiment's $\phi_{s}$ and $\Delta\Gamma_{s}$ measurements are discussed in detail, encompassing the 2011-2012 data set of 3.0~fb$^{-1}$. Future analyses are expected to contribute significantly through the incorporation of additional results derived from decay modes with reduced branching fractions.

Airborne transmission risk in confined environments like buses is intricately affected by the interplay between turbulent airflow, respiration processes, coughing, sneezing, evaporation of saliva or mucus, and gravitational effects. To better understand and quantify this risk, we conducted an in-depth analysis of the bus ventilation system, focusing on the aerosol transport dynamics within it. By employing time-dependent air transport equations alongside Stokes' equation and an energy-based aerosol transport model, we aimed to gain insights into the aerosol's motion. Our results, which are predicated on the assumption that aerosol size falls within the respirable range, reveal a complex airflow inside the bus characterized by a quasi-periodic behavior with varying time periods and intense vertical circulation. This led us to identify three distinct air regions - a near-seat layer, a channel layer, and an atmospheric layer - separated by a boundary layer near the bus windows. The former two layers exhibit a quasi-periodic aerosol circulation caused by turbulence, while the atmospheric layer shows minimal vertical aerosol circulation. Our findings also showed a substantial amount of aerosol accumulation in the near-seat and boundary layers, primarily as a result of vertical circulation. Given these observations, we graded different bus parts based on their aerosol transport efficiency and concluded that the driver's seat is most susceptible to aerosol circulation. Our research can serve as a starting point for further studies on airborne disease transmission on buses, ultimately informing public health strategies and policy decisions.

This study has conducted large-scale shell-model computations for $\beta$-decay attributes. We have calculated the nuclear transition rates, nuclear half-lives, and the interplay between different nuclear shells. Our research focused on 42 transition classes and included 28 distinct nuclear states. We have compiled a comprehensive data set of calculated transition rates and simulated spectra for numerous nuclei. This study has yielded reliable predictions for a wide range of nuclei. Our analysis also revealed an intriguing correlation between nuclear shells and the intershell interactions. These findings could contribute to a deeper understanding of the intricate phenomena governing beta decay.

Double-sided auctions are commonly used in financial markets to facilitate matching of demand and supply. Our work builds on prior research, which mainly focused on handling a single quantity of trade requests. To expand this knowledge, we developed methods to support multiple quantity trade requests and established fully formalized matching algorithms for double-sided auctions. These algorithms come with rigorous correctness proofs. Additionally, we formulated new theorems for verifying the uniqueness of an exchange's output, allowing for automatic detection of potential program violations. To ensure the accuracy of our work, all the mathematical proofs were conducted using the Coq proof assistant, which helped to verify that the properties of an abstract stack data structure are preserved.

We utilized heavy quark effective theory to investigate the $F$-wave bottom mesons, applying both theoretical and experimental data to calculate the mass of these mesons. Additionally, by examining the decay widths of bottom mesons, we derived upper limits on their corresponding coupling values. Our research further included constructing Regge trajectories in the planes of angular momentum (J) and squared mass (M^2), yielding predictions that align neatly with Regge theory lines. These outcomes may hold significant implications for future experimental research on this topic.

Michal Szabados initially proposed a theory in his doctoral dissertation. In this current paper, the proposed conjecture is examined by the authors, specifically a Ph.D. hypothesis by Michal Szabados. Initially, the researchers demonstrate that an evaluation could be narrowed down to a periodic structure, defined over a specific and limited character set. It is further established that Szabados's conjecture is true for a considerable class of non-regular patterns. This includes all low-convex patterns of relatively simple complexity.

In modern research on data-driven systems, a primary focus lies on overcoming challenges presented by high-dimensional dynamics, hidden system states, and the presence of nonlinearity.  The dynamic mode decomposition technique has proven valuable in creating models from complex data sets, yet the effectiveness of this method is limited by its assumption that system states are visible and follow linear time-dependent evolution.  Theoretical work has established that, under specific conditions, a form of mode decomposition can be derived from optimal transport principles, capable of handling high-dimensional data with evident linear components.  A novel approach, involving the solution of a non-linear optimization problem, has been developed to accurately model systems with hidden states and complex dynamics.  The application of this method to real-world problems has been demonstrated, including the modeling of a simple fluid flow system and a more complex air flow system near a virtual obstacle.

The timeless appeal of chess persists, with its strategic intricacies still captivating players across the globe, particularly when it comes to mastering the intricacies of Opening Theory which requires extensive knowledge and years of dedicated study. Our innovative approach harnesses the collective wisdom of online chess enthusiasts to provide insights previously reserved for expert chess players. Firstly, we establish a chess opening network that evaluates the similarities between different opening strategies. This helps us identify clusters of commonly used openings and their connections, insights not easily extracted from existing classification systems. Additionally, our model successfully forecasts future opening preferences and verifies these predictions against actual results, demonstrating superior accuracy over random forecasting. Lastly, by utilizing an advanced algorithm, we assess the level of difficulty for different openings and the skills required to execute them proficiently. This groundbreaking study not only transforms our understanding of chess analysis but also makes possible the use of network analysis to provide individualized suggestions for players, helping them improve their gameplay with data-driven opening recommendations tailored to their needs.

This research explores the observational characteristics of millisecond pulsars in terms of their magnetic fields, rotational periods, and masses. Our analysis is grounded in the concept of accretion-induced collapse of white dwarfs within binary star systems, enabling a more nuanced comprehension of millisecond pulsar demographics. Moreover, our findings underscore the significant evolutionary linkage between neutron stars and white dwarfs within stellar binary systems, particularly through the process of accretion-induced collapse.

A method to derive constants of motion beyond local bounds for ODE-based Lagrangian systems is outlined, including a practical example that illustrates its utility for dissipative mechanical systems and its implications on solution existence and behavior under specific assumptions. The framework is further extended to cover Euler-Lagrange equations with order greater than two, yielding new first integrals for particular models, such as the Pais-Uhlenbeck oscillator, paving the way for potential applications in Euler-Lagrange partial differential equations in the future.

Developing free online 3D model collections has facilitated self-directed 3D learning, yet finding a specific model remains challenging. To bridge this gap, we propose an innovative approach, 'AirWire', which enables users to retrieve 3D models by sketching in a virtual reality space through air-doodling. As sketches lack geometric precision, we devised a two-phase classification method that utilizes a combination of deep neural networks to filter relevant models from AirSketch-Database. During training, air-sketches and 3D-object pairs are classified into two categories:'match' or'mismatch'. In the classification phase, a sample 3D object is fed through a trained model, predicting a confidence score for'match' or'mismatch'. We conducted comprehensive tests, demonstrating the model's performance in retrieving 3D models through air-doodling.

HD80606b, a planet that passes directly in front of its host star, undergoes a significant 1000-fold increase in the heat it receives from the star when it reaches its closest point in its highly elliptical orbit. This intense heat causes the planet's atmosphere to expand, which in turn causes the planet's equator to rapidly heat up and lead to a pronounced atmospheric compression and deformation. Observations of the planet's transit and as it reaches its closest point, known as periastron, have shown a prolonged duration of the transit of almost a day, and further analysis using specific filters has revealed a 7% decrease in the planet's radius as it approaches the closest point of its orbit, and a radius that expands and contracts in a wave like pattern in a day. These findings have raised questions about the possibility of atmospheric loss on this planet, and whether this could impact future searches for similar planets with highly elliptical orbits that may be suitable for supporting life.

In this investigation, we're looking at how a specific type of matter collapse, governed by a certain relationship between pressure and density, behaves according to the general theory of relativity. The effect of this relationship on the mass function is analyzed in terms of its consistency with the general relativity equations, and we find that when this relationship holds, it's usually difficult to get consistent solutions. The outcomes of this type of collapse are then explored, along with the effect of additional factors, such as pressure in a collapsing cloud. Since accurately modeling such a situation is hard due to lack of information about its dynamics, we look at a simplified case where a cloud's pressure is linked to its density in a certain way, and the result is a family of solutions that are consistent with the general relativity equations and have a consistent mass function.

Using the Iyer-Wald formalism, we have developed a comprehensive method for determining corrections to the extremality bounds and entropy of Kerr-Newman black holes following any arbitrary perturbation. This method involves integrating an effective stress tensor and shows, under certain conditions, the correction is equivalent to the standard stress tensor, thereby illuminating the relationship between extremality corrections and energy conditions. Furthermore, we have demonstrated that to lower the mass of an extremal black hole in a canonical ensemble as stipulated by the weak gravity conjecture, the perturbation must breach the dominant energy condition. We have successfully applied this method to compute higher-order corrections to black holes in anti-de Sitter space and to Kerr black holes.

A key goal in reinforcement learning is to invert a target outcome trajectory to perform the action necessary to generate it.  We've found that existing reinforcement learning methods aren't capable of efficiently learning this inversion when there are complications, such as imperfect predictions of the target trajectory.  To address this limitation, we've developed a new motor learning approach that employs 'end-effect drives' - predicted effects resulting from achieving the goal - rather than the goal itself.  We've applied this approach to a simulation of inverting a target throw trajectory in a 2D environment.  We've discovered that pre-training the agent with goal-driven reinforcement learning before switching to end-effect driven reinforcement learning significantly increases the success of the learning process.  We've also demonstrated that end-effect drives facilitate the transfer of learned skills between similar but distinct scenarios.

A generalized three-dimensional Poincaré algebra has been developed that incorporates colour symmetry. This enhanced algebra can serve as a basis for modelling coloured Poincaré gravity and exploring generalised models of massive and massless free particles in three dimensions. Multiple generalised particle models have been presented, which distinguish themselves in terms of the coloured Poincaré orbits they describe. Our methodology provides a potential pathway to describing particles in non-abelian backgrounds and serves as a starting point for the worldline formulation of an associated quantum field theory.

We have devised three new parameterized algorithms for identifying whether a directed graph can be represented in an upward planar layout. Specifically, we've developed a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the number of source vertices, an XP algorithm based on the graph's treewidth, and a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the treedepth parameter. Our novel method combines parameterized techniques with SPQR tree-decompositions, extending previous tractability findings on series-parallel graphs, single-source graphs, and outerplanar graphs.

Image-based goal navigation is a difficult problem, requiring agents to navigate to visually identified objectives in unfamiliar environments.
Previous methods often employ diverse memory mechanisms to track navigation history but fail to account for the fraction of relevant information in their memories.
We propose the MemoNav, a novel memory-based navigation framework, designed to improve performance in multi-goal scenarios by selectively retaining both short-term and long-term memories.
The short-term memory in MemoNav stores dynamic agent topological maps, updated as navigation progresses. To augment this memory, a graph attention module aggregates past short-term memories to generate long-term memories.
A forgetting module using a Transformer decoder retains only the informative fraction of the short-term memory, ensuring that the agent does not overrely on past experiences.
Our experiments demonstrate that MemoNav outperforms state-of-the-art models by maintaining more efficient short-term memories and effectively integrating them into long-term memories to facilitate goal achievement.

To increase cellular capacity, operators initially implemented 4G LTE small cells (Femto Cells) by reusing the same licensed spectrum. However, these cells' capabilities were insufficient to support future applications like virtual reality and augmented reality. As a result, operators have sought unlicensed spectrum in the 5 GHz Wi-Fi band, with LAA being the name later assigned by 3GPP. Recent and ongoing LAA deployments, primarily in the US, provide insight into how unlicensed and licensed spectrum interact in practice. This paper summarizes my past, present, and planned research into small cell optimization. Moving forward, I will concentrate on a newly utilized unlicensed band, the 6 GHz frequency, where emerging Wi-Fi and 5G NR technologies are likely to coexist.

We've developed a comprehensive framework to model complex interactions between multiple entangled systems using hypergraphs. This approach can be applied to several processes and we'll specifically explore how certain conditions lead to spontaneous pattern emergence in systems where individual units interact with each other. Our focus will be on two specific settings: one involving interactions between groups over long distances, and another with diffusive interactions between units. Additionally, we'll demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework through applications to both the generalized Volterra system and the Brusselator model.

This study examines the operator growth phenomenon in Lie-symmetric systems by utilizing concepts from quantum information theory. We specifically focus on the scaling of operator entanglement following the adiabatic turn-on of a boundary Hamiltonian across the entire system. Our analysis, based in part on the Kohn-Sham basis, reveals the intricate relationship between operator growth and entanglement properties. We also explore this connection in both local and entangled operator phases, turning on the Hamiltonian from a central point and observing the resulting growth of operators. Our work is related to recent research on operator growth in open quantum systems, such as the Hatano-Nelson chain and the spin-bath model.

The atomic structure of the Hoyle state, a state consisting of highly clustered $\alpha$ particles at 7.65 MeV in $^{12}\mathrm{C}$, has been a topic of interest for a long time. The question of whether this phenomenon consists of three coupled $\alpha$ particles or an excited state of the 9.58 MeV 0$^{+}_2 level of $^{12}\mathrm{C}$ has not been fully answered. Our analysis of the decay pathways of the Hoyle state, including the relative strength of its direct and overall decay rates, is crucial in resolving this issue. By employing a microscopic two-cluster approach and using the Gaussian Effective Interaction (GEI) model, we were able to calculate the decay widths of the Hoyle state and its neighboring states. Our results show that the direct decay rate of the Hoyle state is significantly lower than its overall decay rate, which implies that the Hoyle state has a high degree of cluster condensation. Our findings also suggest that the 9.58 MeV 0$^{+}_2 state of $^{12}\mathrm{C}$, which is thought to be an excited state of the three-$\alpha$ particle system, has a low degree of cluster condensation and may be stabilized by the effects of the Brody-Moshinsky matrix.

Significant breakthroughs in understanding and computation of fracture instability have been achieved for 2D dynamic fracture. The essence of this advancement is the identification of intrinsic scales in energy-release rate and energy-uptake rate that drive the most likely path of crack propagation. We extend this progress to 3D, establishing a new set of equations that describe the most likely crack trajectory and propagate it accordingly. The validity of our approach is confirmed by having components that are equivalent to those in the 2D case. Through explicit numerical testing on various shapes, such as a triangular applied stress pattern, a bell-shaped applied stress pattern, and a stress concentration at a small hole, we show that our 3D algorithm can accurately reproduce the results of existing methodologies. The implementation of this new approach is available online for others to use.

In a general setting, we examine the properties of finite state channels equipped with feedback and state information, which becomes available to the encoder in a predictable sequence. This encompasses a broad range of channels, including memoryless channels with independent and identically distributed states (referred to as the Shannon strategy), channels with Markovian states that offer the ability to access past states (known as look-ahead access) and energy constraints at the encoder. The concept of feedback capacity is first extended to a sequence of finite state channels with no state information, where the channel outputs are known to the encoder in advance. It is also shown that the channel with look-ahead access has the same capacity as the original finite state channel when the channel states can be accessed. Furthermore, this research confirms a previously proposed lower bound for the feedback capacity of a general DSMC and shows that this bound can be precise under specific conditions. Finally, a survey of previous work on non-stationary channels is conducted, where key findings and challenges associated with non-stationary channels are highlighted.

A novel class of superconductors featuring antisymmetric spin-orbit coupling and placed within a Zeeman magnetic field may be used to create fault-tolerant quantum computations via topologically non-Abelian states. Employing a quantum Monte Carlo dynamical cluster approximation, we analyzed the effects of Rashba spin-orbit coupling and Zeeman field on superconductivity in a two-dimensional attractive Hubbard model with doping. Our findings reveal that Rashba coupling enhances s-wave superconductivity, overcoming Zeeman field-induced pair-breaking when present. Additionally, we demonstrate that Rashba coupling counteracts the spin-imbalanced pair-breaking effect, precisely as seen in spin-orbit coupled systems with no magnetic fields. Lastly, we show that under non-local coupling conditions the Rashba coupling effect further amplifies s-wave superconductivity, yielding a notable enhancement of approximately 50% in the critical Zeeman field required for pair-breaking.

This work focuses on understanding and interpreting tables, requiring the ability to recognize their structure and compare cell information effectively. To address this challenge, we introduced a new dataset for verifying factual information and a detailed classification system to measure accuracy in different aspects of factual checks. By employing a two-part approach consisting of fact collection and evaluation, we classified the task into two main tasks and developed a new benchmark using a dataset with over 7,000 items. This dataset covers various topics like entertainment, education, and medicine from Wikipedia and includes tables from news sources like The New York Times. With a testing phase involving human assessors and a complex machine learning model as our baseline, we were able to establish a new benchmark for measuring the performance of machines in verifying factual information in tables.

This analysis explores the essential role of complex numbers in Quantum Mechanics, delving into common justifications for complex formalism and offering additional perspectives to support its necessity. By examining these factors, we hope to clarify the underlying reasoning for employing complex numbers in Quantum mechanics.

A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint each vertex uniquely by determining their distance to every point in R. A sub-set of R that does this best with the fewest points is known as the minimum identifying set or "metric dimension" of the graph. Here we discuss the version of this property where the shortest distances between points are capped at some number k and call it beta_k of the graph.

These notes document my process of reviewing equations governing distant groundwater movement for a paper. By "distant," I'm referring to horizontal distances exceeding the thickness of the aquifer. They're based on assumptions discussed later on.
