These equations aren't an original contribution but rather a reference guide for those working with simplified groundwater models in computational fluid dynamics.

This work has investigated the potential of integrating an ozone O3 and ultraviolet (UV) light system with biofilters for effectively eliminating volatile organic compounds (VOCs). A laboratory-scale biofilter was tested, using a mixture of sawdust and sand as its support media, alongside an ozone UV system designed to mirror typical field applications. The results from this study indicate that an ozone UV system at a concentration of 30 mg/m3 can significantly enhance the removal of toluene from gas phases by 25-30%, also notably increasing the H2O/CO2 production rates by 200-300%. The simultaneous application of ozone and UV light was found to exhibit synergistic effects, potentially attributing to the enhancement of microbial growth and activity. Future research aims to examine the effects of various UV wavelengths on the system.

As interest in neuromorphic computing grows, engineers face a key challenge in simulating the technology to evaluate and refine their designs. Testing neural network applications on simulated neuromorphic systems requires significant computational power, making it a crucial benchmark for evaluating different architecture designs. To speed up simulations, leveraging the multi-core capabilities of host systems is essential. This paper proposes a parallelized simulation environment based on SystemC for RISC-V multi-core platforms that incorporates multiple computing-in-memory accelerators for neuromorphic computing. The authors also optimize a neural network inference workload to demonstrate a notable improvement in simulation throughput, from 12.5 to 200 milliseconds, by distributing tasks across both the host and the target platform's cores.

Deploying machine learning in practical scenarios can often present challenges,
mainly stemming from uninterpretable models, questionable reliance on imperfect
data, or offering a sole prediction outcome without considering various
probability outcomes.
  This study proposes the concept of Indecision Trees as a modification of the
existing Decision Trees model. These revised models are designed to learn under
conditions of uncertainty, draw conclusions in uncertain situations, produce
reliable probability distributions over potential labels, and be dissected into
clear, logical arguments that can be applied to other reasoning systems.

The DTW distance is commonly applied in time series analysis across classification, clustering, and similarity search tasks, but its time complexity hinders its scalability. To overcome this, PrunedDTW was introduced, offering improved efficiency by halting DTW early based on anticipated distance above a threshold. While effective, the pruned approach often fails to realize its full optimizing potential, leading to additional computations. In response, EAPrunedDTW has been developed as an enhanced version of PrunedDTW, capable of determining whether DTW can be terminated earlier or yield a precisely defined distance lower than a given target, utilizing an enhanced early assessment strategy. If criteria are met, EAPrunedDTW terminates DTW immediately, or refines the pruned distance otherwise. Experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that EAPrunedDTW boosts the pruned rate of typical PrunedDTW and achieves precise distance results in cases where standard PrunedDTW computed incorrect distances. Overall, EAPrunedDTW offers improved efficiency while maintaining the prunability of PrinedDTW.

Current educational tools used in testing can either provide coverage insights comparable to professional tools or highlight instructor-defined test cases that a student has overlooked. While this feedback has some value, it can lead students to rely on guesswork rather than structured verification techniques. Instead of guiding students towards a more disciplined approach, these tools may actually encourage bad testing habits. Furthermore, many educational environments lack a unified data store to simulate diverse database scenarios, forcing instructors to use multiple tools for different data management systems or replicate the functionality of these platforms, which can result in a disjointed learning experience for testing concepts. To address these challenges, we are developing DBQuiz, a comprehensive, web-based quiz platform that utilizes a central data store to facilitate inquiry-based learning for database testing. By leveraging its data store, DBQuiz can simulate various databases, enabling instructors to create exams that demonstrate the benefits of techniques such as data normalization, primary and foreign keys, and transactions, which are often difficult to model with other educational tools. To demonstrate DBQuiz's effectiveness, we conducted two case studies, one of which involved modifying existing syllabi to demonstrate that, even with limited resources, DBQuiz can enhance teaching and make it easier for students to learn about database testing.

In domains requiring reliability or transparency, explainable AI is increasingly becoming essential for handling the unpredictability of black-box machine learning methods, particularly in healthcare and data protection regulations. However, standard visualizations often fall short due to their inability to differentiate between subtle feature variations or accurately represent the interplay between absent and present features. This issue could be addressed by using more advanced symbolic surrogate models but, since these typically require access to the original training data, we explore an approach that incorporates an intrinsic feature importance measure from a standalone symbolic model based on decision rules. This enables us to preserve a reduced and understandable feature set, thus boosting the understanding of visual explanations for users. Our proposed method utilizes a decision table-based feature importance measure to prioritize features and create comprehensive visual explanations that include both text and icons representing the relative importance of each feature. Our experiments involve understanding the features of medical diagnoses using the Prolog representation of decision-making criteria and demonstrate visual explanations of machine learning classifications that can be easily interpreted and modified.

Over-smoothing significantly constrains the complexity of Graph Convolutional Networks, making it crucial to understand the root cause. A thorough examination of the over-smoothing phenomenon and Graph Convolutional Networks is presented in this article, including an estimation of the upper limit for its occurrence. The study also identifies distinct categories of Graph Convolutional Networks based on their architectures and provides a detailed analysis of the effects of varying network components on the over-smoothing problem.

Dark matter particle research has been conducted using a dataset of Z boson candidates accompanied by a significant amount of undetected energy produced between 2015 and 2016. Data collected by the CMS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider amounts to 25.0 fb^-1 of proton-proton collisions occurring at a 13 TeV energy. By examining two distinct decay paths, ZZ and Zγ, into three and one particle states respectively, researchers have found no evidence to support the standard model's predictions. Based on these findings, scientists set new limits on the interaction of dark matter with other particles, restricting cross-sectional values for certain coupling strengths and dark matter masses less than 1.2 TeV and 1.9 TeV respectively.

We propose a new set of functions tied to $k_\perp$ dependencies that differ from the Boer-Mulders function. These functions are connected to quark spin alignment as a collective phenomenon. Additionally, they depend on the movement of partons in the transverse direction, related to parton spin alignment, which is rooted in the interactions represented by corresponding correlators.

Homeomorphisms with compact support on a Tychonoff space can be given several equivalent topological structures by viewing them as either a group under composition with a fixed compact support or as a subset of its own set of homeomorphisms, topologically arranged by compact support. A space has the C-compactly generated property if these two definitions yield the same topological space. In the paper, it is proven that any space with the C-compactely generated property will also have the extension property, defined by the ability to add a continuous function that maps the space to another space without changing the topological structure. The paper also explores the relationship between this property and being second-countable or locally compact, and includes specific examples of spaces that satisfy one but not the other condition.

Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds significant promise, enabling the synthesis of highly lattice-mismatched materials and reducing waste from expensive substrate reuse. Nevertheless, concrete proof of a remote epitaxial process is yet to be found. Many instances are instead attributed to contaminants between graphene and the substrate, or alternative processes such as van der Waals epitaxy. This study discovered that when growing the Heusler compound GdPtSb on clean graphene substrates, it results in a unique 30 degree rotated superstructure, not explicable through other mechanisms. This rotation domain percentage significantly increases at lower growth temperatures. It's suggested that remote epitaxy occurs due to an electrostatic potential, which creates local curvature on the graphene, leading to a preferential adsorption of the third component (sulfur) and the formation of a curvatures-driven attractive force between the Currie and valence band states of Gd. This leads to a 0D quantum state near the interface, which mediates a strong attractive force between the two components, ultimately driving the epitaxial process.

We analyze how to identify common random patterns in large sets of time series data, even when individual observations are rare or unusual. A new method allows us to make this analysis by solving a complex optimization problem with two variables, subject to certain conditions about how these variables relate to each other. This method gives us accurate estimates of how these patterns change over time, even in cases where the data does not follow a smooth or continuous pattern. As a result, we can conduct comprehensive tests of how these patterns affect each other and whether they have any significant connections. This line of inquiry holds significant potential for analyzing the behavior of financial assets over long periods of time. To implement these methods, we develop a new, efficient computational technique that allows us to apply these methods even with large sets of data. We show through simulation studies that these methods give accurate results and can be used to make accurate predictions about future trends. One of the key applications of these methods is analyzing the behavior of the prices of financial assets, which often follows patterns that are both non-smooth and change rapidly. To demonstrate the effectiveness of these methods, we use them to analyze patterns in the prices of financial assets over the course of the last one hundred years, including monthly prices, monthly returns, and annual stock prices. These analyses reveal many interesting patterns and help to confirm previous observations about how these patterns change over time. One of the key advantages of these methods is that they can be used to analyze not just individual time series, but large sets

Recent JWST observations of El Gordo, the massive galaxy cluster, have identified 23 known groups of multiply distorted galaxy images and 8 previously undiscovered ones, all verified spectroscopically by MUSE. By analyzing these groups, researchers created a lens model which allowed them to locate 37 more groups, comprising 28 new and 9 previously identified systems. Based on the initial lens model, researchers estimated the ages of 37 new groups. Their estimates match available information from both spectral and photometric analysis. Furthermore, the estimated ages allowed two further lens models that incorporate all 60 observed multiply distorted galaxy families and range from redshifts of 2 to 6. Data confirm the earlier double-peak distribution of mass within the cluster and that the northern and southern masses are similar. Data confirm that El Gordo has a mass spanning approximately 3 megaparsecs. Data confirm that the cluster's mass does not change much with redshift. Data confirm that the cluster's inner structure is similar to its outer structure. Data confirm that the cluster has a smooth mass distribution. Data confirm that the cluster's mass is concentrated in its central areas. Data confirm that the cluster has a smooth mass distribution. Data show the cluster has a smooth mass distribution. Data show the cluster has a smooth mass distribution.

Internet Service Providers have long requested that Content Providers contribute financially towards improving network infrastructure, with promises of better Quality of Service. This research examines profit-sharing agreements between a single Content Provider and multiple Internet Service Providers, with the Content Provider agreeing to split profits in exchange for enhanced service quality by the ISPs. We find that for ISPs to invest in better service, the Content Provider must compensate them sufficiently, otherwise, ISPs will choose the lowest cost action and Quality of Service will be subpar, potentially deterring some ISPs from participating in the agreement. We identify specific conditions under which an equilibrium is reached, involving profit-sharing terms that balance the interests of both parties.

The GNS construction forms a correspondence between abstract collections of physical observables in a C*-algebra and associated physical states. This process essentially amounts to a reverse operation to obtain the algebra given a state. We demonstrate that the GNS construction behaves as a kind of inverse procedure for state representation through an abstract adjoint relationship, capturing fundamental aspects of the algebra's underlying properties. This abstract adjoint relationship can be understood within a category theoretical framework, offering a generalized representation of the algebra's underlying structure. This representation is not limited to the specific context of bounded operators on a Hilbert space but can be applied more broadly within the realm of C*-algebras and more general functional spaces.

The $\alpha$-attractor models in inflationary theory hold great promise in the context of upcoming cosmological observations, also having connections to supergravity. Exponential and polynomial models of this type are compared against recent data from the field, particularly with regards to their ability to address the angular scale problem in the cosmic microwave background. The models' predictions are highly consistent with this observational data, also exhibiting versatility in their potential solutions to the weak anthropic gravity fine-tuning problem.

In the context of a quasi-Fuchsian hyperbolic three-dimensional manifold with a boundary that approaches infinity, its foliations measured at infinity directly relate to the horizontal leaves of the natural projection from the manifold's compact core onto its boundary. For a given hyperbolic surface that becomes Fuchsian after a finite number of laminations, adding these measured foliations does not change its hyperbolicity, but it does increase its curvature. There are, however, situations where the additions result in a foliation that is bounded by the surface, causing it to become Fuchsian. These unique combinations, which are relatively rare, occur on certain types of surfaces that have a hyperbolic core that is a tunnel or a fillings sequence.

This study seeks to create advanced mathematical methods and computational tools to model portfolio returns, establishing essential formulas and efficient algorithms using techniques from computational geometry and splines. By leveraging these methods, our approach can efficiently handle large portfolios and accurately compute moments of the probability function within seconds. We primarily focus on the long-only strategy and develop an adaptable method for this type of investment. By representing the stock market as a geometric space, our cumulative distribution function enables a score for each portfolio based on the percentage of its returns exceeding a certain threshold. We derived closed-form equations for the first four moments and an innovative algorithm for computing all other moments, demonstrating a direct connection between the cross-sectional stock market returns and the probability function's moments. All of our methods are highly versatile, covering the scenarios where the cross-sectional returns follow any distribution. Furthermore, our score and moment formulas remain applicable even when the portfolio size exceeds the number of stocks.

Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate abnormality detection from cardiac auscultation sounds is hampered by background noise and the variability of heart conditions.  To address this challenge, a deep learning approach is presented that employs a dual structure to minimize the influence of noise and capture key abnormal heart sound features.  With its ability to adapt to different levels of noise, this method can effectively identify cardiac disorders even when its audio input is obscured by significant noise.  Testing on over 800 cardiac condition recordings reveals that it achieves a high accuracy of 91.7% in identifying condition records, along with an 87% accuracy rate in correctly classifying condition types.  Furthermore, this method demonstrates a 90% success rate in distinguishing condition recordings that have been artificially distorted with noise.  By mitigating the impact of noise and capturing key sound elements, this method offers a powerful tool for diagnosing heart conditions.

In a 2021 study, we had developed a more accurate calculation for a specific nuclear transition in $^{133}$Cs using relativistic coupled-cluster theory. Recently, Roberts and Ginges raised concerns about a part of this calculation that they disagreed with, but it aligns with earlier calculations. In response, we thoroughly justify our method and highlight that all components were treated equally, whereas other calculations relied on sum-over-states methods. Additionally, we address concerns about the approximate treatment of some corrections that were not the main focus, but rather included for completeness, and reiterate that the primary calculation can be improved only by using more sophisticated cluster-cluster diagrams.

A twist is utilized as a localized element in the formulation of topological K-theory. 
Within the framework of equivariant analysis, twists are categorized into four distinct forms, 
which can be visualized as four points within an XY plane. 
This classification is achieved by applying a selection of continuous motions 
that adhere to specific rules, effectively "shaving the elephant" of topological K-theory. 
These continuous motions serve as a means to deform one type of twist into another, 
thus establishing a connection between the four forms of twists. 
This paper provides an in-depth examination of these continuous motions, 
as well as the geometric processes that give rise to them.

Pomona College's Mathematics & Statistics Department has been dedicated to
establishing an inclusive and welcoming environment for all students to
engage in mathematical study. In response to low diversity among majors, the
department initially attempted to address this through targeted programs aimed
at enhancing students' mathematical abilities. Conversely, recent efforts have
shifted to an anti-deficit strategy, which prioritizes modifying the
department's internal culture to foster a more cohesive community. Our
initiatives to boost collaboration, atmosphere, and overall department
climate are detailed below.

We examine the boundedness of the fractional series operator $T_{\gamma}$, with its given function form $(T_{\gamma}b)(j)$, in the context of $H^{p}(\mathbb{Z})$ to $\ell^{q}(\mathbb{Z})$. Furthermore, a counter-example demonstrates that the operator $T_{\gamma}$ does not yield a bounded mapping from $H^{p}(\mathbb{Z})$ to $H^{q}(\mathbb{Z})$.

This study offers the first empirical evaluation of the influence of auction format integrity on bidding tactics and outcome profitability. Through a controlled lab experiment where human auction participants earn revenue, we assess whether a credible or uncredible auction environment impacts bidding. We discover that the majority of bids in an uncredible second-price auction occur within the revenue-maximizing range of both a credible second-price auction and a first-price auction. Sellers often deviate from the auction rules, but when participating in an uncredible auction, typically don't prioritize maximizing revenue. We explain the outcomes of our experiment using a theory that combines bidder misperception and a seller's reluctance to break auction rules, as confirmed by a test of actual preferences.

The explanation of accelerated cosmology is partially satisfactory but challenges to understanding the universe's early development persist. Our research focuses on the promising potential of a new symmetric teleparallel theory of gravity, denoted as $f(Q)$, where the non-metricity scalar $Q$ facilitates gravitational interactions and addresses the issue of gravitational screening. To study the universe's initial phase, we establish a model based on a specific type of spacetime with the complete set of embedded spaces having spherical symmetry. By solving the resulting equations in the framework of a specific $f(Q)$ model, we model a universe with its own gravitational dynamics, which is consistent with observational evidence that a universe existed before the Big Bang. Our research also reveals implications for the Friedmann equations and the relationship between energy density and Hubble's constant, which are observed to differ from the Big Bang cosmology's fundamental principles. Our findings demonstrate that a universe with its own gravitational dynamics is possible, and this has significant theoretical and observational repercussions.

We initiate a study of local defining ideals of Hessenberg varieties, specifically focusing on regular nilpotent Hessenberg varieties of type A, utilizing an affine coordinate chart based on the maximal element of the Weyl group corresponding to GL(n,ℂ). Key findings include the following. Firstly, we prove that the local defining ideal associated to a given Hessenberg function within this specific coordinate system can be decomposed into vertices. Furthermore, combining our result with existing work on generators, we demonstrate that this set of generators constitutes a Gröbner basis for this local defining ideal under a suitable monomial order. Lastly, applying our analysis, we derive an explicit splitting of the associated fiber product, encapsulating the local defining ideals of all Hessenberg varieties of type A within this specific coordinate system.

Neural Painters, utilizing a GAN-based approach, generate brushstrokes that are assembled into paintings. Despite GANs' superiority in AI-generated art, their training can be exceptionally challenging. To address these difficulties and accelerate Neural Painter training, we employed Transfer Learning, achieving a notable time reduction from days to just hours without compromising visual quality. Our findings are presented in this study.

We tackle current, striking discrepancies in flavor anomalies within the Standard Model, specifically with CP-violating Kaon decay and lepton-flavor universality violation in $b\to s\ell\ell$ transitions, through a multifaceted approach. Our primary tool is a low-energy symmetry, known as $G_{23}$, that arises from a set of high-energy transformations characterized by the $G_{23}$ symmetry. As a result, the Wilson coefficients of several operators are constrained by this symmetry, leading to relationships between CP-violating Kaon decay and $b\to s\ell\ell$ transitions. Our analysis shows that this approach resolves the epsilon' / epsilon anomaly at the experimental values and predicts the outcomes of forthcoming CP-violating Kaon decay experiments. Furthermore, the framework also constrains $R_{K^{(*)}}$ in line with the LHCb's observations and is compatible with the Littlest Higgs model with a dark gauge boson (LHDM+) with a heavy $b'$ boson.

Academic researchers who read research papers usually seek specific information to answer particular questions, but current systems fail to efficiently provide the desired information due to their limited ability to reason complex relationships between paper sections. Developing effective Question Answering tools necessitates large datasets that capture the challenging nature of this task, including interpreting claims from multiple parts of a document. Unlike traditional information-seeking datasets that typically consist of fact-based questions, the proposed QASPER dataset contains a diverse range of questions over 1,585 NLP research papers. These 5,049 questions were posed by NLP specialists who relied only on paper titles and abstracts, requiring answers that would appear in the full paper, accompanied by supportive evidence from separate NLP practitioners. We observed significant performance disparities between existing models that excel in other Question Answering tasks and human capabilities, with models struggling to answer these queries by at least 27 F1 points when using the entire paper, underscoring the importance of further investigation into document-grounded, information-seeking Question Answering, an area where the QASPER dataset can play a pivotal role.

In order to understand fast neutrino flavor instability in supernova events, researchers studied an axisymmetric, neutrino-driven explosion in a core-collapse supernova.  This fast instability occurs when neutrinos escape from a region where neutrino spheres would ideally exist.  It was found through simulations that this fast instability only develops under specific conditions and requires considerable amounts of neutrinos and a specific geometry to manifest.  This involves neutrinos being deposited into a region near the center of the proto-neutron star, and where matter is dense and convection is active.  When this condition is met, a fast instability can occur, leading to an explosion in the scenario simulated.  This has implications for how we predict and understand supernova events, particularly in how neutrinos and other processes contribute to it.

ADHD is a widely prevalent psychiatric condition that has been challenging to diagnose accurately. The advancement in computational capabilities and machine learning techniques has enabled researchers to investigate the use of resting-state fMRI imaging data for classifying ADHD. In contrast to prior studies that relied on the entire brain, this study aimed to optimize ADHD diagnosis by identifying and prioritizing the most relevant brain regions. Using data from the ADHD-200 Global competition, this study leveraged deep learning models to create robust features from RS-fMRI data and conducted an extensive search over multiple classification models and feature extractors. The results revealed that a simplified model featuring 18 key regions of interest achieved the best classification performance, surpassing existing state-of-the-art methods by 2%. More importantly, this study demonstrated that reducing the number of brain areas did not significantly lower the classification accuracy, ultimately yielding an error rate of 75.8% for the optimal model. By pinpointing the crucial regions of interest and refining the classification systems, this study facilitated the development of more efficient, user-friendly ADHD diagnosis systems.

In a discrete-time epidemic SISI model where population growth is constant and balanced, the per capita mortality and fertility rates are equivalent, and the model's evolution operator is a nonlinear function of seven parameters. When we reduce this operator to a quadratic stochastic one, we show that it has a unique interior fixed point and examine the long-term trajectory behavior under specific conditions regarding the model parameters.

Acronyms and abbreviations serve as shorter versions of lengthy phrases, commonly found across diverse writing mediums. While they are instrumental in saving space and time in written communication, they also introduce comprehension hurdles if not clearly defined, particularly if the acronym's origin is unclear in lengthy texts. To address this, concerted efforts from both researchers and software developers are directed at creating systems capable of accurately identifying and interpreting acronyms within various contexts. This report summarizes a competition held on processing acronyms and abbreviations, hosting a competition where participants contributed 21 submissions.

Quantum interference, evident in low-dimensional systems, is one of the most notable manifestations of quantum physics. Recent findings have shown that phase-coherent phenomena are not limited to charge transport and can also occur in heat transport. This discovery has prompted us to investigate heat transfer and electrical conductivity in systems of two coupled quantum wires with varying lengths. Using a text-based simulation, we examined how these systems behave under different scenarios and observed that the simulation accurately represents both thermal and electrical properties. Moreover, we were able to simulate two distinct physical experiments: a time-dependent measurement and a study of a system subjected to a temperature gradient. Our simulation revealed a surprising correlation between heat and current fluctuations. Despite differing time scales, both effects are rooted in the same physical phenomenon. By validating our simulation against existing experimental data, we demonstrated its reliability and effectiveness.

Our proposed DNA-storage system presents a new, flexible structure that establishes a hierarchical relationship among data objects identified by the same primer pair and facilitates efficient data revisions. Unlike existing approaches, in this architecture a pair of twenty base PCR primers no longer defines a singular object, but rather a distinct, independently managed storage segment with its own index. We've discovered that, although there are limited sets of primer pairs compatible with one another, each segment offers essentially limitless storage potential. Our design leverages this versatility to provide enhanced and versatile data storage properties, including organized hierarchical data and efficient data updates with flexibility. Furthermore, to fully utilize the prefix-based nature of PCR addressing, we've developed a method for converting any indexing system into a compatible PCR format. This enables us to utilize primers that can be variably extended to include desired parts of the index, allowing us to precisely locate specific objects within a segment with minimal scope, resulting in the reduction of sequencing costs by up to 140x for the retrieval of smaller data objects.

Topological insulators represent a significant phenomenon in modern condensed matter research, characterized by exceptional properties of exotic matter states that facilitate unidirectional and unobstructed electron flow while blocking it in the interior of the material. Current research has revealed that certain characteristics of topological insulators, such as the spin Hall effect and the transverse photoresponse, can also be replicated in rare-earth ferromagnets using external stimuli like light. By combining theoretical calculations and experimental measurements, our study examines the presence of the light-induced spin Hall effect and the transverse photoresponse in the rare-earth ferromagnet EuFe2As2. The results of our research show that in EuFe2As2, the application of a laser beam results in a vector field that varies laterally and is aligned perpendicular to the beam, which can be modified by adjusting the polarization of the light. The presence of this vector field can induce a lateral current of spin and a longitudinal magnetization, which can be observed and controlled through the adjustment of the laser's polarization. The unique properties of this vector field make EuFe2As2 an appealing material for the construction of spin-based optoelectronic devices and the investigation of related phenomena, such as the generation of magnons and the interaction of light with magnetization.

In oscillatory media, regions that oscillate faster than their surroundings can give rise to outgoing waves, which are crucial for synchronization across entire systems and are prevalent in many biological and chemical processes. These waves, typically triggered by pacemaker-generated activity, serve as a means of transmitting information at a constant speed over extended distances. This research utilizes advanced analytical tools to explore the determinants of wave velocity, focusing specifically on singular perturbation and phase reduction techniques in the context of two distinct types of oscillators, one built on bistability and the other featuring time delay in negative feedback mechanisms. We examine how temporal separation of oscillatory scales impacts resulting wave speeds and assess the influence of pacemaker size and oscillation frequency. Our analytical findings are further validated by numerical simulations described previously, which were designed to model this phenomenon.

A fundamental concept, entropy, has significant implications in both classical and quantum physics and computer science, leading to diverse applications across theoretical and practical domains. The focus is on determining approximations within a factor $\gamma > 1$ of the Shannon entropy in probability distributions and the von Neumann entropy in mixed quantum states. The key contributions are two algorithms: a quantum one for approximating Shannon entropy that requires $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{\frac{1+\eta}{2\gamma^2}})$ queries, and another for approximating von Neumann entropy that necessitates $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1+\eta}{2\gamma^2}})$ queries. These results hold provided the entropy is bounded away from zero by a quantity linked to $\eta > 0$, and a no-go result indicates the non-existence of polynomial query algorithms for distributions with very low entropy. The analysis considers the most general input model - the quantum purified query access model - enabling handling of both classical distributions and quantum states. The study also accounts for the statistical measurement uncertainty when estimating entropy, leading to improved understanding of its estimation.

Implementing and deploying effective artificial intelligence (AI), particularly deep learning, necessitates substantial datasets for training, testing, and validation processes. Establishing comprehensive data collections, annotated in accordance with standardized protocols, necessitates the setup of imaging biobanks to ensure organized access. Achieving this, however, involves intricate design, careful compliance with current regulatory frameworks and technical standards to facilitate seamless data management. Simply collecting and storing imaging data does not suffice; additional value is derived from providing accompanying clinical data and technical image acquisition parameters to enhance data utility. To address these complexities, a recommended reference architecture for AI data processing and management has been developed, featuring specific components that cater to imaging data management and incorporate AI-specific elements. This framework is now being utilized in the establishment of multiple imaging biobanks across Europe.

Physicians' written assessments and interviews with patients, stored as unstructured clinical text notes (CTNs), have been analyzed by recent studies using machine learning techniques to forecast diagnoses based on nine possible outcomes. This research confirms that these advancements have delivered high levels of accuracy in specifying diagnoses from CTNs, a process known as ICD coding. A novel diagnostic system was developed using neural networks to identify ICD codes from raw CTN data without pre-processing or labels from a single country. Its effectiveness was confirmed by evaluating the model's ability to recognize and encode ICD codes by comparing its output with what actual physicians encoded during the initial assessment process. Further validation involved verifying the model's agility in adapting to new data from different regions by comparing its performance on data from an unfamiliar area. Overall, this research validated the use of deep learning-based models for encoding ICD codes from CTNs, a process known as deep ICD coding (DIC).

Let $R$ be a polynomial ring in $n$ variables over a field $k$. A monomial ideal $I$ within this ring is considered. This paper explores almost Cohen-Macaulay simplicial complexes and provides specific classifications for certain types of ideals, including polymatroidal Veronese type and transversal polymatroidal ideals, along with illustrative examples.

Due to the diverse applications of machine learning, its ability to identify patterns in datasets is well-regarded, yet it often overlooks the underlying rules within these datasets. Developing an algorithm capable of discovering these underlying rules using classical methods is complex and often requires extensive expertise. We propose a protocol that uses a quantum computing approach to process data, potentially accelerating the analysis by a factor of thousands to millions. The protocol, inspired by the search algorithm of the quantum simulation of animal cognition, leverages quantum fluctuations to generate possibilities that then undergo a classical filtering process to exclude impractical solutions. Following this, the remaining possibilities are ranked using a quantum-inspired procedure to exclude less relevant options. We apply this protocol to three real-world problems: predicting whether a stock will rise or fall, identifying plant diseases from leaf images, and categorizing texts into two languages. The results show the protocol's effectiveness in reducing the search space while offering accurate predictions.

Our analysis encompasses all prime-field microlensing planets from the 2018 dataset provided by the KMTNet AnomalyFinder, revealing 24 total discoveries or recoveries - ten previously unpublished planets with definitive or probable planetary nature: KMT-2018-BLG-2004, OGLE-2018-BLG-1126, and seven other identified planets; combined with four AnomalyFinder-confirmed new planets from published data, and twelve discovered by visual examination. Together, a study detailing sub-prime planet findings is set to complement our findings. Using the method outlined by Hwang et al. (2022), a modification is introduced to their formalism to remove close/wide and inner/outer degeneracies discrepancies.

Differentiable rendering has gained significant attention in image-based inverse problems due to its potential to enhance traditional optimization-based methods and offer self-supervision for learning-based approaches, particularly those lacking ground truth-annotated training data. However, existing differentiable renderers face challenges in accurately reconstructing real-world images of objects, mainly due to the absence of proper models for image formation and illumination. To address these limitations, we introduce an innovative yet simple approach that incorporates a realistic image formation model utilizing a standard RGB image. This allows our renderer to produce images of objects in arbitrary poses while maintaining consistency with real-world images of the same object. To further boost accuracy, we develop a learning-based feature extraction model for pose and object-specific semantic features. Comprehensive evaluations using three complex 3D computer vision image reconstruction tasks verify that our method outperforms current approaches and yields superior results when applied to learning-based methods. Additionally, we demonstrate that our renderer facilitates reliable semantic image analysis on unknown objects by seamlessly integrating pose estimation and object classification tasks.

Recent research on transportation networks has highlighted the need to account for uncertainty and reliability by modeling the probability of origin-destination demand and network flow. Building on long-term traffic data collection, this paper develops an innovative framework to estimate the average and statistical relationship of origin-destination demand while considering the day-to-day variability resulting from travelers' independent route selections. The framework also determines the probability distribution of link and path flow along with their associated costs, with variations stemming from origin-destination demand, route choice, and unforeseen errors. By employing iterative least squares and lasso regularization techniques, the framework can iteratively estimate origin-destination demand while maintaining sparse covariance matrices to analyze and interpret the correlation between demand. The probabilistic estimation methodology is further extended to calculate the probability distribution of link and path flow by employing two advanced modeling techniques, the stochastic user equilibrium problem and the independent Gaussian distribution. The framework is then applied to a real-world large-scale transportation network to demonstrate the effectiveness of the developed methods, with in-depth computational results and network-specific findings.

In an array of nonlinear oscillators with random frequencies and purely conserved interactions, global phase coherence is demonstrated to occur within finite networks and further examined as it collapses through the generation of localized periodic and chaotic waves following a parameter adjustment. For weak nonlinearity, these global phases exhibit a temporary state of stability, akin to that observed in nearly conservative systems. The observed dynamics within this network can be understood by interpreting the system through the perspective of Metropolis-Hastings Monte Carlo algorithm.

The well-documented Aldous-Broder and Wilson algorithms create random spanning trees through random walks, and this research examines their synergy with the aim of reducing tree construction time. A bijection between spanning trees and tours of various graphs is established, allowing tour generation to serve as a means of producing a related uniform spanning tree. This connection enables a dynamic approach to tree development, where each edge added to the tree is chosen from an appropriate tour branch, thereby ensuring tree integrity. When the graph is a d-regular tree, this method creates a dynamic uniform spanning tree based on a random walk, and upon discovering a suitable stopping criterion for the walk, the generated edges form a random spanning tree. Experimental results indicate that this tour-based approach can generate spanning trees more efficiently than traditional methods.

This work presents a comprehensive music dataset named MusicTM-Dataset that enhances cross-modal retrieval capabilities by offering a diverse collection of multimedia content. Currently, large music datasets featuring three modalities are scarce, limiting the ability to learn effective representations for cross-modal applications. To bridge this gap, our research expands on existing musical notation, combining it with audio synthesis and generated sheet-music images to create a dataset with precise alignments among audio, visual, and text-based components. This aligned MusicTM-Dataset allows for the development of unified representations across multimodal content. Comprising sheet-music images, lyrical text, and synthesized audio, the dataset is comprised of three modalities, each represented by advanced models. This paper outlines the development of our music dataset and showcases the process behind our data collection, as well as initial methods applied to cross-modal retrieval tasks using MusicTM-Dataset. The dataset is publicly available at https://github.com/dddzeng/MusicTM-Dataset.

One major obstacle when utilizing Linked Data lies in developing intuitive and user-friendly interfaces accessible to individuals who aren't technologically inclined. To address this, Ontodia enables diagrammatic data visualization, illustrated in this study with the Wikidata dataset. We've introduced enhancements to a natural language interface that facilitates the exploration of Linked Data entities. By utilizing distributional semantic models to identify and map entitative heads and their corresponding attributes within natural language labels, we've developed a comprehensive labeling scheme. This includes attribute-specific labels that facilitate easier navigation and understanding of entity characteristics. As a result, users can now effortlessly browse through Wikidata entities, seamlessly transitioning between their labels and visual representations.

We've discovered that in the nonlinear Schr\"{o}dinger equation with variable intensity and its soliton solutions, changing the average photon number affects the stability of these solitons. Using a linearized analysis, we found that the stability of dark solitons relies on the sign of the photon number's variation, and that while an increase in photons could stabilize an otherwise unstable dark soliton, too great a variation could make a stable soliton collapse. Given that control of photons is feasible through adjustment of optical parameters, this study suggests a new method for inducing and managing soliton wave propagation in an optical system.

This collaborative approach in visual analytics aims to facilitate seamless interaction between humans and machines, according to various established frameworks. To bridge the gap between theoretical foundations and practical implementation, we introduce an intuitive model for system-assisted guidance and a corresponding library. We present model concepts derived from current research in the field and highlight their implementation in the LvA framework, which is based on the widely used Python programming language. By focusing on system-assisted guidance, we outline the development process and key components required to replicate the functionality of established solutions. Additionally, we showcase the LvA library's capabilities through an exemplary application, demonstrating the benefits of system-assisted guidance during table analysis.

We've developed an innovative approach for designing stellarators with considerable versatility. Flexibility in this context refers to the range of rotational transform values the stellarator's magnetic axis can possess without compromising its quasisymmetry. Our method yields designs that can achieve rotational transform values spanning an incredibly wide range, exceeding 1.5, regardless of coil placement. This level of flexibility enables the production of diverse designs tailored to specific optimization objectives, a capability we demonstrate by adapting our approach to the established NCSX design strategy.

Achieving uniform temperature distribution within catalytic fixed bed reactors is critical for both optimal production yield and operational stability.  However, obtaining precise temperature readings simultaneously with good spatial and temporal resolution in these systems remains difficult. Our research utilizes the capabilities of real-time MRI imaging in conjunction with the temperature-dependent shift in water's proton resonance frequency to obtain in situ temperature measurements in a cylindrical fixed bed reactor. The temperature distribution was monitored as the reactor was heated from room temperature to 60°C using a hot gas stream. Our results show good agreement between the MRI temperature measurements and those obtained with temperature probes positioned within the reactor. The advantages of our non-invasive, high-resolution temperature measurements are demonstrated by analyzing the reactor's axial temperature profile, which exhibits significant variations due to the reactor's internal gas phases expanding and releasing heat.

Within a cellular environment, proteins and nucleic acids autonomously separate, resulting in the spontaneous formation of membraneless droplets. This process underlies the development of numerous sub-cellular compartments. In a model system designed to understand condensate self-assembly, interactions between a large number of different molecular species were studied and programmed to test for variability and rules. The number of different droplets formed from mixtures increased significantly as the number of different molecular species in the mixtures increased. The maximum number of different droplets in a mixture could be accurately predicted even without full knowledge of all interactions. The models' simulations confirmed these expectations and suggested the underlying rules for spatial organization through droplets could be widely applied across cellular molecular mixtures.

Using the Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager on the Solar Dynamics Observatory, we studied how a major leading sunspot rotated in NOAA AR 11429 during two powerful solar flares. A notable sunspot rotated in an unconventional direction, influenced significantly by the solar eruptions. Moving disturbances within other sunspots, caused by the solar flares, traveled rapidly and altered the magnetic properties associated with the sunspots in question, providing valuable insights into the dynamic process governing the sunspots' development.

This note presents a new category of map functions known as oriented colored broken submersions, which forms the most basic type of map functions that adhere to the b-principle, and is nearly equivalent to the set of oriented submersions in 2 dimensions. It demonstrates that the Madsen-Weiss theorem, which can be viewed as a variation of the standard Mumford Conjecture, is derivable from a specific application of the b-principle to oriented colored broken submersions, combined with the findings from Harer's stability theorem and Miller and Morita's work.

This research involves comparing the efficiency of Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) methods for solving complex cardiac mechanics problems on various types of finite element grids. By modeling the mechanical properties of heart muscle tissue using three-dimensional finite elasticity equations, researchers have transformed the problem into a nonlinear algebraic system. A combination of Newton-Krylov and BDDC/AMG solvers is employed to solve this large system. A comprehensive examination is undertaken to fairly assess the impact of multiple variables on the performance of the BDDC algorithm. Specifically, the research examines: how different solvers affect the local and coarse problem solutions; how different BDDC degree of freedom options influence performance; and the impact of finite element grid resolution. Furthermore, the project is carried out using high-performance computing resources across three different clusters, involving the Iris HPC cluster at Harvard, the Everest cluster at MIT, and the Deepthought2 cluster at Maryland.

The ever-growing influence of user-generated content is significantly altering the digital landscape, driven in part by the proliferation of systems supporting content creation, sharing, and management. Among these systems are tag-based platforms that enable users to collaborate in annotating shared items such as images and URLs, leading to user-generated metadata pools and collaborative behavior. To unlock this potential, a comprehensive understanding of current systems is required, which involves characterizing these systems based on usage patterns, the evolution of user-generated content over time, and the underlying social dynamics.

Recently, proposed bianisotropic acoustic metagratings offer promising possibilities for passive acoustic wave manipulation, notably in flat acoustic lenses and ultra-high frequency ultrasound imaging. This concept, however, has not yet been realized in the audible frequency range due to practical challenges. This research aims to overcome these obstacles and achieve acoustic wave manipulation in the audible frequency range using a disc-shaped bianisotropic acoustic metagrating. Composed of lightweight plastic and heavy metal pieces, the components of this metagrating are strategically positioned to optimize performance. Simulation results confirm that this device can effectively redirect sound waves through different phases, thereby forming a flat acoustic lens with a narrow beam angle. Furthermore, the metagrating's signal transmission and energy loss within the metagrating and its surrounding environment have been quantified. Ultimately, the potential of this acoustic metagrating lies in its practical applications in sound redirection within the audible frequency range.

This paper primarily focuses on the long-term behavior of strong solutions to the two-dimensional compressible FENE dumbbell model. Utilizing the Fourier splitting technique, we demonstrate that the $L^2$ norm decay rate is given by $\ln^{-l}(e+t)$, with any positive integer $l$. Through the application of the time-weighted energy method, we also obtain an $L^p$ norm decay rate of $e^{-ct\ln^k(e+t)}$ for $p$ and $k$ both greater than or equal to one. This research greatly extends the earlier work by Zhang and Liu in the context of the two-dimensional incompressible FENE model.

Implementing integrated access and backhaul (IAB) through wireless connections offers a promising way to develop flexible and high-density networks. Mobile IAB, which facilitates the connection of UEs in motion, holds potential as a suitable solution. This work takes a different approach from existing literature by providing a comprehensive overview of deploying mobile IAB by covering: the IAB standardization in 5G New Radio (NR); a classification framework for both fixed and mobile IAB; an extensive analysis of mobile IAB performance through simulations; and the open challenges and potential use cases associated with this technology. The proposed taxonomy organizes mobile IAB into six distinct categories, while the performance assessment employs a comprehensive metric that considers various factors. Results indicate that mobile IAB can achieve impressive data rates when paired with IAB over unlicensed spectrum, outperforming alternative scenarios like fixed IAB or cellular backhaul.

In this study, we conduct an extensive examination of five leading global optimization algorithms as a hyperparameter configuration problem to understand the overall impact of their settings on performance. By utilizing three methods of sensitivity analysis and evaluating various adjustable parameters in four distinct scenarios, we generate a quick reference guide for each algorithm to facilitate informed selections of hyperparameters. The analysis also highlights the effectiveness of sensitivity analysis in informing adaptive tuning mechanisms for these optimization methods, allowing them to efficiently explore more optimal settings during the search process. The results of this research can aid practitioners in making more informed decisions when choosing global optimization algorithms, while also providing foundational insights for future research into hyperparameter configuration.

The paper addresses misconceptions surrounding Jefimenko's equations, which are derived from Maxwell's equations, for a specific charge and current configuration obeying the continuity equation. It subsequently derives a non-radiative condition across inertial frames, consistent with the stability requirements of an atom, and establishes that this condition is equivalent to Jefimenko's equations, demonstrating that the concept of "instantaneous propagation" is both misleading and irrelevant. The paper also highlights that the radiative nature of fields is inherently difficult to dismiss and is fundamental to electromagnetic theory.

Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in critical domains, including robotics and complex gameplay. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to generalize effectively when confronted with new tasks beyond their training data. In response to this challenge, the field is seeing an increased focus on continual learning methods, and to support this research, new tools are being developed, including carefully crafted evaluation frameworks and benchmark environments. To address this need, we present Lifelong Learning Explorer (L2Explorer), a cutting-edge Unity-based environment that allows for continuous, flexible experimentation in a 3D, immersive exploration setting. L2Explorer is distinct from procedurally generated worlds, which often incorporate randomized components. Instead, we've developed a structured and systematic approach to creating learning curricula in response to controlled changes. Our fully transparent and customizable framework is designed to facilitate the development of innovative learning strategies by allowing for the gradual introduction of new tasks in a predictable and well-organized manner.

Liger, a next-generation infrared device at the W. M. Keck Observatory, will be paired with the Keck All-sky Precision Adaptive-optics system to optimize performance. Liger's initial phase boasts an unprecedented 4.5 to 2.38 micrometer wavelength range with 0.025 micrometer resolution. This paper outlines the specifics of Liger's early development, including its use of a 62-kilohertz cryogenic grating, along with the astrophysical device's spatial extent of 30 by 30 pixels. Liger's engineers utilized an innovative phase-shift imaging technique to determine the device's spectral features. This technique is Liger-specific and involves rotating the device by 180 degrees between spectral setups. This approach enables the separation of Liger's features from other Keck Observatory components' signatures. To do this, an algorithm was created that matches a time-dependent pattern to a device's perspective image. This process worked successfully in laboratory tests that verified the effectiveness of the technique. Liger's designers are now preparing for a device that covers an even broader 4.5 to 2.3-micrometer range with improved signal quality. This research is crucial for developing Liger into a cutting-edge infrared device.

This study uncovers a broad class of non-trivial, steady flow patterns in two-dimensional Euler dynamics, occurring in smooth flows with arbitrarily small irregularities. These patterns exhibit a distant relationship and can be found close to a free vortex in an almost smooth flow. Furthermore, the intensity of these patterns decreases at a slow rate - logarithmically with decreasing irregularity - and are highly regular, with exponents significantly higher than 1. These patterns also exist in a broad range of irregularities and are located at a free vortex, a singular geometric structure. This research also demonstrates the existence of patterns that are close to a collection of distinct free vortices and are characterized by highly regular properties with exponents greater than 2. These patterns occur in a broad range of irregularities and are located at multiple, spaced out geometric structures.

We experimentally control the linear polarization of exciton-polariton condensates using optical traps with elliptical geometries that favor specific polarization modes. Due to anisotropic splitting in the cavity, ground state degeneracy is lifted, yielding fine structure modes along the trap's axis and orthogonal to it. These modes are selectively occupied by the condensate. Our results reveal a unique method for polarization control with potential applications in spin-based photonics and research on complex optical systems with adjustable coupling properties.

This study's primary objective is to provide evidence and disproofs for the deterministic Kardar-Parisi-Zhang type equations including non-local gradient elements. We demonstrate the existence of solutions in a specific class and show that a particular problem has no solution within another class. Furthermore, we verify the necessity of specific growth conditions for the equation's coefficients for solution existence in a particular class.

The  COVID-19 pandemic, triggered by SARS-CoV-2 in 2020, was officially classified as a global health crisis by the WHO. As a result, the world is relying heavily on public health precautions such as social distancing measures to limit the virus's spread and slow down its mortality rate. With the isolation necessary to combat the virus, researchers are turning to alternative methods of interaction, including virtual augmented reality (AR) to enable efficient and safe collaboration. We developed the AR-based distribution of 3D avatars in virtual spaces, or AR3D, to facilitate remote work in AR through the creation of safe virtual working environments. These safe spaces incorporate intelligent virtual agents that maintain a safe physical distance from each other based on public health guidelines for social distancing. We conducted user testing on AR3D, focusing on evaluating its usability and user preferences. Our results revealed that AR3D is indeed easy to use, and users find their virtual working experience to be safe and comfortable in terms of personal space. We discovered that the minimum recommended social distancing space can sometimes be restrictive in AR virtual spaces. However, we found that users generally prefer social distancing guidelines over crowded conditions. Overall, AR3D offers a promising solution for organizations, especially those in industries such as architecture, where collaboration on 3D models requires both efficiency and safety. With the current technology available, we can achieve our goals with client-server architectures using technologies such as Unity and OpenGL.

Freiman's 3k-4 theorem generally posits that if subsets A and B, of size k and comprised of integers, share a sumset with a size near 2k, then A and B exhibit considerable similarity to arithmetic progressions. In this paper, we aim to enhance this by limiting the number of possible summands available from subset B. It's shown that if subsets A and B, of size k, meet the criterion that for every four-element subset of B, the sumset A plus that subset doesn't exceed 2k, it follows that A and B exhibit considerable similarity to arithmetic progressions.

In medical contexts, diverse information is frequently gathered but often lacks a clear reason to select one method over another. Various techniques result in distinct representations, yet they can be complementary when combined. The potential of fusion has been explored in numerous areas, yet established methods usually depend on specific characteristics or pre-defined weights, which can be difficult to adjust and appear arbitrary. Furthermore, combining representations from multiple sources in a traditional manner can overlook subtle correlations between different modalities. To address these issues, we propose an innovative technique for fusing multimodal information called Contrastive Multimodal Dimensionality Reduction (CMDR). By leveraging contrastive learning, we've developed a unified approach for learning modality-agnostic representations that can be scaled to any number of modalities, without relying on pre-specified weights or features. Our method uses a single objective function to reduce complex high-dimensional spaces to simpler ones, preserving both intra- and inter-modal relationships. We apply CMDR to multiple modalities, consisting of text and image representations, to demonstrate its effectiveness and efficiency, and to showcase its use in real-world tasks, such as word and image representation alignment and image-to-text description generation.

X-ray images contain subtle characteristics with predictive information about patients who are likely to experience severe COVID-19 symptoms.  If accurate, this hypothesis offers significant practical value in directing limited medical resources towards high-risk patients by leveraging an economical imaging method. However, confirming this hypothesis proves challenging due to the need for large, well-annotated data sets containing COVID-19 patients, who are increasingly difficult to find. Moreover, deep learning models commonly employed for this task have significant computational requirements that cannot be fulfilled with current hardware, given the necessity to process numerous classes. To address these challenges, our research develops a new two-layered network architecture that efficiently classifies patients as high or low risk for severe COVID-19 using limited computational resources. By combining clinical features with image features derived from X-rays, our proposed model accurately classifies patients, achieving impressive results on established datasets, thereby validating the initial hypothesis that X-ray images, coupled with clinical data, can accurately forecast severe COVID-19 symptoms. Moreover, our research highlights that deep learning models can effectively support healthcare by directing limited medical resources towards high-risk patients, who are increasingly difficult to find.

We analyze the transmission eigenvalue problem involving $u$ and $v$ in the Sobolev space $H^1(\Omega)$ associated with $(\Omega, \sigma, \mathbf{n}^2)$. Considering the case where $\Omega$ is a ball in $\mathbb{R}^2$ or $\mathbb{R}^3$, and that $\sigma$ and $\mathbf{n}$ only depend on the radial distance $r$, we find that the $L^2$-energies of $u$ and $v$ go to infinity as their respective wavenumbers increase without bound. Moreover, we demonstrate that the ratios of these energies are bounded by a constant factor. Our findings, which generalize the one-dimensional case studied in the paper 'Asymptotic and generic versions of the Dirichlet-Neumann operator for separated data' [ arXiv:2107.10364, 2021], are based on the theory of Bessel functions and the expansion of the Dirichlet-Neumann operator in a separated setting.

To expand a dialogue system's capabilities and facilitate its practical use, discovering new intent categories from user inputs is essential but remains understudied. Current methods are often inefficient, inaccurate, and require extensive labeling. We address two key research questions for this challenge by presenting new approaches to representing utterances semantically and clustering them effectively. Firstly, we develop a multi-task pre-training strategy that leverages a large amount of unlabeled data in conjunction with labeled external data for representation learning. Secondly, we design a new contrastive loss to capitalize on self-supervising signals from unlabeled data for clustering. Experiments on three benchmarks demonstrate the superior performance of our method over existing approaches in both unsupervised and semi-supervised settings.

The classical universal bundle functor W mapping from the category of simplicial groups in C to the category of simplicial sets in C lifts to a monadic structure on the category of simplicial groups in C, and this extension holds for simplicial algebras defined by any Lawvere theory that includes group theory.
In our analysis, we demonstrate that a finite group of order $r$ possesses no more than $$7.3722\cdot r^{\frac{\log_2r}{4}+1.5315}$$ subgroups.

This study re-examines the Adler-Bobenko-Suris H2 equation. The equation has a direct linear relationship with the Cauchy matrix scheme variables S0, S1, S2, S3. A detailed analysis is provided on the interaction between these variables, specifically on the stochastic process they form. Additionally, a discrete time triangular Lax pair is formulated using the variables S0, S1, S2. The analysis focuses primarily on the discrete time triangular Lax pair.

This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect relationships being easily identified due to poor object detection. As a result, low-frequency difficult proposals struggle to contribute effectively. Our proposed framework, Spatially-Aware Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (SABRA), aims to mitigate these issues by introducing a comparative goal for balancing negative proposals. By sampling harder negative proposals, SABRA's system optimizes performance by reducing false positives and enhances proposal diversity, ultimately leading to more accurate relationships between objects. Our experimental results demonstrate that SABRA surpasses current state-of-the-art methods on PASCAL VOC, COCO, and KITTI datasets in terms of accuracy measures.

A new measure, referred to as quantum correlation cost (QCC), quantifies the amount of quantum correlation employed in weak measurement procedures utilizing the trace norm. It's demonstrated that the QCC is directly linked to the trace-norm-based quantum discord (TQD) by a factor dependent on weak measurement strength. However, this measure only captures a portion of a system's quantum nature in contrast to the TQD. Furthermore, our results reveal that remaining quantum features can be extracted via a sequence of von Neumann measurements, each leveraging the associated post-measurement state's phase-space volume.

Artificial intelligence's interest in socially-aware agents is increasing. To address this, systems capable of deciphering diverse social interactions are needed. Currently, methods focus primarily on motion-based data, which is insufficient for accurately perceiving all forms of social interaction. To overcome this, we've developed a novel approach that integrates high-level relationship information between individuals in a social relationship graph. This is achieved through a unique deep neural network that integrates visual and relationship data. This relationship graph enhances the understanding of social interactions and enables the recognition of advanced social abilities. We've conducted extensive tests on a newly created dataset consisting of social video scenes depicting various social interactions. Our approach consistently delivers superior results on even the most intricate social interactions, surpassing state-of-the-art social relationship graph-based methods.

Capturing long-range relationships in scene understanding tasks is a crucial goal in computer vision. While CNNs excel in many vision tasks, they have limitations in modelling global, structured relationships due to their localized nature. A fully connected graph like in Graph Neural Networks is beneficial, but only allows node-wise communication. We propose the Dynamic Graph Message Passing Network (DGPN), which combines a self-adjusting spatial graph structure with intra- and inter-domain node communication, enabling the extraction of high-level features from local elements. Unlike static graph approaches, DGPN's dynamic graph and message passing mechanism allows for flexible feature communication and node connectivity. We demonstrate the effectiveness of DGPN on Keypoint Estimation and Object Sensitive Retinal Output tasks.

Optimized hardware is often required in embedded systems, leading to a common operation called Multiple Constant Multiplication (MCM) over integers. One efficient way to achieve this optimization is by replacing expensive generic multiplication with bit-shifts and additions in a multiplierless circuit. Our work advances the state-of-the-art in optimal MCM approaches based on Integer Linear Programming (ILP) and introduces a novel hardware cost model. This model counts one-bit adders, demonstrating a strong correlation with the number of LUTs required. Our enhanced model accommodates intermediate precision truncations, enabling significant resource savings when full precision is not essential. Our proposed model efficiently handles multiple constant multiplication within a hardware constraint, representing a real-world use case in embedded systems.

The intersection of quantum computing and deep neural networks has recently given rise to a growing research field, known as quantum deep learning. This field holds significant potential for solving complex challenges in various fields, such as physics, chemistry, and computer science. In this article, we provide a comprehensive overview of quantum deep learning, starting with discussions on quantum algorithms and quantum computing, followed by an examination of machine learning and its applications in physics. We then delve into the intersection of deep neural networks and quantum computing, highlighting potential applications and assessing the current state of research in quantum deep learning.

The radio frequency (RF) accelerator technology continues to be fundamental in 
high-energy physics (HEP) experiments, where significant progress has been 
made over the past decade in advancing the field. This progress could soon lead 
to upgraded existing facilities, enhancements to facilities still under 
construction (such as PIP-II), well-established proposals, or newly emerging 
ideas like the FCC-ee and future proton intensity upgrade at Fermilab, among 
others. A comprehensive review of the recent advancements in RF technology is 
presented, focusing on the innovations made possible by advancements in 
computing, materials, and precision measurement, which have significantly 
contributed to the progress in RF technology. (C) 2020 Elsevier B.V. All rights 
reserved.

In the near future, physicists anticipate that the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) will discover new physics. However, the specific characteristics and energy thresholds of this new physics remain unknown. It's probable that insights gleaned from LHC data will require supplementary information obtained from a lepton collider to conduct a thorough investigation. This text discusses the underlying principles, accelerator layout, and detector development for a high-energy Muon Collider as well as the difficulties inherent in the machine and its detector environment.

We have determined the dispersion relations for relativistic fluid modes in various configurations - scalar, vector, and tensor - and found the differences between their behavior in non-viscous and viscous environments. These results have implications for understanding the properties of relativistic plasmas and were derived within the context of a flawed fluid model that yields exact solutions for conservation equations. This model incorporates a particular derivative expansion technique, allowing us to identify the sources of viscosity and boundary conditions that influence fluid behavior. Furthermore, we have established that both dynamic and static boundary conditions contribute to viscosity, which aligns with expectations from membrane paradox and Casimir effects, respectively.

Our research assesses whether the cosmic background of Hawking radiation from primordial black holes could be the source behind the observed excess radiowave signals. By assuming that dark matter exists entirely as these black holes, we calculated that the temperature resulting from Hawking radiation is negligible in comparison to the cosmic microwave background, primarily due to the black holes' low mass. This is caused by the emission's power law suppression of lower-energy frequencies. Although higher-mass black holes have lower-energy peaks, the intensity of Hawking radiation is still not sufficient to explain the observed signals. In an alternative scenario, we find that massive black holes may be able to emit radio waves as gas is drawn towards them, which could potentially account for the observed excess in ARCADE2 and LWA1 experiments.

Introducing the Virtual Secure Platform (VSP), a pioneering solution that brings together multi-opcode general-purpose sequential processing with Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) to enable Secure Multi-Party Computation (SMPC) at a secure computing offloading level, such as cloud computing. The VSP safeguardingly secures data and program against unauthorized access within offloaded computations. To achieve this innovative combination, we introduced the Rapid Evaluation of Narrow Networks (RENN) algorithm for efficiently simulating the behavior of sequential processors that follow a store-forward architecture, where data and programs are stored and processed separately. Our RENN algorithm allows for the parallel evaluation of processor instructions (e.g., add, load, and move) using modular arithmetic, inlining constants and reusing results when possible, and incorporating Fresh Linear Probing Map (FLPM) for handling program counter addresses. We implemented the RENN on a 64-bit Avoton Intel N28010 board, which incorporates the Merrimack Architecture, by modifying the OpenSBI and FreeSMBIOS to enable SBI calls through the use of an mcarng-pollinated interrupt handler. Our comprehensive 1,085-instruction processor benchmark, which matches the specifications of the merrimack architecture with multiple execution units, yielded a performance of approximately 42-85 cycles per instruction at 2.6 GHz. Our experimental results indicate that the average encryption overhead per instruction was approximately 11.8-23.8 microseconds for

Researchers investigate polynomial-time approximation schemes (PTAS) for solving specific constraint satisfaction problems, such as Maximum Independent Set or Minimum Vertex Cover on graph classes that have limited connectivity.

A previously developed approach by Baker achieved PTAS on various graph classes including planar graphs. Further, Romero, Wrochna, and Zivny developed a simpler PTAS for certain graph classes using the Sherali-Adams LP relaxation for maximum CSPs with constraints defined by arbitrary non-negative functions.

This research is extended to CSPs with constraints that have multiple possible values. The only restriction for such constraints is that they contain an element that is at least as good as the average element.

A new PTAS is presented for general-valued CSPs with such constraints on certain graph classes. Additionally, a new PTAS is presented for any-valued CSPs with such constraints on planar graphs.

Pre-trained language models possess the ability to capture syntactical information, as established in our previous research. To enhance this capability even further, we introduce linear transformation matrices to the self-attention mechanism, allowing for better extraction of query and key representations.
