For deep learning models, understanding how complexity is controlled has been a challenging task, given that many conventional methods are unsuitable for their inherent complexity. Our research introduces a concept called geometric complexity, quantifying the variability of model functions using a discrete Dirichlet energy metric. By applying this metric to various network architectures, we can analyze the complexity of their layer configurations and demonstrate the method's effectiveness in optimizing geometric complexity, ultimately improving the capacity of deep learning models to generalize.

A new approach for directly extracting the Wilson coefficients of rare $b\to s$ processes is developed using $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ decays within an unbinned maximum likelihood framework. This novel method outperforms traditional Wilson coefficient determination by utilizing all available data and accounting for experimental correlations. Its effectiveness is tested using a combination of Monte Carlo simulations and real-world data from LHCb.

Automated essay grading has been a persistent challenge in Natural Language Processing.  Despite years of research, it remains an only partially resolved issue, with notable practical applications and research implications.  Techniques such as transfer learning and data augmentation have significantly improved the accuracy of state-of-the-art models in this domain.  Past research has explored the potential of Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and variants like Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), among others, in solving automated essay grading.  Our study focuses on the effectiveness of transformer-based architectures, specifically BERT and RoBERTa, in conjunction with data augmentation methods for developing a versatile and efficient automated essay grading model across diverse topics.

Given a simplicial complex defining a tensor's marginalizations, we restrict them to rank one, an idea developed from Kirkup and Sullivant's work on toric models. We delve into the toric ideals arising from such marginal independence models, with a specific focus on models for random graphs and matroids' independent set polytopes. We also explore numerical methods for parameter estimation through both Euclidean distance and maximum likelihood techniques and establish a database for small model examples.

A higher education system or similar opportunities can drive social mobility across generations by allowing individuals to rise above their family's economic status. To examine this dynamic in societies with social mobility limitations, a new model allocates opportunities to maximize the benefits they provide to current and future generations. Our model reveals that, in order to maximize long-term payoffs, it's beneficial to give priority to lower socioeconomically situated individuals who have greater potential to rise to better socioeconomical standings. The result can lead to socioeconomic affirmative action. The duration and intensity of this practice vary depending on specific conditions. The proposed model also offers avenues for exploring more intricate relationships between different socioeconomical groups in various societal settings.

The symmetry of wavefunctions under parity for particles of arbitrary spin is responsible for determining the wavefunction exchange statistics when the particles are permuted. According to non-relativistic quantum mechanics, the properties of angular momentum alone account for the sign factor resulting from the particle permutation, which relates spin to particle exchange statistics in this context.

We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports stealth addresses in conjunction with Delegated Proof of Stake, resulting in Delegated RingCT.
The Delegated RingCT scheme is comprised of an integrated signature and encryption framework, combining a public key encryption protocol and two types of signatures along with linkable ring signatures, alongside non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs.
A comprehensive description of Delegated RingCT, along with security evidence and an implemented prototype, are presented, which we subsequently test through benchmarking analysis.
While Delegated RingCT may not possess the same level of anonymity compared to other RingCT implementations, we propose that its ability to be compatible with DPoS consensus mechanisms provides a reasonable trade-off for enabling a more efficient and scalable decentralised cryptocurrency with preserved anonymity capabilities.

If more specific subclasses of linear systems can be solved in near-logarithmic space, this capability can be applied to solve a broader range of linear systems within a similar space complexity. Our findings build on work by Kyng and Zhang who previously made similar discoveries in terms of time complexity, utilizing reductions between approximate solvers; our own proof demonstrates that these reductions can be implemented using threshold circuits with specific characteristics.

Researchers have made the initial detection of three massive gauge bosons simultaneously produced in high-energy collisions between protons.  These collisions were performed at the CERN LHC with the CMS experiment's data set that contains 137 fb$^{-1}$ worth of information.  Separate searches for individual combinations of bosons, including W boson variations, have been done using several patterns of final particle arrangements.  Together, the signals for these processes indicate a cross-section of boson creation that is slightly larger than that predicted by the standard model, occurring 26.2 standard model-like times with an uncertainty of 5.1 statistical and 8.2 systematic combined.  Also, searches for signals of new physics in these processes have been done, constraining various theoretical models of such physics, including ones involving expanded particle spectra and others involving interactions between additional particles.

Previous foundational Hebrew NLP tasks have heavily relied on the 30-year-old Hebrew Treebank. This outdated single-source corpus lacks the diversity of modern Hebrew, found primarily on the web. This research paper addresses this issue by presenting a new, open-access UD Hebrew treebank. This corpus, created by sampling various topics from Hebrew Wikipedia, provides a much-needed upgrade to NLP's understanding of contemporary Hebrew. The project validates its annotations through multiple reliability checks and undergoes quality evaluation, demonstrating a high level of accuracy. The project also introduces the first udpipe model for Modern Hebrew, utilizing the new annotations.

We maintain the maximum value of any $p$-dimensional vector composed of $n$ elements from the $L_p$ space with $p\geq 1$ and scale factor $S_n$ can be represented by a vector of at most $(n+1)^{1/\alpha}$ elements from the $L_\alpha$ space for $\alpha>p$, and specifically for $\alpha=2$, a scale factor of $S_2=(2^{1/p}-1)^{-1/p}$. This discovery generalizes a 1989 finding by Matouk and complements a 2017 result by Naor and Zagdilov. Furthermore, we propose the maximum value of any $p$-dimensional vector composed of $n$ elements from the $L_p$ space with $p\geq 1$ and scale factor $T_p$ can be represented by a vector of at most $2^{1/p}\sqrt{2n}$ elements from the $L_2$ space, and specifically for $p=1$, a scale factor of $T_1=\log(2n)/\log(2)+1$. This discovery addresses a 1991 problem proposed by Alon and Borgs.

Recent breakthroughs in artificial neural networks have accelerated the growth of data-driven research in mental health, but advances in machine learning have long been hampered by two core challenges: the limitations of scalable training and the enigma of catastrophic forgetting.  We introduce a groundbreaking technique called Continual Learning through Neural Compiler Design (CLNC), which employs compiler tools to establish robust, forget-resistant models capable of learning continuously.  We demonstrate the effectiveness of CLNC by testing it on benchmark tasks in image recognition, where we observed an error reduction of approximately 80% compared to conventional methods, and further improvements can be achieved through variations in compiler strategies.

Current studies examining the performance of randomly assembled low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes usually assume the independence of degree distributions from edge endpoints. In contrast, our research extends this understanding by investigating LDPC ensembles that incorporate degree-degree correlations. We propose novel techniques for generating degree-degree correlated LDPC ensembles, derive density evolution equations applicable to binary erasure channels, and employ numerical simulations to illustrate how degree-degree correlations impact LDPC code performance. Interestingly, our findings indicate that negative degree-degree correlations can enhance the maximum error tolerance of LDPC codes, with further gains achievable through adjustments in degree distribution parameters.

An advanced modular system, which is known as the safety filter, has been designed to enhance potentially unsafe control inputs with safety assurances through constraint satisfaction. This paper presents a detailed review of the safety filter's effectiveness in fulfilling its purpose and also introduces a refined version of the model predictive safety filter, which utilizes system level synthesis techniques to optimize its performance. This improved model predictive safety filter is capable of fulfilling tighter safety constraints compared to traditional MPSF approaches, which often fail to account for the system's inherent properties such as predictability and robustness. Moreover, this paper provides a comprehensive analysis of the safety filter's performance in various systems, which often exhibit smooth and safety-compliant trajectories that closely mirror the original control inputs, with these benefits being attributed to the integration of system level synthesis with MPSF.

A critical flaw exists in the current application of quantum key distribution (QKD) systems due to their vulnerability to quantum hacking. Our novel approach incorporates a hybrid measurement attack, achievable with only basic components such as linear optics, homodyne detection, and single photon detection, which poses a significant threat to the widely adopted vacuum+weak decoy state QKD system. Specifically, if the source phase is randomly altered to a limited degree, we discovered that the proposed attack can bypass the system's security, resulting in the entanglement-breaking channel without being detected by the users. Our findings suggest that randomizing the source phase to a limited degree may not be sufficient to safeguard phase-encoding QKD systems using coherent states.

Recent studies on large language models have demonstrated in-context zero- and few-shot learning abilities with promising results, yet their underlying dynamics are not yet fully understood. For instance, there is limited knowledge about how learning in-context changes when using varying training corpora. Our research aims to explore the influence of a pretraining corpus's origin and size on the performance of a Korean-centric model. Notably, we discovered four crucial findings: Firstly, a pretraining corpus's domain significantly affects the model's ability to learn in-context. Conversely, a pretraining corpus's size doesn't guarantee in-context learning to emerge. Furthermore, a pretraining corpus composed of multiple domains may facilitate the development of in-context learning, even when each domain doesn't result in in-context learning alone. Lastly, a pretraining corpus related to a downstream task may not always lead to in-context learning, especially when it comes to tasks outside its domain, such as natural language inference.

Galaxy cluster observations have primarily focused on the formation of central nebulae, yet little is known about what happens when the initial, intricate structure of these formations disintegrates. To investigate the long-term effects of this process, we conducted 30 magnetohydrodynamic simulations of kiloparsec-scale, kiloparsec cold clouds under conditions typically found in galaxy clusters. Our results indicate that filamentary segments of these clouds quickly cool and separate from the rest, only to be torn apart by winds, and ultimately fragmented into smaller, kiloparsec patches. We discovered that factor affecting cloud growth and evolution were gas temperature, density, and absorption. Clouds with thin external layers and a stable base tend to persist, whereas clouds with a uniform density are fragmented and lose cooling capacity. These findings imply that galaxy cluster formations involve multiple phases, and the primary cold clouds are broken down into kiloparsec patches that fuel starbursts.

The examination of $C\!P$ violation in beauty- and charm-hadron decays serves as
a crucial test of the Standard Model's predictions, also acting as a sensitive
indicator to uncover physical phenomena not accounted for within the SM. The
presentation includes precise measurements of observables connected to the
unitary triangles stemming from unitarity constraints on the Cabibbo-Kobayashi-
Maskawa matrix describing quark mixing, alongside recent $C\!P$ violation
measurements in beauty- and charm-hadrons. Specific emphasis is given to an
analysis that initially identified $C\!P$ violation in beauty baryons and made
the most accurate measurement of this effect within the charm system to date. 
These analyses rely on data gathered from proton-proton collisions in 2011 and
2012, collected by the ATLAS, CMS, and LHCb experiments.

New high-energy string interactions have been discovered in 10D open superstring theory. These amplitudes have unique polarization properties and their counterparts in bosonic string theory are significantly weaker. A remarkable relationship exists among these amplitudes, where one is proportional to the others. Calculations of their ratios confirm a long-standing theory prediction made by Gross in 1988. Additionally, the total count of newly calculated high-energy amplitudes in superstring theory is consistent with those from recently discovered fermion interactions in string theory.

To effectively manage the vast amounts of data being generated by a growing number of mobile and IoT devices, future mobile networks (MNs) must shift from traditional resource allocation methods. By integrating computation capabilities into Base Stations, we can optimize resource usage and efficiently manage resources near the edge of the network. Leveraging techniques such as time-series forecasting and control theory, we propose using neural networks and optimizing strategies within the Multi-access Edge Computing paradigm. Our approach involves online algorithms for virtualized resource scaling, reconfiguring computing and communication assets, and enabling dynamic BS switching to minimize energy consumption and ensure Quality of Service (QoS). Numerical results demonstrate that these strategies lead to significant reductions in edge computing and communication energy consumption, promoting energy self-sustainability in MNs through the use of green energy sources.

The objective of zero-speech synthesis is to create a vocabulary-independent speech system without transcription data, requiring the transformation of training data into acoustic units for test synthesis. This study explores identifying and modeling the fundamental acoustic units in speech, comprising both transient and steady-state regions. The transient regions are equivalent to consonant-vowel and vowel-consonant units, while steady-states include singles and combinations of vowels and consonants. The speech signal is first segmented into CVC-like units based on a short-term energy contour and then grouped into acoustic units using graph clustering. Excitation patterns of these units, obtained by analyzing the autoregressive power spectra and glottal reflection signals, facilitate the determination of unit types. The synthesized speech quality of the developed graph units is superior to that of the short-term energy contours.

Optimizing multi-limbed robots' motion under posture and force constraints poses a challenging nonlinear optimization issue, often accompanied by extensive computation times. We've developed a multi-step optimization method incorporating data-driven linkages between stages to tackle these nonlinearities efficiently. Both cluster analysis and evolutionary strategies are applied to determine the specific parameters of McCormick envelope relaxations, allowing us to leverage specialized solvers for sub-problems while maintaining global optimality, thus achieving faster solution times. Our planner was thoroughly tested and validated through various experiments on a 6-legged walking robot, the Hyq-14, demonstrating the efficacy of this approach.

We have developed two overarching methods to quantify the manipulation of quantum states using probabilistic protocols constrained by specific quantum resource limitations.
Initially, we formulated a fundamental criterion for achieving a physical transformation between quantum states using a previously introduced resource metric.
This approach led to the discovery that the metric is not only necessary, but also sufficient, for one-shot resource conversion in various resource theories, effectively rendering more restrictive protocols unnecessary.
By employing this metric, we were able to refine the performance limits of one-shot and multi-copy probabilistic resource distillation protocols.
Concurrently, we introduced a comprehensive technique for calculating achievable probabilities in resource transformations through a series of convex optimisation problems.
This approach enabled us to precisely assess the trade-offs between probabilities and errors in the distillation of maximally resource-rich states.
Furthermore, we successfully demonstrated the efficacy of our methods in the analysis of quantum entanglement distillation.

We investigated the dynamic behavior of a cup of coffee being carried while in motion, by applying a lumped model that combines characteristics of a planar nonlinear pendulum. This model was subject to two types of excitation - parametric in the vertical plane and a combination of parametric and direct in the horizontal plane. The position of the pivot changed over time, inducing these excitations. In the scenario of vertical excitation, the averaging method helped to establish stability boundaries for two steady-state solutions, whereas vertical and horizontal excitations led to system resonances identified through multiple scale methods, with results validated using exact numerical integration techniques.

In our research paper, we address the challenge of a regularized distributionally robust learning problem in decentralized networks by taking into account the changes in data distribution. By incorporating the Kullback-Liebler penalty into the robust min-max optimization framework, we transform the problem into an efficiently solvable form and propose a robust decentralized optimization method, specifically DR-DSGD, based on the Decentralized Stochastic Gradient Descent (DSGD). Under specific conditions and a sufficiently large regularization parameter, we analytically prove that our algorithm achieves a rate of convergence of $\mathcal{O}\left(1/\sqrt{KT} + K/T\right)$. Furthermore, experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of DR-DSGD, yielding an approximation within a factor of $\mathcal{O}\left( \sigma^2 + \tilde{T}^{-1/2} \right)$, where $\sigma^2$ represents the worst-case data variance and $\tilde{T}$ denotes the total number of iterations. DR-DSGD exhibits substantial communication savings over traditional DSGD, reducing the amount of data exchanged by a factor of $\mathcal{O}\left( \tilde{T}^{1/2} \right)$.

We utilize the concept of hydrodynamic attractors to establish a universal relationship between initial energy states and the number of produced particles in high-energy collisions. By combining this with an in-depth model of energy release, our findings demonstrate that entropy generated before equilibrium is established naturally accounts for the common trend of decreasing particle production with increasing centrality observed in nucleus-nucleus collisions.

Using complex simulations of star-forming clouds, the process by which powerful jets form is studied under different magnetic field strengths and mass accumulation rates. The data show that strongly magnetized clouds produce fast-moving jets only when the protostar gains a relatively small amount of mass per year, typically no more than 10 to the minus 3 solar masses. When the magnetic field is very weak, however, high mass accumulation rates can still lead to the formation of powerful jets. In the middle range of magnetic field strengths, slow-moving jets can sometimes appear due to the protostar gaining too much mass too quickly, and this can also lead to the blockage of jet material and the formation of dense knots. These findings suggest that powerful protostellar jets require a delicate balance of strong magnetic fields and slow mass accumulation, and this balance can sometimes be disrupted, resulting in less powerful or irregularly shaped jets.

This study investigates the optimal equilibrium between performance capabilities and operational limitations for a specific category of nonlinear systems, encompassing balanced command filtered backstepping (BCFB) and balanced performance control (BPC). A novel approach involves introducing a performance safety assessment (PSA) metric that measures system safety in the presence of destabilizing influences, such as saturation and filter error, which ultimately enables comprehensive compensation and performance restoration. It is acknowledged that within a safety zone, certain thresholds can be tolerated for these destabilizing factors, prompting the need for corrective action only when the system's status poses a significant threat. Numerical simulation examples effectively demonstrate the proposed strategy's merits.

This research project seeks to offer fresh perspectives on how various gravitational interactions affect an object orbiting the Earth, specifically considering its shape and the impact of sunlight pressure. To achieve this, it provides mathematical models that take into account how the object's area-to-mass ratio influences its equilibrium positions. This includes deriving key equations that describe how the object's orbit changes due to the interactions with the two principal resonances, specifically in terms of its variations in altitude and inclination. Throughout the study, references are made to the work of a previous author, specifically regarding the object's shape and the two-resonance scenario. This research project also explores how the object's shape affects its orbit, particularly with respect to its equilibrium positions. Additionally, it considers the impact of sunlight pressure on the object's orbit, which causes it to wobble in response, and also causes its equilibrium positions to wobble in a larger sense. This research project offers a comprehensive analysis of how the object's shape and the two resonances affect its orbit, which provides valuable insights into its general shape and the role of sunlight pressure in its orbit.

We examine the techniques of simulating light-matter interactions within tight-binding models that derive from first-principle theory. The conventional method for describing optical properties uses a velocity-based approach tied to the vector potential. An alternative method exists, where a finite system is represented through the electric field, resulting in a dipole-based model inspired by Peierls substitution. This study evaluates the accuracy of both methods in relation to gauge invariance, utilizing TB models constructed from maximally localized Wannier functions and applied to two-dimensional paradigm materials. We calculate the electromagnetic responses under linear and strong excitations, comparing the outcomes to converged first-principle simulations to validate our TB models' accuracy. The results indicate that the dipole-based model yields a more precise description than the velocity-based model. We attribute this to the imperfect compensation of diamagnetic and paramagnetic currents in the velocity-based model. To rectify this shortcoming, we formulated a sum rule that explicitly addresses the compensation issue, allowing the correction of velocity-based models to match dipole-based models and guarantee gauge invariance.

In a problem focused on category-level perception, we consider utilizing sensor data to identify and understand objects within specific categories despite variations within those categories. An active shape model, where pre-defined CAD models of various objects are used as a reference, is employed to determine object pose and shape. Our first achievement is developing PACE3D* and PACE2D*, which are novel optimisation algorithms handling intra-class variability by jointly optimising multiple sample objects' poses and shapes using a single observation. These algorithms are based on an novel approach where observation data is directly weighted against model variations using weighted alignments, thereby enabling the efficient use of complex observation data in object pose and shape optimisation. Our testing reveals that PACE3D* and PACE2D* perform superiorly when compared to existing techniques in both 3D and 2D formats, as well as that active shape models are adaptable to various complex datasets.

We will define a confidence area for parameter estimates of a sample of size $N$ derived from random variables following a Cauchy distribution. By considering the Cauchy distribution's parameters as a single complex parameter, combining location $\mu$ and scale $\sigma$ as $\gamma = \mu + i\sigma$, we will determine a region within the complex plane, ultimately defining it as both a disc and a square using a straightforward formula.

A new statistical method is developed for basket trials to assess the effectiveness of a novel treatment in multiple patient subgroups under one protocol. This approach uses Bayesian statistics to optimize sample size and allows information sharing between groups. We develop formulas to ensure each subgroup trial has the required sample size to meet statistical goals. This consistency property maintains the robustness of inferences across all groups. We also develop a scoring system to evaluate trial performance in real-time and propose a scoring threshold to stop trials that are unlikely to meet statistical goals. This approach is scored retrospectively to show how it could have altered the course of actual trials. We score simulated trials to demonstrate the method's effectiveness in predicting trial outcomes and propose a scoring system to guide trial management. We score basket trials containing multiple armier to assess treatment differences while controlling for bias. We develop formulas to optimize armier sizes and show the results of simulated trials. Our approach combines the strengths of two popular Bayesian methods for detecting treatment differences and unbalanced designs.

To satisfy the rising demands of high-throughput in the industry, advanced motion systems must now be designed with a delicate balance between high-speed and high-accuracy. However, conventional control strategies often struggle to meet these requirements, particularly in motion systems that are susceptible to changes based on their position. This research introduces a cutting-edge modification to traditional control designs to address the performance limitations in these systems, effectively reducing the impact of disturbances and errors, and allowing for tighter control over key parameters, such as motion, velocity, and vibration. A demonstration of the new control strategy's effectiveness is achieved through simulation-based testing of a precise motion platform that must maintain ultra-stable vibrations while enabling high-speed operations.

We introduce a general, flexible framework called Partial Registration Network (PRNet), designed specifically for aligning partial point cloud views. Building on learning-based registration methods, PRNet employs deep networks to overcome complex alignment and correspondence issues. Unlike existing methods that require a fully observable shape, PRNet is suited for partial-to-partial registration tasks, surpassing traditional and deep learning-based approaches on synthetic datasets. Our approach features self-supervised learning of a suitable geometric representation and a keypoint detector for common point identification, alongside learned keypoint-to-keypoint correspondences. Experimental results demonstrate that PRNet achieves superior performance on synthetic datasets and shows potential for real-world application in pose-guided pose estimation and single image-based 3D object reconstruction.

A group G exhibits property $R_\infty$ if all automorphisms $\varphi$ of G produce an infinite number of twisted conjugacy classes. In such cases, we determine the $R_\infty$-nilpotency degree by finding the least integer c such that the quotient $G/\gamma_{c+1}(G)$ possesses the $R_\infty$ property. In this research, we derive the $R_\infty$-nilpotency degree of Generalized Solvable Baumslag-Solitar groups $\Gamma_n$ and explicitly calculate the lower central series for $\Gamma_n$. Additionally, we decompose the nilpotent quotients $\Gamma_{n,c}$ as semidirect products of finitely generated abelian groups, and we identify which invertible matrices can be extended into automorphisms of $\Gamma_{n,c}$.

Instead of presuming hypothetical new physics will be found at future colliders, 
we consider a different possibility where there isn't any. In this case, 
our main goal would be to find out if the unusual Standard Model fits within a vast landscape of possibilities. A crucial step towards achieving this would be to determine the stability of the Higgs potential, which relies on a precise measurement of the top quark mass. Reaching top quark mass precision beyond 0.6 GeV will likely require the use of information from top quark pairs at a 100 TeV collider or through the development of advanced top quark production techniques at the LHC.

A new technique is developed to process time-sensitive data from ultra-fast experiments using an approach based on optimization in a pathway framework. This technique is successfully tested on data from experiments involving X-ray scattering and electron diffraction to analyze the breakdown of molecules. Results from applying the technique accurately match experimental findings and highlight key molecular movements, further aligning with other independent experimental evidence. What's more, this approach effectively considers the continuity of molecular structures and is resilient against noisy data.

We present the results of the first calculations of the longitudinal and transverse light-front distribution amplitudes for several mesons, specifically $D^*$, $D^*_s$, $\rho$, $\phi$, $K^*$, and $\J/\psi$. This calculation also yields distribution amplitudes for the vector kaon, providing confirmation of lattice QCD predictions; in contrast to other calculations, our results show a significant difference between the left and right distribution amplitudes.

We investigate key properties of the space ${\Sigma}_s^{\sigma}$, which arises from combining the standard sigma-algebra on the set $\{1, 2, \ldots, s\}$ with an arbitrary countable index $\sigma$. The nontriviality of this space, ${\Sigma}_s^{\sigma}$, depends on whether the probability measure $P$ assigns a value of less than $1$ to the event $\{1\}$, and we derive essential facts about its structure, including measures ${\mathcal{E}}$ and ${\mathcal{F}}$ that satisfy specific consistency conditions. Our results also concern a game played between players $P$ and $Q$, who take actions $\tau$ and $\zeta$, respectively, which are then evaluated against measures ${\mathcal{E}}$ and ${\mathcal{F}}$ that are in an opposing sense 'dominated'.

Segmentation of unseen imaging modalities without manual labels presents significant difficulties due to the considerable time and resources needed for annotation. Current techniques typically rely on either domain adaptation or semi-supervised learning, however these approaches have notable limitations.  To overcome these challenges, we propose cutting tool, a simple yet efficient segmentation pipeline for unseen modalities that requires minimal supervision in the form of rough masks.  Unlike traditional approaches, cutting tool does not involve complex step-by-step processes but rather utilizes a single easy-to-interpret loss function that guides segmentation.  We validate the effectiveness of our method by applying it to two complex segmentation tasks and the results demonstrate its superiority over existing techniques.

Our proposed algorithm, Feature Mapping RNN, leverages key concepts in machine
learning, including neural network-based feature learning and transfer learning
in a novel way by combining them. It employs an RNN to forecast future video features
and actions by using only the initial frames of each video. Feature Mapping RNN
uses a two-part approach with a primary feature extraction layer based on RNN and
a secondary prediction layer also based on RNN. This results in an highly efficient
network with minimal computations that can operate in real-time even on mobile
devices, making it suitable for widespread use. Our research assesses the algorithm's
performance on action recognition datasets and demonstrates that it significantly
surpasses all comparable state-of-the-art techniques while achieving fast processing
speeds.

Thousands of white-light stellar flares are now being observed through high precision, long-baseline photometry from space missions including Kepler, K2, and TESS, which provide vital information for assessing exoplanetary biosignatures and the habitability of planets in low-mass stars' UV environments. Despite this advancement, a critical limitation remains in assessing these variables, which stems from the lack of data on near-ultraviolet spectral stellar flares. As such, we have developed an empirical approach that uses visible and near-infrared plasma emission data to estimate UV emission from flare stars, specifically focusing on M dwarfs. By combining spectral data from the Hubble Space Telescope, the Galaxy Evolution Satellite, and the International Ultraviolet Explorer, we created two empirical templates for all-sky and equatorial regions, respectively. These templates cover the range of UV radiation from 1,550 to 3,000 Angstroms. Next, we applied these templates to visible and near-infrared spectral data from 30 M dwarf flare stars observed from space and ground, which revealed a strong correlation between UV and IR emission during a flare. Furthermore, we found that all-sky template fits surpassed those from the equatorial region, indicating that solar UV radiation may be an underestimation. Lastly, we fitted our all-sky template to visible and near-infrared data from 88 stellar flares observed from space and ground, which provided crucial data for calculating and comparing total energy releases and energy fluxes in

We are exploring the deformation theory of G2-instantons on nearly G2-manifolds. A one-to-one connection exists between nearly parallel G2 structures and real Killing spinors, enabling the deformation theory to be formulated through the use of spinors and Dirac operators. We establish that the space of infinitesimal deformations for an instanton is equivalent to the kernel of an elliptic operator. With this approach, we prove that abelian instantons exhibit rigidity, and subsequently apply these results to define the deformation space of the canonical connection on nearly G2-manifolds with a normal homogeneous structure of four dimensions.

A bounded linear operator $T$ on a complex Hilbert space with a countable basis is referred to as C-normal if it satisfies a particular condition under the action of a conjugation operation. Specifically, $T$ can be said to be C-normal if there exists a conjugation operation $C$ on $H$ such that $TC^\ast CT = C^\ast T^\ast T$. In the context of function mappings, a self-map $\varphi$ of the open unit disc can be described using a linear fractional expression. This work investigates the conditions under which the composition operator $C_\varphi$ and weighted composition operator $W_{\psi, \varphi}$, where $\psi$ is another function, are both C-normal operators for specific conjugation operations $C$ and $\psi$.

This paper delves into a type of partition that excludes elements divisible by p. Specifically, the study targets p-core p'-partitions which adhere to these constraints. Notably, the largest of these p-core p'-partitions can be modeled by a long walk through a p-vertex graph, with edges assigned via the modulo p addition rule. Moreover, the research also identifies a systematic collection of significant p-core p'-partitions that establish a substantial lower limit on their maximum size.

Neural network-based point cloud models have achieved great success in various domains but it's crucial for them to handle test-time transformations efficiently.
Currently, applying the same transformation to input point clouds results in a common set of learned features, which means the models lack versatility in handling diverse 3D transformations such as rotations, reflections, and translations.
To overcome this limitation, we propose a new approach called Point Transform Networks (PTNs), which allows multiple 3D transformations to be applied to point clouds at test time using learnable transformation parameters.
PTNs consist of three key components: a feature extractor, a position encoder, and a prediction head, utilizing the principles of multi-task learning to generate features for various transformations.
By introducing an auxiliary classifier for related tasks like position prediction and reflection identification, PTNs enhance the robustness of learned point cloud features.
Through extensive experiments on three 3D transformation-related datasets, we demonstrate PTNs' ability to generalize well across different 3D transformations such as rotations, translations, and reflections.

We're investigating medium access techniques in Frequency-Modulated Continuous-Wave (FMCW) radar networks with all radar units utilizing identical settings, such as sweep duration and frequency characteristics. We're developing and evaluating ALOHA and CSMA protocols to minimize the impact of narrowband interference, introducing a new metric to gauge performance based on network throughput. In the case of ALOHA, we analyze the probabilities of interference and system efficiency under different system parameters. We observe that FMCW network behavior diverges from typical wireless communication patterns. In some scenarios, increased packet transmission can decrease interference probabilities. We introduce a clear channel assessment process, known as medium sensing, for CSMA, also defining metrics to gauge its effectiveness. In our analysis of CSMA, radar units transmit data after confirming an empty transmission path. We examine CSMA's medium sensing success rate, interference probabilities, and system efficiency. We introduce a new medium sensing success rate model that considers the combined impact of system parameters. In the case of multiple access, we introduce a new metric to gauge performance, measuring the combined interference and system efficiency. We also introduce ALOHA and CSMA comparison methods that minimize interference in FMCW radar networks.

Recent experiments employing various methods have sought to detect the entangled two-photon absorption phenomenon across a range of materials. A new investigation adopts a distinct approach, focusing on analyzing changes in a Hong-Ou-Mandel interferogram resulting from entangled photon interaction. Utilizing Rhodamine B solution as a model nonlinear material exposed to 800 nm photons generated through type-II spontaneous parametric down conversion, researchers have explored conditions facilitating detection of HOM interferogram visibility modifications. A supporting model portrays the sample as an energy-preserving spectral filter, aligning with the observed results and providing insight into the entangled two-photon absorption process. By combining cutting-edge quantum interference techniques with a detailed mathematical framework, this work presents an innovative perspective on ETPA research.

We calculate rational T-equivariant elliptic cohomology of complex projective spaces derived from finite dimensional T-representations V. This is accomplished by establishing that the T-equivariant elliptic cohomology theory constructed in Gre05, and the T^2-equivariant theory constructed in Bar22, share a key decomposition. This key decomposition facilitates reducing the T-equivariant cohomology computation to T^2-equivariant cohomology of complex spheres, whose computation is already available from Bar22.

Temporal knowledge graph completion has emerged as a leading approach for
inferring accurate and missing event and temporal knowledge graph information.
Building upon successful applications of tensor decomposition in static graph
completions, we introduce Time-LowFER - an extension of the low-rank factorization
model that is both efficient in parameters and attentive to time constraints.
We recognize current time representation approaches' shortcomings and suggest a
cycle-aware time-encoding framework for time characteristics that is universally
applicable and provides a more comprehensive time representation. Our unified
framework focuses on processing time-sensitive data within temporal knowledge graph
embeddings. Comprehensive experiments are conducted on multiple time-aware
knowledge graph benchmarks, and our model surpasses state-of-the-art time-sensitive
approaches in inferential tasks by 3%. The project code is available at https://github.com/hugehelpertg/Time-LowFER.

In the field of rigid-body impact sound synthesis, the sound produced by the ground is often overlooked.  This research aims to rectify this by providing a model that enables the simulation of sound ground can produce when an object drops onto it.  The model relies on a simple mass-spring diagram to analyze the sound ground generates.  This diagram consists of a mass representing the ground anchored in a spring-damper system that represents the sound wave propagation.  The equation of this diagram is solved using the implicit Newmark method.  This solution, in turn, informs a wave equation that describes sound propagation in the ground.  The solution to this equation is achieved through the Monte-Carlo simulation of a wave packet.  This simulation allows for the numerical calculation of the sound produced by the ground when an object drops onto it.  The model is verified through the simulation of an object dropping onto different ground materials.  The model also allows for the calculation of a ground sound frequency spectrum that will help designers and analysts to optimize the sound produced by a dropping object based on that sound's characteristics.

A prevalent form of demonstrating Bell nonlocality known as the all-versus-nothing proof is presented without the use of inequalities. This concept consists of two main species, referred to as "always-type" and "sometimes-type", which have received significant research attention. Past studies on "always-type" all-versus-nothing proofs have primarily involved perfect correlations from stabilizer states. This has led many researchers to conclude that perfect correlations are the sole means of yielding "always-type" all-versus-nothing proofs. Contrary to this prevailing notion, our study offers a "always-type" all-versus-nothing proof rooted in non-perfect correlations. This research aims to clarify an enduring misconception and potentially expands our understanding of Bell nonlocality while also opening avenues for advancements in quantum information technologies.

In flat band systems, constrained environments result in atypical behaviors influenced by randomness, indicating minimal movement. Molecular orbital representations of these systems introduce random MO models, retaining the degeneracy of the flat bands even in the presence of disorder. The zero modes in chiral systems with an imbalance in sublattices fall into this category. Following a general description of constructing flat bands through MOs, various examples are examined with numerical proof, including the sawtooth lattice in one dimension and the hyper-Pyrochlore lattice across any number of dimensions, extending the principles seen in two-dimensional Kagome and three-dimensional Pyrochlore lattices to higher dimensions.

A newly created hydrogen boride monolayer, existing in the Cmmm phase, exhibits potential as a superconductor due to similarities with MgB2 and an abundance of hydrogen within its structure. Utilizing density functional theory, we've used first-principles calculations to investigate its electronic, vibrational, and superconducting properties. Our results show that this system possesses a typical s++-wave superconducting state characterized by a strong attractive electron-phonon interaction, primarily resulting from hydrogens' presence. Moreover, hydrogen's impact on lattice stability plays a crucial role, as observed in MgB2. Ultimately, we've discovered that this hydrogen boride monolayer can achieve a relatively high superconducting critical temperature, specifically between 1.10 K and 1.61 K, depending on the phonon model used.

Research on flattened partitions, a concept identified by Andrew V. Slae through OEIS number A124324, is conducted. A distinct counting method is developed for them and relates to the reduced partitions counted by Euler. Additionally, a specific fluctuation statistic is examined. It alternates between a positive and zero values, much like a random walk, and follows a known distribution that can be proven using two different methods: one method links to the multiplicative congruences considered by Carlitz and Levine, and another method involves enumerative combinatorics connected to the number of distinct terms in ascending flattened partitions.

We categorize and understand a certain aspect of attractiveness in groups that use arithmetic, and derive statements indicating a dual nature related to their stable components, characteristics, patterns, and associated algebraic structures. To accomplish this, we study the movement patterns over the characteristics of the part of these groups that are stable and have manageable properties, particularly demonstrating the rigidity where any stable movement remains unchanged, which is a more comprehensive interpretation of Furstenberg's earlier work concerning patterns on the torus. Additionally, under the assumption that the group has a certain higher-level structure, we prove that the movement patterns over the characteristics of these groups that are stable and have manageable properties, and have a certain complexity structure, exhibit rigidity as well.

Highly automated driving systems designed to operate in case of failure demand robust architecture and contingency planning mechanisms. To safeguard against electric and electronic failures, a backup system is triggered by an arbitration logic that prioritizes functional safety above all else. To uphold the standards set forth by ISO 26262, rigorous testing of this logic is mandatory. Through this validation, one can confidently ensure the reliability of system responses in times of crisis and prevent aberrant system states from materializing. Traditional safety assessment tools are often inadequate in this capacity, prompting us to propose an advanced method centered around formal verification, leveraging model checking in particular. To demonstrate the efficacy of this approach, we carefully recreate the driving system's dynamics, define and formalize key safety criteria, and scope the analysis within the guidelines specified by ISO 26262. Upon successfully verifying a high-automation fail-safe logic aligned with industrial standards, we discovered critical errors previously unaccounted for in more conventional evaluations, thereby significantly enhancing the reliability of automotive safety-critical systems.

Identifying clusters in complex systems across various fields such as power, genetics, finance, and astronomy is a pressing challenge. These systems often evolve dynamically, rendering traditional static clustering methods ineffective. In this paper, a novel approach is presented that leverages time-series data to detect communities within dynamic systems by defining a state similarity measure that reflects mutual influence and utilizes the Koopman operator to handle nonlinear relationships, thus extending the approach to a broad spectrum of applications. This method's effectiveness is demonstrated through clustering of a linear system, the non-linear 39-bus transmission network, and variables derived from atmospheric data in the Amazon rainforest.

Recent research into Leibnizian calculus has centered on evaluating different fundamental approaches to describe its mathematical processes.  Many scholars, such as Ishiguro and Levey, rely on a Weierstrassian perspective; others, like Leibniz, employ an infinitesimal method using the law of continuity.  However, a fresh analysis by Arthur and Rau of Leibniz's earlier writings has uncovered evidence of a reliance on a distinction between abstract and concrete notions of function.  They propose that a logic-based approach, known as Kuczarski logic, provides the most accurate representation of Leibnizian calculus, ultimately informing their understanding of the Leibnizian differential calculus.

Using the Effective Field Theory of Large Scale Structure, we make predictions for HI intensity mapping power spectrum multipoles based on perturbation theory. These predictions will allow us to constrain cosmological parameters using mildly non-linear scales from data that will be obtained from interferometric HI intensity mapping experiments. Assuming that the experiments will be like CHORD and PUMA, we run a series of analyses on mock data that accurately represents how these surveys are conducted at redshift z=0.5, comparing these to the performance that can be expected from stage 4 optical galaxy surveys. The impact of removing foregrounds using methods that rely on simulations is accounted for in the analysis which also looks at how much information about the universe is lost by not including the cross power spectrum in the analysis. Based on this analysis, we revise our previous forecast that stage 5 HI intensity mapping surveys could constrain the parameters A_s, n_s and w_0 in a range of 10 percent to 20 percent, but that stage 6 surveys would be needed to constrain Omega_m and sigma_8. However, our new findings show that with the help of foregrounds mitigation, stage 5 surveys could already achieve this level of precision while stage 6 surveys would achieve a maximum deviation of 9.5 percent. The inclusion of the cross power spectrum is also found to increase the precision of the parameter constraints to 6-13 percent.

Christensen and Hasannasab established that if a hypothetical operator T transforms sequence vectors $e_n$ into $e_{n+1}$ for all natural numbers, then the sequence is linearly independent only when the dimension of the sequence's vector space is infinite. In our research, we derive this result as a specific instance of a more comprehensive model-theoretic finding. Then, focusing on vector spaces, we demonstrate that if a condition such as $T(e_i)=e_{\phi(i)}$ is to replace the previous operator assumption, $\phi$ must be equivalent to the successor function, defined as incrementing a number by 1. Finally, we explore a more complex generalization of this result, substituting the earlier operator assumption with a more complex condition.

One key limitation of recommender systems is data scarcity resulting in considerable variability. Various approaches have been implemented to optimize the bias-variance equilibrium utilizing supplementary information. In particular, methods incorporating text-based document modeling have significantly improved accuracy by incorporating data like reviews, summaries, and narratives when user-item rating matrices are sparse. However, these models have limited ability to learn user preferences and item representations due to the absence of sequential user-item interactions. In contrast, the proposed PaperRank method leverages contextual representations of users and items by analyzing the temporal co-occurrence of users and items within recommender systems datasets. It fuses the obtained representations with embeddings produced by supplementing data using pre-trained word models. Finally, the recommended outputs are generated through a straightforward ranking of rated items by their total score. The effectiveness of PaperRank is validated on two real-world datasets by measuring its performance on two critical metrics against existing approaches. The empirical evaluation confirms that PaperRank achieves superior performance and regularizes models effectively.

Independent unitarily invariant self-adjoint random matrices $H$ and $M$ are examined in this study, where it's known that the asymptotic freeness of $H$ and $M$ holds true. Building on a finding by Benigno and Chula in a previous study, our research expands upon their result by showing that the central limit theorem for non-commutative random variables, as defined by Baisch and Bun in a different context, can be satisfied by the spectra of the random matrices $H$ and $M$. This is accomplished while requiring only a linear dependence on the size of the matrices, rather than a quadratic dependence, as might be expected. To achieve this result, our research involves establishing a new Banach space, which we term $S^2_2$, and demonstrating that the random matrices $H$ and $M$ can be mapped into the $S^2_2$-valued Banach space $S^2_{2,\infty}$ in a way that's consistent with the central limit theorem. This involves a number of technical difficulties, particularly in dealing with the potential singularity of the random matrices and the challenges of handling operator-valued Banach spaces. As a result, our research may have the effect of broadening the scope of the non-commutative central limit theorem, while also revealing connections between the properties of random matrices and the characteristics of non-commutative Banach spaces.

This paper revisits monitoring real-time systems by leveraging properties described either in Metric Interval Temporal Logic or as Timed B\"uchi Automata. We propose effective, symbolic, and online monitoring methods in several contexts that take advantage of 'zones', a concept familiar from efficient model checking of Timed Automata. These contexts encompass improved treatment of timing discrepancies, monitoring under timing ambiguity, and the extension of monitoring to provide earliest time estimates for when decisive verdicts can be rendered.

The decay reactions $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi f_0(980)$ and $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi
a_0(980)$ are examined in detail. Attention is focused on isospin breaking and
the mixing between $f_0(980)$ and $a_0(980)$, both of which are generated by meson-meson interactions. Our analysis indicates that the primary source of isospin breaking arises from transition matrix $T$ terms exhibiting isospin breaking and that additional isospin breaking arises due to the presence of loops containing kaons, which necessarily produce isospin breaking as a result of the mass differences between kaons and anti-kaons. Our calculations demonstrate that the presence of $T$ terms and $K\bar K$ loops yields acceptable descriptions of existing data for $a_0(980)$ and is consistent with current understanding of the scalar resonances $f_0(1710)$ and $a_0(980)$.

The GRAVITY acquisition camera is utilized in the Very Large Telescope Interferometer's (VLTI) internal data stream, capturing images of the formed optical focal plane array. It employs four distinct optical functions: a 0.6 micrometer short-pass filter, an image orienting prism, an equalizing lens, and an electronic camera. The camera's objective is to visualize the interferometric array's point-spread function, facilitating the alignment of individual telescopes and the validation of our knowledge of the array's optical parameters. The GRAVITY acquisition camera operates in a standalone mode, facilitating the alignment of VLTI's Gaussian beam array, which is a crucial step in achieving the desired full-field diffraction-limited sensitivity.

We examine $k$-Center variants in graphs of reduced diameter and sparse edge connectivity. Our study focuses on the Capacitated $k$-Supplier with Outliers (CkSwO) issue, which incorporates supplier capacity constraints. For CkSwO with a subset of the center selection options, we demonstrate scheme complexities that complement the interaction between supplier and client capacities. This leads to an efficient scheme for solving ApX-CkSwO in graphs with a logarithmic diameter and obtain a near-optimal approximation for this problem in networks with a polylogarithmic diameter. Similarly, we address the Metric Tree Survivor problem and develop a scheme to solve ApX-Tree Survivor in graphs with an approximate logarithmic diameter, achieving a near-optimal result. Moreover, we propose an algorithm for the Metric TSP with a 2-approximation in cubic planar graphs, extending the same for the Control $k$-Center problem in tree networks and deriving a near-optimal result for Control $k$-Center in bipartite graphs.

In our paper, it's demonstrated that every entire solution of the equation $\Delta_{\eta}^{m}f-Q_1=(\Delta_{\eta}^{k}f-Q_{2})e^{P}$ exhibits hyper-order with the same degree as the polynomial $P$, and based on this result, we establish the differential difference counterpart to Bruck's conjecture. Furthermore, we have successfully proved Bruck's conjecture for the specific instance where the hyper-order of $f$ is less than $\frac{1}{2}$.

This research paper explores solving polynomial linear systems in the presence of errors using an evaluation-interpolation technique, with a focus on minimizing the number of computations required to recover the solution. This is crucial because it depends on parameters like the degrees and size of the linear system as well as the error rate. As part of an ongoing series on solving polynomial linear systems with errors, we build on our previous work which focused on a specific case scenario. In contrast, this paper provides a comprehensive approach that is applicable across a wide range of polynomial linear systems and error rates. Additionally, the paper includes a detailed analysis of the evaluation and interpolation steps, leading to a formula that estimates the minimum number of computations required. This formula is then expressed as a continuous problem, with a related variational equation analyzed to determine key properties, including solutions, boundedness, and homotopy invariance. This research enables the development of a finite-element method that solves a related discrete problem, providing a practical solution to the original problem in the realm of computer algebra. This problem is distinct from the numerical field and requires a multi-parameter analysis, making it challenging to extend our results to other problems in this domain, such as polynomial factorization with errors.

In the ultrastrong coupling regime of cavity QED, we show that symmetry protects a type of photon bundle emission. The parity symmetry of the Rabi model allows for the creation of super-Rabi oscillations, resulting in the periodic production of even photons in the cavity. This phenomenon occurs through a laser-driven qubit flip and transitions influenced by Rabi interaction, preserving parity. By introducing dissipation, the system only emits photons at specific intervals, producing an intense light pulse. The intensity and spectral properties of the light it emits can be adjusted by modifying the Rabi coupling. We have demonstrated that the parity symmetry of the Rabi model can be utilized to create a logical qubit zero-spin operation, either a single $\pi$-rotation of the Rabi model or a super-$\pi$-rotation protected by parity, depending on the parameters.

A unified analytical equation of state for the equilibrium gas phase of pure alkali metals is developed, covering the entire pressure range (up to 1000 GPa) and temperature range (up to 1000 K). This comprehensive equation of state is based on experimental and theoretical data for six specific elements (Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs, and Fr). By incorporating interatomic interactions and using a generalized Maoutian-Fortov equation, an analytical solution is achieved. This precise analytical equation of state permits the derivation of important properties, including isothermal compressibility, anisothermal compressibility, adiabatic index, and sound wave velocities, among others. Additionally, an analytical expression for the chemical potential is included, enabling the identification of critical points for each element. By applying this equation of state, various phenomena, such as the interaction between sound waves and their coupling with a superconducting pair, are investigated.

In the context of vector-meson dominance model, properties of light vector mesons in local parity breaking mediums with chiral imbalance are explored. By utilizing a finite lowest-order local effective Lagrangian derived from QED for vector ρ and ω mesons, a mass spectrum as a function of momentum and chiral chemical potential is determined. Furthermore, in addition to the existing Chern-Simons effect, which differentiates the transverse polarizations of these mesons, a significant radiatively induced contribution arises at a few hundred MeV for momentum and chiral chemical potential.

We examine the fundamental challenge of estimating a sparse network's node count under conditions of uncertainty, specifically when the network contains a large number of malicious nodes with complete network knowledge, unbounded processing power, and the ability to manipulate the protocol freely. Our main achievement is a probabilistic algorithm designed to estimate a sparse, complex network's size, even in the presence of an unspecified number of malicious nodes not exceeding O(n^(1-delta)) - where delta can be any arbitrarily small positive number. The algorithm generates an approximate estimate with a fixed constant factor, specifically a fraction of the logarithm of the network size, and this estimation is accurate to a large extent (up to 1 - epsilon) among the genuine nodes for any arbitrarily small positive epsilon. The algorithm runs on genuine nodes with limited processing power, relying on randomly generated nodes for additional processing power, and is resistant to tampering by malicious nodes. The algorithm's efficiency is determined by the parameter beta, which is a function of delta and can be adjusted to tolerate a larger number of malicious nodes. Our results show that this algorithm is precise, accurate, and meets the specified conditions. The algorithm requires a one-time network fluctuation, involving a small delay and minimal communication, to establish a common reference point for subsequent executions. Our results also show that this algorithm can be used in iterative scenarios to constantly monitor the network and detect a growing number of malicious nodes.

In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter configurations, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data. Our novel approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by replacing the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint with an algebraic equation, allowing for a choice of conformal factor instead of mean curvature. By bypassing the issues of solution existence and non-uniqueness associated with the Hamiltonian constraint, we leverage a conformal structure to simplify the decomposition process and bypass the issues typically encountered with conformal 3-manifolds. Our method is particularly beneficial for scenarios involving fundamental fields, where conventional methods are often too simplistic or unwieldy.

The main objective of the JUNO experiment involves identifying the neutrino mass ordering by utilizing a large, 20-kt liquid-scintillator detector equipped with photomultiplier tubes. For optimal results, the experiment's instruments are placed at a 53-degree angle from which they can collect data influenced by the neutrino background, external light, and other factors. To achieve accuracy, researchers use various techniques, including the recovery of event timing, charge integration, and event topography. By selecting high-quality events and applying convolution and event reconstruction methods, researchers can obtain accurate data which is then utilized in analyzing the neutrino mass ordering. The experiment's instruments are placed at a 53-degree angle from which they can collect data influenced by the neutrino background, external light, and other factors. To achieve accuracy, researchers use various techniques, which will be further detailed in this presentation.

In practical scenarios like power consumption forecasting and air quality analysis, long sequence time-series forecasting (LSTF) is indispensable. The complexity of multidimensional time series data presents significant model demands, necessitating precise representation of long-term input-output relationships and relationships across multiple dimensions. Recent advancements in the application of long short-term memory (LSTM) models have shown promise, but multidimensional LSTM models are difficult to optimize and suffer from inadequate theoretical foundations. This research presents a new LSTM-based framework, dubbed Lifestyle-LSTM, incorporating the following key distinct features: Lifestyle-Selection LSTM and Lifestyle-Merging LSTM. The former utilizes a filter layer that enables the selection of most relevant dimensions and series, while the latter integrates the remaining series through an LSTM process that produces a consolidated forecast. When compared to state-of-the-art models, such as Vectorized LSTM and Multivariate LSTM, the Lifestyle-LSTM framework has consistently surpassed them on various numerical and symbolic metrics and achieved a 1.2% improvement in accuracy. The results are based on a extensive dataset consisting of 1000+ numerical time series, including the famous UCI dataset, as well as a large collection of air quality data.

Astronomical observations from ground-based telescopes can be distorted by Earth's atmosphere due to differential dispersion that varies by wavelength. Observations made off-axis, other than directly through the atmosphere's center, are further distorted. The Atmospheric Dispersion Corrector addresses this issue by using lasers to measure the atmosphere's dispersion, thereby allowing telescopes to correct for this effect. We've developed an ADC prototype that incorporates an f/5 supernet telescope specifically designed for this purpose, along with a dual-laser system to perceive the atmosphere from both ends of the observable spectrum. By pairing this with the IPAC Heritage Code that models the atmosphere, we've simulated the ADC's performance and calculated its expected outcomes.

Recently, pre-trained models have significantly impacted ranking systems, delivering outstanding results. To balance high performance with computational efficiency, knowledge distillation is now extensively employed. In this research, we address two critical challenges in knowledge distillation for ranking models: 1) leveraging multiple teachers; and 2) utilizing label data within the distillation process. We introduce the Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble (PILE) framework to concurrently address both concerns. By iteratively combining multi-teacher logits guided by label information, PILE has shown superior performance in offline and online experiments. Furthermore, our method has been successfully integrated into a real-world commercial search platform.

Bosonic dark matter with a very low mass can be detected through the analysis of an untraditional astronomical signal related to the matter's wave-like properties. This signal arises from changes in the matter's density within a certain mass range, affecting the frequency range of $10^{-14}$ to $10^{-8}$ Hz. The importance of accurately matching the detector's response to the signal frequency and reducing non-bosonic background noise are crucial elements in the detection method. The signal's components at or near zero frequency are particularly relevant because they are not affected by environmental factors such as seismic activity. The use of ultra-low-temperature nuclear spin detectors near rooms that are thermally isolated from each other could facilitate the detection of ultralight bosonic dark matter.

This paper explores the recovery of one-dimensional Radon measures on a torus from their low-frequency Fourier components up to a given cutoff frequency, denoted as Kc. The proposed method involves minimizing the total variation among all compatible Radon measures through the problem of basis pursuit in the continuum (BPC). A characterization of BPC's solution set, including uniqueness and sparse solutions, is established in terms of a Toeplitz matrix. The uniqueness and characteristics of BPC's solution rely on the eigenvalue properties of this matrix. The solutions range from a single, weighted Dirac mass for certain conditions to infinitely many Dirac masses in other cases. The number of Dirac masses in each case is influenced by the rank of a positive or negative semi-definite matrix. The positive or negative definiteness of the matrix also determines the weights of the Dirac masses as either nonnegative or nonpositive, respectively.

P4 has become the standard language for configuring reconfigurable programmable switches, with the V1Model architecture being the most widely used implementation. An open-source compiler for the P4 consortium allows for syntax analysis and translation of P416 programs into hardware-independent code, but a compiler backend to map this code to V1Model switch resources is needed. A freely available compiler backend for P416 programs and V1Model architecture-based switches has been lacking, with some vendors providing proprietary compilers for their specific switch models. Our research fills this gap by presenting a novel compiler backend that transforms hardware-independent code into V1Model resources. Our approach is based on an initial parsing technique to analyze the P416 program and identify its functions. Then, a resource allocator is activated to ensure there are enough resources for the program in advance. Next, a data-path builder and initiator/driver generator are used to create the initial data path configuration. Finally, an optimizer is employed to optimize the data path configuration based on network traffic patterns. Our compiler backend was tested and validated by mapping different P416 programs onto an Apstra INF1 fixture and an NetFPE switch, representing both fixed function and customizable use cases. Our results show that our compiler backend's resource utilization closely matches the actual values measured on the NetFPE switch, while there were discrepancies between the allocated and utilized resources on the INF1 fixture.

In numerical simulations involving fluid dynamics, the Raviart-Thomas elements are widely used to approximate vector-valued variables like velocity or momentum. Nevertheless, the standard finite element methods that employ the lowest-order quadrilateral Raviart-Thomas elements tend to have low spatial accuracy in the vector transport equation. This paper explores two methods that elevate the accuracy of transporting such vector-valued fields across curved surfaces in two-dimensional environments. One method enhances the transported field by projecting it onto a higher-order function space before solving the transport equation. In contrast, the other method utilizes a mixed finite element approach to concurrently solve for both the transported field and its vorticity, introducing a stabilisation strategy via a Streamline Upwind Petrov-Galerkin method. These schemes are validated and their performance compared in a series of numerical experiments involving both specially designed and standard rotating shallow-water models.

The remarkable effectiveness of deep learning has sparked various concerns regarding ethics, encompassing skewed predictions and data security risks. To address these problems, experts are introducing ethical considerations into the prediction process through the use of standardized metrics like fairness metrics and risk assessment tools. Nevertheless, for more intricate applications such as medical diagnosis, decisions are increasingly reliant on the expertise of specialists. To bring decision-making inline with medical professionals' expertise and values, researchers are integrating ethical metrics into expert judgment, including optimizing diagnosis policies to minimize medical risks. This research delves into the development of a novel method to balance fairness and safety, utilizing a two-step process based on the maximum relaxation technique and an optimization algorithm sourced from the realm of game theory. Our proposed method successfully balances the need for accurate predictions and risk aversion in predictive analytics, ultimately contributing to safer and more transparent decision-making.

Scientists analyzed collision data from the LHCb experiment to identify excited states of a particular subatomic particle, known as the B-c plus. They found two peaks in the data, each corresponding to a possible state. One state has a mass of around 6841.2 MeV and fits expectations for a particular predicted state. A second state has a mass of around 6872.1 MeV and may be consistent with a different predicted state.

In the last few years, the creation of accurate numerical solutions for problems with Hamiltonian dynamics led to the establishment of a specific class of energy-preserving Runge-Kutta methods known as Hamiltonian Boundary Value Methods (HBVMs). These methods can be interpreted as a continuous, multi-step approach, similar to Runge-Kutta methods but with continuous stages, and are explored here in the context of more general differential problems.

This paper introduces an innovative approach called local critic training, a model-parallel learning method utilizing specialized networks to refine neural network updates. By segmenting the main network into separate layer groups and applying error gradients from corresponding critic modules, the learning process is efficiently decoupled for both CNNs and RNNs. We demonstrate that this method not only converges to an optimal solution, but also facilitates structural optimization. The proposed method also significantly reduces training time and decreases the memory usage per machine. The code is openly accessible on the GitHub repository https://github.com/hjdw2/Local-critic-training.

Three-dimensional chaotic scattering has garnered less attention than its two-dimensional counterpart. In this research, a three-dimensional open Hamiltonian system is analyzed where the non-dissipative boundaries initially deviate from Wada's characteristics, changing topologically. Focusing on the effects of dissipation, this study investigates how this system alters when weak dissipation lowers the system's energy below its critical value. Interestingly, this investigation reveals that non-Wada basins transition into partially Wada basins under such weak dissipation. Moreover, numerical results demonstrate the emergence of Wada points on the boundaries of these basins in three-dimensional systems. Ultimately, this research indicates that Wada basins in three-dimensional systems exhibit increased stability when subjected to low levels of dissipation.

A theoretical model involving an intricate scalar field that connects to (e+, e-) pairs is considered within the realm of non-abelian gauge theories. This type of scenario might arise in certain left-right symmetric models. If the scalar's real component becomes heavy, it will decay into these e+ e- pairs. These e+ e- pairs will then interact with a similar scalar field, causing them to become confined within "strings". These e+ e- pairs will then remain within these "strings" until they are dislodged and can decay, typically propagating a considerable distance between their creation and decay points. Potential drawbacks to this theory include its high energy requirements, exceeding what's currently available, and its predicted lifespan of the "strings", significantly shorter than the decay time of the e+ e- pairs.

Human action understanding in complex videos has far-reaching implications, 
which this study addresses by proposing the Hierarchical Attention Network (HAN).
Compared to current deep learning-based methods, HAN stands out due to its
capacity for (1) extended temporal structure capture; (2) explicit modeling of 
temporal transitions between frames and segments, and (3) the ability to learn key 
regions in frames and temporal segments through its multi-step attention mechanism.
Evaluations of the model on established action recognition benchmarks indicate
remarkable performance improvements.

Investigating the thermodynamics and cosmic censorship conjecture in Reissner-Nordström anti-de Sitter black holes through scalar field scattering yields results that support the first law of thermodynamics for non-extremal black holes, confirming that the singularity in such black holes is hidden by an event horizon. The validity of this theory near the extreme boundary is confirmed, but it fails for true extremal black holes. This study also analyzes the interaction between a spin-2 particle and the Reissner-Nordström anti-de Sitter black hole, verifying that the principles of conservation for both momentum and energy hold for non-extremal black holes.

This article will examine the concept of star formation (SF) through observation, and its progression over time, offering a fresh understanding of the process, particularly relevant since planet formation emerges from it and sheds new light on the origins of life in the universe.

This paper proposes a new computational method to estimate uncertainty and relevance metrics, like Shannon entropy and mutual information, for complex probability distributions that can't be directly calculated. By leveraging Nested Sampling, this approach enables evaluation of such quantities even when only sampling data is available. Three case studies are provided to illustrate its effectiveness: one with a straightforward Gaussian distribution; another with a real-world experiment involving observation scheduling for signal period estimation; and a scenario with predicting future outcomes from past data under heavy-tailed conditions.
