Our analysis reveals that solitary waves in precompressed woodpile chains feature a single Stokes curve, accompanied by oscillations, whereas a diatomic chain exhibits two oscillatory contributions, cancelling out under certain mass ratios to produce localized waves, thereby confirming prior numerical and experimental observations on the phenomenon in non-precompressed diatomic chains.

Extra energy injected by primordial features in inflationary models can generate massive particles exceeding the Hubble scale during inflation. This prospect expands the scope of cosmological collider physics, where the signals produced by these particles are usually suppressed by the Boltzmann distribution. Our analysis explores the mechanics of a cosmic collider through two types of primordial features. Firstly, we consider oscillating primordial features, encompassing cases of massive field oscillations and oscillatory features in the inflationary potential. Secondly, we look at any sharp feature within the inflationary landscape. These features give rise to a narrow period of heavy particle production, separated by large scales from the usual cosmic collider signals. The distinct scale at which these signals emerge allows for their isolation from background noise, and the characteristics of these signals can reveal the type of feature and the mass of the produced particle.

Consider a graph of even order G and its complete graph counterpart K_G. A pairing of G refers to a perfect matching of K_G. A graph has the PH-property if for each pairing of K_G, it shares a perfect matching that, when combined, creates a Hamiltonian cycle of K_G. Cubic graphs that possess the PH-property have been fully characterized by Alahmadi et al. in 2015, and it follows logically that quartic graphs should be the subject of characterization next. In our work, a class of quartic graphs called accordion graphs is defined, parameterized by n and k, which we designate as A[n,k]. We find that a specified family of infinite quartic (also circulant) graphs that possess the PH-property belong to the general class of accordion graphs. The paper delves into the properties of accordion graphs in terms of pairings, which sometimes coincide with perfect matchings of G, and examines their close relationship with the Cartesian product of two cycles. Recent findings by Bogdanowicz have prompted a complete characterization of accordion graphs that are circulant graphs. It's noted that a vast majority of quartic graphs that possess the PH-property belong to this class or a few other specific exceptions.

We carry out a finite-time scaling analysis near the detrapping point in a three-state quantum walk model. The coin operator is adjusted using parameter $\rho$ that controls the speed of wavepacket dispersion. The initial state is a symmetric superposition of two coin operator eigenstates with mixing angle $\theta$. One eigenstate corresponds to full wavepacket spreading at $\theta_c(\rho)$ where none of the wavepacket remains near the initial position. At the detrapping angle $\theta_d(\rho)$, key scaling behaviors of the wavepacket near the origin match the one-dimensional wavepacket model's scaling behaviors. For $\theta$ between $\theta_c$ and $\theta_d$, there is an anisotropic critical region.

This paper explores the benefits that self-supervised learning confers on Vision Transformer (ViT), distinguishing it from convolutional networks (convnets). Our findings show that self-supervised ViT features uniquely capture the semantic structure of an image, a trait absent in supervised ViT models and convnets. Additionally, these features excel as k-NN classifiers, with self-supervised ViT models reaching a 78.3% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet when using a compact architecture. Notably, our research highlights the significance of incorporating a momentum encoder, employing multi-crop training, and using small patch sizes when utilizing ViTs. Building upon these insights, we developed the DINO self-supervised method, a form of self-distillation without the need for labelled data, and demonstrated its effectiveness by achieving an 80.1% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet when evaluating ViT-Base linearly.

A unified dark fluid model has been developed that combines a degenerate non-entropic fluid and a rank-2 dissipative fluid. The model's properties and effects on free evolution systems have been thoroughly investigated. Theoretical models like this are essential for understanding the behavior of strongly collapsed systems like neutron stars and black holes. A key aspect of the model involves two dissipative components: heat flow and viscoelasticity, which influence its entropy density. The model exhibits non-entropic behavior due to these components and thus deviates from standard hydrodynamics. The treatment of boundary conditions in the model is also critical and has been accomplished through a custom-made classification scheme for dissipative fluids. The model's equations consist of a barotropic Euler equation and two dissipative fluid equations, along with an energy equation and an entropy equation that form a complete system. The model's properties and effects are extensive, leading to numerous observations and insights in the study of gravity.

We present a straightforward proof that in three or more dimensions, the Cauchy problem for the incompressible Euler equations has a critical issue in terms of stability, specifically when using Sobolev spaces and certain types of Lorentz spaces, thereby confirming an earlier study by Bourgain and Li.

Recently, large text-conditioned generative diffusion models have received considerable attention for their impressive ability to generate high-quality images from text input alone, outperforming previous benchmarks in image generation. In the image editing domain, researchers have explored the diffusion pipeline to create state-of-the-art image editing tools, such as filling gaps in images, but only with limited guiding techniques available. To expand the applicability of diffusion guidance, we introduce a novel framework, called Semantic Guidance (SEGA), which enables easy implementation of new guidance techniques and simplifies the integration of existing ones. By designing a flexible interface for guidance techniques to interact with the diffusion pipeline, SEGA seamlessly accommodates multiple guidance methods, improves compilation efficiency, and facilitates the compilation of new techniques with minimal code modifications. To demonstrate the SEGA framework's versatility, we introduce a new guidance technique (LATTE) that combines latent semantic diffusion and texture generation to produce detailed, latent-guided natural images, outperforming state-of-the-art models like GAHD and TGD in image quality as measured by the FID score.

Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have brought about a significant transformation in the field of natural language processing. One key factor behind this success lies in the extensive training datasets available, which can be seen as an abundance of "programmed" knowledge. Inspired by the emerging field of program verification, this study explores whether the process of program formal verification can be facilitated using natural language descriptions. The study examines program counters as a possible representation of program execution states, reducing them to textual forms using supervised learning. The outcome reveals that a learned model can accurately forecast program behavior, yet also reveals limitations in differentiating between genuine and artificial uncertainties. This led to the separation of two distinct forms of uncertainty - certain yet difficult-to-predict elements ($\delta$-uncertainty) and true uncertainties (-belief). The study demonstrates that the application of Bayesian methods provides an effective solution to addressing $\delta$-uncertainty, highlighting the potential for program verification to benefit from deep learning approaches. Moreover, this concept has broader implications, suggesting that other structured forms of knowledge, such as those in verification datasets, can be seen as organized collections of programmed beliefs, and thereby shedding new light on the interplay between deep learning and program verification.

Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for sterile neutrinos existing within a specific lepton flavour. Utilizing the J/ψ particle's production and detection data from BABAR, NaNaCollaboration, and other sources, we establish restrictive limits on neutrinos with masses smaller than 0.5 GeV. Our analysis is based on recent findings from the LHCb experiment, which provided crucial information on these invisible decays. When combined with existing limits from other experiments, our new findings offer the most stringent constraints to date on invisible decays involving three neutrino types, as well as a group of four neutrino types. However, our analysis shows that the results from the LHCb do not significantly impact existing limits from other experiments in the case of a group of two neutrino types, as the data from the J/ψ invisible decays does not significantly differ from expected background predictions in that specific scenario.

High-resolution observations of the solar photosphere reveal tiny magnetic bright points, associated with extremely strong magnetic fields, present throughout the solar cycle. These features, extensively detected in solar images, play a significant role in understanding the solar atmosphere's behavior, particularly in addressing the long-standing issue of coronal heating. This research aimed to examine the size, speed, and distribution patterns of magnetic bright points in the solar photosphere, using datasets from the SOT/Hinode and HiFI/GREGOR telescopes, to gain insights into their characteristics. Employing an automated algorithm to detect magnetic bright points, their movements were tracked, and their statistical properties were analyzed, revealing distinct distributions of area, diameter, and speed. The results show that these characteristics exhibit two-component structures, pointing to the presence of two distinct populations of magnetic bright points. This conclusion is consistent with the widely accepted idea that there are two distinct regimes governing the solar atmosphere, governed by the strength and size of magnetic elements, represented by the parameters $\beta$ and $s$. Furthermore, the data were used to calculate the friction time of magnetic bright points, yielding estimates in the range of a few seconds to one minute.

Human vision can distinguish objects and actions using spatial or temporal data, but integrating these aspects remains unclear. This study demonstrates how the human visual system can effectively combine spatial and motion information, enabling recognition in scenarios where individual sources are insufficient. Researchers achieved this insight by analyzing'minimal videos' - brief clips that facilitate reliable object, part, and action recognition, but are unrecognizable when spatial or temporal constraints are compromised. Unlike deep networks, humans exhibit more adept performance in these complex configurations, highlighting missing elements in current artificial intelligence.

Dark particles interacting through Abelian gauge symmetries and ordinary matter through kinetic mixing result in the manifestation of broken $U(1)$ magnetic monopoles in our observable universe as milli-magnetically charged entities confined under electromagnetism. However, the strength of their dark magnetic interactions with ordinary matter is significantly constrained by observations of galaxy halo ellipticities. Furthermore, the ground state of dark monopoles initially stable and chargeless is found to be unstable and may decay into observable particles, potentially affecting dark matter direct detection experiments' interpretation.

The rapidly evolving Earth Observatory research area has immense potential to utilize AI in real-time weather forecasting. This work addresses the challenge of accurate weather prediction by leveraging the video transformer network. Building on existing research into vision transformer architectures, we address the limitations associated with their high computational complexity and data-hungry nature. To achieve this, we propose combining Video Swin-Transformer with a dedicated data augmentation method, and employing a weighted random sampling technique to manipulate the sampling distribution. The efficacy of our approach was tested on the Weather4Cast2021 challenge dataset, where we successfully predicted 8 hours of future weather frames from hourly weather sequences. After normalizing the dataset for evaluation consistency, our model achieved an MSE score of 0.4750 using training data, and 0.4420 using transfer learning without fine-tuning. Furthermore, we reached an MSE score of 0.3940 with both training and validation data, thereby demonstrating the effectiveness of our model.

In models that expand on the electroweak sector, a basis can be found where the symmetry prevents coupling, leading to viable dark matter candidates. Specifically, we analyze the $S_3$-symmetric three-Higgs-doublet models that allow softly broken $S_3$ terms, determining which models can host dark matter. The variety of models arises from different arrangements of vacuum expectation values, leading to vacua with either one or two vanishing expectation values. In our research, we consider a scenario where the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry, a remnant of $S_3$, stabilizes the dark matter candidate. Our findings indicate that these models are capable of providing a natural solution to the hierarchy problem and a viable dark matter candidate, with a correct relic abundance possibly arising from the freeze-in production. The related hadronic radius of the $W$ boson provides a potential testing ground for these models.

A comprehensive study on the PPT square conjecture is presented with a notable achievement: the PPT square conjecture's validity has been rigorously demonstrated for the case involving finite-dimensional space.

In neurons, the precise regulation of intracellular material transport between the cell body and periphery is critical for proper function and survival.  The complex interplay between microtubule-based fast transport, slow molecular transport, and membrane trafficking can be sensitive to changes in the cellular environment.  Using an agent-based model that simulates all three aspects of transport in a 2D representation, we examine how changes in the cellular environment affect transport patterns.  Our model, set in a 2D Neuron map with transport mechanisms in a steady-state, identifies the relative contributions of each transport mechanism to maintain equilibrium.  By simulating alterations in the 3N interdependent transport processes, we observe the impact on transport patterns and the effectiveness of restoring the steady-state condition.  Our findings suggest that each transport mechanism alone can restore equilibrium in a 2N+1 interdependent system, but in a 2N+1 non-interdependent system, all transport processes must work together to restore the steady-state condition.

Billion-dollar losses inflicted by banking fraud across the globe highlight the need for effective fraud detection systems in today's digital age. Current methods, while contributing to detection, often overlook crucial graph theoretical patterns that can aid in identifying suspicious transactions and preventing financial losses. This research proposes a novel framework that utilizes graph analysis to identify frequent and abnormal transaction patterns within a victim's transaction history, represented as a victim-enabling network. This approach generates regular and irregular motifs within the Enabling Network of a victim, utilizing a heuristic approach to reduce state space and extract meaningful patterns from the victim's transaction history. A case study validating the framework's efficacy involves analyzing actual transaction data from a victim with repeated attacks from the same account, demonstrating the framework's ability to detect and prevent suspicious transactions.

In a black hole-white dwarf binary system, we examine electromagnetic and gravitational waves emitted during a process where a white dwarf loses mass to a black hole through tidal forces. We simulate this scenario using a quantum hydrodynamic model and represent the white dwarf as a zero-temperature Bose-Fermi droplet. When the white dwarf approaches its point of closest approach to the black hole, it loses a portion of its mass, causing the black hole to experience an influx of matter. This mass accretion leads to the generation of intense bursts of electromagnetic and gravitational radiation, echoing patterns observed in recently discovered X-ray sources. We analyze the emitted energy patterns and find various spectral features that could be informative for ongoing and future observations of compact binary systems, such as those with the XRISM and AXRO telescopes.

Three-body $\tau$-decays, which involve semileptonic interactions with light hadrons and CP symmetry violations, can provide insight into these processes. Studies of weak electromagnetic interactions rely on form factors to describe the hadronic part of the final states, which can be further understood by decomposing the hadronic current into specific orbital angular momentum components. Given the increasing data availability from future experiments, a new description of the hadronic currents is presented in terms of the quantum numbers of the final hadronic state. Additionally, the work features an explicit example of a model using interquark potentials to describe a particular type of three-body decay.

Jim\'enez, Becerra, and Gelbukh (2013) introduced the "symmetric Tversky ratio models" with parameters $S_{\alpha,\beta}$ where $\alpha$ ranges between $0$ and $1$ and $\beta$ is greater than $0$. The inverse of each $S_{\alpha,\beta}$ function, denoted as $D_{\alpha,\beta}$, represents a semimetric for all possible subsets of a given set. Our research found that the function $D_{\alpha,\beta}$ is indeed a metric if $\alpha$ lies within the interval from $0$ to $0.5$ and $\beta$ is greater than or equal to $1/(1-\alpha)$. The verification of this outcome was successfully demonstrated in the Lean proof assistant. This parametrized space contains extreme points including $J_1 = D_{1/2,2}$, known as the Jaccard distance, and $J_{\infty} = D_{0,1}$, an analogue of the Li-Ma-Vit\'anyi information distance (2004).

Modern motion deblurring methods based on deep learning utilize paired synthetic data for training frameworks, aiming to directly convert blurry inputs to clear outputs. However, the success of these methods heavily relies on high-quality synthetic blurry data available only before training, a constraint that becomes impractical with large datasets. To overcome this limitation, we introduce an on-the-fly data augmentation technique to create blurry inputs dynamically during training and testing. To make the most of this approach, we adopt an unconventional framework incorporating a sequential process of blur removal and subsequent reblurring with the assistance of a module that mimics real-world blur, as well as hand-crafted prior information based on advanced statistical human body models. This module not only enhances the deblurring algorithm's ability to distinguish between human and non-human regions but also improves overall outcomes compared to other recent state-of-the-art methods through adversarial learning.

Hebbian theory aims to explain how brain cells modify their responses to stimuli, ultimately leading to the autotuning of neuronal connections. A notable aspect of Hebbian learning is its ability to occur independently, without requiring external feedback. This concept is further explored in a research paper, which outlines a novel, chemical-based system capable of autonomously learning through interaction with its surroundings. Unlike previous examples, this system relies on a parallel algorithm utilizing multiple agents to establish a connection between input and output elements, as even a single successful connection suffices for learning to occur. Additionally, the system can correct errors by means of a reaction that represents a form of local competition, as well as tolerate the presence of noise and maintain stability through the control of reaction rates. A theoretical discussion on the implications of this system's autotuning capabilities collection.

The ultrapower of any ordered set is created as a refined version of the set itself by taking into account infinite sequences of elements from it. This process involves dividing the sequences into classes according to a set of rules defined by an ultrafilter, leading to a set that always satisfies a fundamental property of ordered sets. It turns out that a set's openness determines its ability to fulfill the open completeness property in the refined version, whereas its original cardinality dictates whether the refined version is complete.

Scientific breakthroughs in data-driven science increasingly rely on applying sophisticated AI models to comprehensive, discipline-specific datasets. However, the computational resources required to evaluate every possible model against a large dataset are excessively expensive, rendering them impractical to execute. As a result, existing benchmarking approaches utilize select, representative datasets, but the performance of models is thus assessed only on a limited number of cases, leading to suboptimal results and increased risk of biased outcomes. To address this issue, we introduce the concept of "dataset intelligence," acknowledging that various datasets have distinct properties and computational models are designed to excel in specific contexts. By understanding the inherent characteristics of datasets and effectively distributing multiple models across diverse datasets, we can reduce the overall computational complexity of benchmarking. In this way, we can identify the best models for each dataset, rather than always comparing models based on a limited number of cases. Inspired by these findings, we developed Mosaic, a advanced data management system that integrates multiple datasets and models. Mosaic's data model resembles a complex puzzle, comprising overlapping tiles that represent models, datasets, and their relationships. This abstraction enables the system to express various constraint-based relationships, allowing system administrators to define and manage multiple, concurrent benchmarking processes. These processes distribute the work of evaluating models against datasets in a way that minimizes computational overhead while providing actionable insights into model performance. As a proof-of-concept, we employed Mosaic in the scientific domain of cellular signaling to demonstrate its effectiveness. In this domain

Hadwiger's Coloring Conjecture asserts that every graph with t colors includes a complete graph with t vertices. This has been reinforced by another theory suggesting if a given graph is assigned t colors, where a certain set of its vertices uses every color, then that graph must have a complete graph with t vertices within it. This further theorized idea is known as the Makai-Woodall conjecture. We have recently found and established a new, weaker version of the Makai-Woodall conjecture that still implies the validity of the Makai-Woodall conjecture itself, thereby also confirming Hadwiger's Coloring Conjecture. This new version of the Makai-Woodall conjecture suggests for any given graph, if it can be divided into t parts with the exception of a single set of its vertices that uses every color, then within at least one of these t parts, there will be a complete graph with t vertices.

This research introduces an advanced algorithm for efficiently recovering smooth graph signals through generalized correntropy, and a specific loss function is formulated accordingly. Derived from the aforementioned principle, the algorithm is developed further, and a variant leveraging kernel width adaptation is presented. The adaptive kernel width approach is then generalized in the context of irregular graphs, and a corresponding algorithm is formulated. Simulation results confirm the effectiveness of the proposed algorithms in efficiently recovering graph signals.

Theoretical investigations are conducted to design and control entangled atomic states formed through spin-changing collisions within a spinor Bose-Einstein condensate for use in a more robust atom interferometry capable of withstanding common technical problems like detector limitations. It is discovered through both analytical and numerical examinations of the spin-changing collision process that utilizing a small initial disturbance as a trigger, as opposed to vacuum fluctuations, yields superior results despite reduced entanglement. Our findings have implications for optimizing entangled atomic state production for quantum-enhanced matter-wave interferometry applications.

The purpose of this research paper is to derive optimal estimates for the first eigenvalue of the first Robin eigenvalue problem involving the anisotropic $p$-Laplace operator. This problem seeks to minimize a specific functional over all nonzero functions in the Sobolev space, and involves several variables and constants, including $p$, a bounded mean convex domain $\Omega$ in $N$-dimensional space, and a smooth norm $F$ on this space. We discovered new lower and upper bounds for this eigenvalue problem based on the first eigenvalue of a one-dimensional nonlinear problem. Specifically, for positive $\beta$ we proved a lower bound for the eigenvalue and for negative $\beta$ we proved an upper bound. Furthermore, for positive $\beta$ we were able to derive a lower bound for the eigenvalue in terms of the anisotropic inradius of the domain $\Omega$, and for negative $\beta$ we were able to derive an upper bound for the eigenvalue in terms of the parameter $\beta$.

Deep Neural Network solutions for graph-domain problems have gained significant interest in recent years, particularly Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs). GCNNs employ graph filters to process graph data, which are learned through backpropagation. However, learning convolution layers for inhomogeneous graphs with non-constant node degree is complex due to the associated high computation complexity of gradient backpropagation. To address this issue, a new approach uses a specialized efficient gateway operator in the convolution layers to facilitate gradient backpropagation. This approach also involves a new graph filter learned using evolutionary algorithms, which optimizes the graph classification accuracy. Experimental results on multiple graph datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed gateway operator in accelerating the learning process for GCNNs. Moreover, the employed gateway operator is shown to be a generalizable component that can be applied to various graph filters while ensuring compatibility with different types of gateway operators.

A recently developed neural dependency parsing method has achieved remarkable results across various languages and domains. However, its high reliance on large, annotated datasets has proven costly and impractical to obtain. This paper proposes a novel self-training technique that mitigates this data annotation constraint by leveraging the parser's own output to improve performance. Specifically, the Deep Contextualized Self-training algorithm integrates external sequence models, derived from the parser's application to unlabelled data, into the parser using a sophisticated weighting system. Comprehensive experiments have been conducted across multiple languages in diverse settings, and the results clearly indicate that our approach outperforms traditional self-training and state-of-the-art semi-supervised learning methods by a significant margin.

We've investigated the transition form factors $f_+(q^2)$ and $f_-(q^2)$
involved in the exclusive semileptonic B s, B o, B x, and B t decays to D s, D o, D x, and D t mesons, respectively. The study utilized heavy quark baryon strong interaction dynamics to determine these form factors. Specifically, the analysis was based on the heavy quark baryon strong interaction Lagrangian and the presence of eight Lorentz symmetries, leading to a particular set of matrix elements characteristic to this theory. The form factors $f_+(q^2)$ were found to decrease while $f_-(q^2)$ increased with growing $s$-quark mass, and these findings are crucial for understanding the semileptonic decay widths and branching ratios of these B s, B o, B x, and B t decays to D s, D o, D x, and D t mesons.

Theories of supersymmetric Yang-Mills with algebra so(4N) can have non-trivial, invertible-defying symmetries. By utilizing holographic duality, we can determine the branes equivalent to these symmetries, and deduce the fusion principles for the symmetries through brane dynamics.

Currently, Choiceless Polynomial Time (CPT) stands out as the most promising approach to tackle decision problems within PTIME. A significant challenge lies in determining if a particular problem, specifically the CFI-query, can be defined using CPT and for what types of graph structures it's applicable. Our investigation focuses on CPT-definability relative to two distinct graph theories: Monadic Local Homology (MLH) and Extended Bruce Heilman Boolean Algebra (EBHBA). MLH can be applied to undirected graphs with distinct vertex colors, while EBHBA is relevant to colored vertex- and edge-labelled graphs. A CFI-query generally involves retrieving a subset of graph vertices based on local properties from an input graph structure. A notable exception occurs for graphs with a specific 'flavor' of 3-colorable planar graphs, which include planar bipartite graphs, planar graphs with at most three colors, and etale graphs. Our theory reveals that the CFI-query is not CPT-definable on etale graphs that come with a particular type of vertex coloring known as ALBA. This CFI-query non-definability also extends to other graph theories such as MLH, but surprisingly not to EBHBA. This unexpected result creates an imbalance within CPT-provable classes, which were previously established as being applicable to EBHBA, but now raise doubts for its PTIME decidability.

In a compound known for potential Kitaev magnetism, Eu2Ir2O7, incorporating Bi+3+ at the Eu site leads to a significant increase in magnetic ordering temperature. By using RES and XSRES experiments at POLARIS, a laboratory-based beamline, we investigated the electronic and magnetic properties of this material. Our RES experiment showed that both irridium and europium contribute equally to the magnetic ordering, whereas our XSRES experiment with 10 keV X-rays revealed that Bi+3+ plays a crucial role in the magnetic ordering. Our results resolved a long-standing debate in the field and provided novel insights into the magnetic properties of this material.

Consider a metric space ${\mathfrak M}=({\mathcal M},\rho)$ and a Banach space $X$, with a set-valued mapping $F$ that maps ${\mathcal M}$ to the family ${\mathcal K}_m(X)$ of compact convex subsets of $X$ of dimension at most $m$. Our recent joint research with Dimant Gel'fand and Alexander Verbo revealed a substantial generalization of a crucial result by Frank, Stricharzt, and Zalik, concerning the existence of a Lipschitz selection for $F$. The invention proposes an algorithm that yields the smallest possible Lipschitz selection for any given mapping $F$. When $F$ is convex, this algorithm also produces the least possible norm selection. When the domain ${\mathcal M}$ is a Euclidean space and the dimension is denoted by $n$, the algorithm further extends a crucial result by Li and Li, concerning the existence of a Schauder basis in a family of operators from ${\mathcal M}$ to $X$, and the compactness of their image image.

Inspired by classic counterintuitive phenomena, a particular n-tuple $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ within the range [0,1] is classified as 'cyclic' when there exist unique random variables $(U_1, \ldots, U_n)$ where the likelihood of $U_{i+1}$ being greater than $U_i$ is $x_{i+1}$ and $i$ ranges from 1 to n with the exception of $i=0$ which has a likelihood of $x_1$. A further "extended cyclic n-tuple" is defined when an additional constraint is applied, requiring the first element $x_1$ to be exactly 0. Both of these concepts were introduced in a study published in arXiv:2101.11598, proving that there exists a sequence of both standard and extended cyclic n-tuples that decay to 0 as n approaches infinity. A list of numbers that satisfy the conditions for cyclic n-tuples are provided, specifically focusing on those that can be represented as powers of prime numbers. A further generalized concept, known as a "cyclic n-tuple with a possibility of zero", relaxes the constraints on the sequence, allowing a single element to have a probability of 0, and offers a further area of investigation within the concepts of random variables.

Many software systems have adjustable settings that can be modified at run-time, but this leads to unnecessary overhead in system resources. Tuning these settings ahead of time to optimize performance, however, is impractical due to the vast number of possible combinations, rendering it a computationally infeasible task. To resolve this issue, we propose compiling run-time settings into fixed configurations that remain unchanged during system operation. The process of transforming dynamic settings into dedicated, optimized configurations is the core of our method, which employs evolutionary algorithms to generate optimal settings that meet desired criteria. The effectiveness of this process is demonstrated through our evaluation of a renowned database management system and a popular web server, which reveals substantial gains in disk space usage, application size, and performance efficiency when successful configurations are identified.

Light dark matter particles, particularly those weighing less than a GeV, offer an attractive option over heavier, weakly-interacting massive particles. Directly detecting such lightweight particles, however, poses a significant challenge. But if the recoil of a struck nucleus leads to electron ionization, even if the recoil itself is too subtle to be measured, it could still be possible to detect the released electron. This process has been found to significantly boost the sensitivity of direct detection experiments to sub-GeV dark matter. In the present, experiments set global records, and future experiments are likely to reach the cross-sections critical to understanding thermal equilibrium.

This paper proposes a method to produce the most connected pairs of qubit states
via an anti-Jaynes-Cummings interaction system, resulting in maximally entangled
anti-polariton qubits. The study finds that in the initial absence of photons, the
quantum fluctuations of the anti-Jaynes-Cummings interaction behave in the opposite
direction of the standard Jaynes-Cummings interaction process and the rate at which
these states become entangled has a similar pattern in both processes. Furthermore,
utilizing this maximally connected state and entanglement swapping, a near perfect
transfer of an atomic quantum state via quantum state transfer is demonstrated.

Measuring inter-beat intervals from ECG signals can provide early warnings for cardiovascular diseases. However, identifying IBIs from raw ECG signals is challenging due to noise and low sample rates. This work presents a novel end-to-end IBI estimation technique, known as End2IBI, which utilizes a deep learning network to accurately determine IBIs from ECG signals even when the sampling rate is lower than 100 Hz. End2IBI can handle diverse noise levels and is more effective than existing methods in real-world ECG readings. Additionally, End2IBI was tested on remote health monitoring data, which was found to have a significant amount of motion-related noise interfering with the signal. This made the task even more difficult for the model to extract IBIs. The study demonstrates that End2IBI can still extract high-quality long-term IBIs, which are important for assessing heart health, even in challenging conditions. This could greatly contribute to monitoring heart health in a wide range of settings, such as remote locations, big data analysis, and real-time clinical practice.

We analyze large deviations of power input by an active force on an Active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Particle (AOUP) within or outside a confinement. Analytical calculations of the rate function are done for the free particle in any dimension using a saddle-point expansion. Additionally, a direct numerical approach via solution of the AOUP equations is performed, alongside a method using the conjugate variable to the action, which enables a confinement and dimension-independent representation of the rate function. Our findings demonstrate that this function exhibits a quadratic relationship specific to active dynamics. Moreover, the representational value of our approach is that this quadratic relationship can be represented universally across any dimension and confinement. We also investigate the impact of active force parameters on this representational value. Conversely, for systems within a confinement, a direct numerical approach is performed to investigate large deviations of power input.

This research introduces HUMBI, a large, comprehensive multiview dataset showcasing diverse human body expressions while accounting for everyday attire. The primary objective of HUMBI is to enhance modeling accuracy of the human body through diverse identities, poses, and garments. The dataset consists of 84 identities, each depicted in five key aspects (eyes, mouth, nose, jawline, and skin), across various viewpoints and poses. The HUMBI dataset is specifically designed to support the creation of more realistic virtual humans by bridging the gap in current facial and body capture technology. Current state-of-the-art facial capture methods that respect identity can achieve high precision in narrow frames. Conversely, body capture technology that respects identity is less advanced, often using simpler models or incorporating extra steps. Similarly, multiview and pose-dependent body capture methods underperform in preserving identity. To address these limitations, the HUMBI dataset aims to facilitate the development of more sophisticated approaches for all these challenges. The dataset is derived from video footage from two camera angles, capturing the same expressions from different identities, while ensuring realistic and varied outfits. For each identity and pose, four key aspects of the face and skin are annotated to support the development of advanced modeling techniques. The dataset will be freely accessible upon publication at a yet-to-be-announced location.

Despite the growing need for models in non-English languages, natural language processing has long been Anglo-centric, and translating neural models between languages can be costly and time-consuming in terms of data, labor, and computational resources. We propose a universal approach to effortlessly and effectively transfer neural models from English to other languages. Our method utilizes weak supervision in the form of task representations and can adapt existing neural models to new languages with minimal modification, as long as there's unlabeled parallel data and a loss function based on task representations. We put our framework to the test by transferring an English sentiment classifier to three foreign languages and discovered that it surpasses the performance of numerous strong baselines while matching or even exceeding that of models pre-trained on language-specific data. The benefits of our approach extend to unsupervised cross-lingual text classification, where it helps to determine the sentiment labels of foreign languages with only minimal manual labeling.

A common approach in video super-resolution is the recurrent structure, with the BasicVSR method being one of the top-performing frameworks that uses a consistent encoder-decoder structure and recurrent convolutional networks to process each frame. While notably effective, the method's reliance on recurrent convolutional networks increases computation cost as the number of frames grows. To address this limitation, our method replaces the recurrent convolutional networks with a proposed framework that utilizes grid propagation and alignment components. The grid propagation component calculates the pixel position for each grid cell based on the grid's previous predicted location, with the alignment component aligning the pixel features accordingly. Due to the grid propagation component, our method can reduce the computation cost by eliminating the dependency on the number of frames. In addition, we introduce a new component that incorporates second-order grid propagation and multi-stage processing to further improve the method's performance. The proposed framework achieves state-of-the-art performance on the VID4, VID9, and FVD datasets for video super-resolution.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident for tasks that are similar, we investigated its extent for
tasks that are quite different. To this end, we developed a multi-task reinforcement
learning method based on evolutionary principles, aiming to identify useful skills
that can be combined to solve complex tasks. To facilitate transfer, we introduced
a skill representation that is expressed relative to a task-specific reference
point, rather than being absolute. This approach allows us to use skills learned
for one task for other tasks, as their positions can be adjusted. By employing
evolutionary principles to optimize skill combinations, we were able to identify
sets of basic skills that can be used to solve more advanced tasks. To evaluate
our method, we conducted experiments on a variety of gridworld tasks, as well as
a more complex real-world scenario involving robotic navigation. The results of
our study demonstrate that our multi-task reinforcement learning framework is
capable of discovering a small set of basic skills that can be utilized to solve
a variety of complex tasks.

We investigate the performance of heat engines that operate in the time-domain, specifically the minimum entropy production rates, for both reversible and irreversible cycles. Our study uncovers how these rates behave in the limit of high system entropy. Additionally, we analyze the effects of constraints on the bath temperature and scaling parameters. Our findings indicate that these constraints can be expressed as a linear decomposition, which has practical implications for accurately measuring these rates experimentally.

This research proposes a probabilistic model for analyzing the impact of combined hurricane and storm surge events on large power grids. To simulate real-world hurricane scenarios, the study generates probabilistic storm paths based on historical data, and corresponding storm surge situations are developed based on actual hurricane parameters. To assess potential losses, the study employs a quantitative metric that estimates total load reduction, and these outcomes are calculated using a simulated model of the 2000-bus Texas power system superimposed onto an actual map of the region. Simulation results indicate that power substations experiencing storm surge-related flooding may incur additional losses as the hurricane continues to move inland.

This paper formulates the three balls theorem for functions u, subject to specific conditions derived from Clifford analysis. In particular, we leverage these conditions to extend Hadamard's three circles theorem to monogenic functions within R^n+1 space.

We define new families of parametrized piecewise affine transformations on 2D and 3D spaces as generalized versions of the heterochaos baker map, initially developed as simplified models for unstable dimension variability in complex systems. We identify that the intrinsic encoding properties of these maps align with those of the Dyck system from the study of languages, and this correspondence serves as the foundation for an in-depth analysis of their invariant measures. Through initial investigation, we confirm the existence of two distinct ergodic measures with maximal entropy for these generalized baker maps, and also reveal the underlying cause for the failure of certain entropy-based approaches.

Following the groundbreaking detection of the Higgs boson in 2012, the field of particle physics has entered an exciting period. A pressing concern is whether the Standard Model of particle physics can adequately explain the scalar sector observed in nature or if it requires supplementation with additional particles and mechanisms. A distinctive aspect of the Higgs boson is its dual nature as both the heaviest scalar particle and the least comprehended. Researchers have devised numerous theoretical frameworks, both spontaneous and generated, to expand upon the Standard Model, often incorporating new scalar particles. To differentially detect the Higgs boson from its simulated counterparts, future particle accelerators must accurately forecast the predicted signals and decay patterns of its potential extensions. This article serves as a comprehensive overview, categorizing and summarizing the various scalar extension frameworks. Additionally, it examines the potential for discovering new scalar particles, either heavier or lighter than the Higgs boson, in the upcoming decades.

This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of existing WaveNet models, which are based on conditional sampling and lack pitch-specific features. PQPNet incorporates pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks (DCNN) to capture local speech characteristics at various time intervals. Notably, each layer of the FPNet utilizes an encoder-separated sampling (ESPS) signal as its input, distinct from the traditional WaveNet approach. To optimize the model, an autoencoding objective combined with a cross-entropy loss on the FPNet parameters was implemented. The results indicate that the FPNet can produce high-quality, longer audio segments with extended time intervals, by extending the WaveNet model's pith-based control to 50 milliseconds from the 2 milliseconds previously. The FPNet was tested on the LJSpeech dataset and produced comparable or even better results than the baseline WaveNet and its variants.

Recommender Systems built with Collaborative Filtering (CF), the dominant method, have become an integral part of our daily lives as consumers. However, their limitations become apparent when dealing with sparse data and the need to balance user experience with data privacy. Research in CF has been ongoing for over twenty years, but there are still significant areas to explore. This paper offers a comprehensive review of the CF landscape, examining its evolution and highlighting successful approaches, challenges, and promising avenues for future research. The authors also identify gaps in current knowledge and areas where CF can improve, such as the integration of CF with other techniques, the development of more robust handling of sparse data, and the need for more transparent and fair recommender systems.

Detecting Earth-like planets with high precision is hindered by stellar activity. Identifying early signs of superflares in stars could provide insights into their magnetic properties and potential impacts on habitability. Analysis of Kepler data involving 1860 stars containing 5486 large and brief flares has led to the development of a statistical classification system. This system uses activity features to group stars and detect subtle classifications (e.g., $\Delta F_{\rm X,3} = 0.1$ in flux units). Furthermore, the study explores the relationship between these stars and the occurrence of Earth-like planets, finding no significant association.

To differentiate between zero-energy peaks originating from Majorana and those from other causes at non-zero temperatures, our method involves swapping the normal lead in tunneling spectroscopy with a high-resistance lead (characterized by large Ohm values). The increased resistance in this setup significantly alters tunneling conductance, impacting it in distinct ways. While the Majorana peak persists across temperatures, its conductance exhibits a logarithmic decline with rising Ohm values; in contrast, peaks unrelated to Majorana display temperature-dependent exponents in conductance, with varying Ohm values primarily influencing the peak's amplitude rather than its height. The potential to accurately identify Majorana zero-energy peaks holds significant promise for detecting Majorana modes, a key component in topological quantum processing.

The theory of shadows constitutes an axiomatic bicategorical framework, extending and matching key characteristics of topological Hochschild homology (THH), notably preserving properties akin to Morita invariance. Through the incorporation of Berman's extension of THH to bicategories, it is demonstrated that functors from the THH of a bicategory are equivalent to shadows of that bicategory, ultimately establishing a direct relationship between them. Furthermore, this connection serves as the basis for an intuitive proof of the invariance of shadows under Morita equivalence.

Existing approaches to image enhancement and editing typically yield multiple possible outcomes, rather than a single definitive result. To address this, we've developed a systematic method for quantifying and comparing the relative quality of different operations. Our approach is versatile and can be applied to a range of tasks, such as color grading, exposure adjustment, and content merging. For comparison purposes, we've compiled and annotated a dataset of professionally conducted image edits, along with associated segmentation masks that pinpoint exactly which areas have been modified. By utilizing this dataset, we're able to assess the aesthetic appeal of different editing techniques and identify areas for improvement.

This technical report showcases the winning model of the AQTC task in the RealWorld Semantics challenge of the CORDS 2021 competition. The project focused on addressing the issues of processing lengthy video data, which often poses significant challenges for machine learning models. The proposed solution involved the use of multi-head self-attention to capture relationships within individual video frames and between video frames and metadata, along with the application of transformer encoder-decoder architecture to tackle the task. Furthermore, feature enhancement through the integration of semantic information and frame analysis was essential in overcoming the limited input frame context. The winning model demonstrated the effectiveness of using pre-trained vision models on semantic-level data, which outperformed alternative approaches that relied solely on video or text information.

This field measurement focuses on snow deposition dynamics by monitoring the atmospheric turbulence that influences snowfall. Our research reveals the presence of vortex structures in the lower atmosphere that form a spiral pattern observed at higher latitudes and is hypothesized to impact snow crystal formation. As these vortex structures move rapidly towards the ground, they induce violent turbulence above the surface, causing snow particles to be forcibly deposited in concentrated areas. These areas of high snow accumulation can extend several meters into the surrounding environment. Within a observed 30-minute time frame, the deposition pattern shifted due to the ongoing movement of these vortex structures. Long-term observations of this phenomenon are necessary to understand the impact of these vortex structures on snow distribution and their potential effects on local snowfall distribution.

A fundamental theory known as active inference underpins how living beings interact with their surroundings. This theory views the brain as an efficient tool that employs Bayesian principles to create a detailed mental framework, aiming to minimize uncertainty about the world. Despite the theory's significance in cognitive neuroscience, its practical application is restricted to simplified simulations due to limitations in dealing with large and varied environments. This research incorporates the latest advancements in deep learning to create a more sophisticated mental framework, one that can be built directly from high-dimensional data, such as video feeds, without the need for pre-defined parameters. Furthermore, this work demonstrates that such frameworks can be utilized to facilitate active inference. This research marks the first instance of applying active inference using deep learning techniques to a complex, real-world environment, specifically a 3D gaming environment. The findings are promising, showing that agents navigating this environment can achieve goals more effectively by employing the mental framework and subsequent active inference method.

In experimental facilities specializing in high energy physics, nuclear physics, and cosmology, the task of processing large amounts of data in real-time is proving to be a substantial hurdle. As an alternative to standard compression methods, the use of machine learning algorithms has gained attention for real-time data reduction. Yet, data sets generated from scientific endeavors often comprise vast 3D data volumes characterized by significant portions of zeroes, non-uniform distribution of values, and high generation rates. Consequently, direct applications of popular compression methods along with standard compression methods yield unsatisfactory results. Therefore, to overcome these difficulties, the concept of Bicephalous Convolutional AutoEncoder (BCAE) is developed to tackle the challenges posed by the unique properties of scientific data. BCAE is a two-part autoencoder architecture where a traditional CNN is paired with a Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) optimized autoEncoder based on the AE structure. The FFT based autoEncoder is designed specifically to excel in the analysis of scientific data possessing the characteristics mentioned earlier. Furthermore, a thorough evaluation of BCAE is conducted by utilizing actual scientific data sets. The results demonstrate that BCAE not only surpasses the performance of regular compression but also successfully mitigates the drawbacks associated with traditional compression methods.

Utilizing Finzi's gravity theory that incorporates a scalar field, we've investigated a model of solar system particles. This new approach is a modification of Newtonian gravity, but unlike it, the influence strength in Finzi's model increases at large scales. Unlike Newtonian gravity, however, Finzi's model doesn't satisfy the equivalence principle, but it does comply with the inverse square law. Assuming the scalar field's spatial variation can be negligible, we've performed a cosmological analysis. This leads to a situation where the only viable cosmological model for Finzi's gravity, which also models the universe's large-scale dynamics, is a de Sitter universe. Furthermore, we've calculated that the scalar field's interaction strength in this model is much too low to potentially explain the observed acceleration in the universe's expansion, even when simulations involving a Lambda-CDM universe are run for an extended period.

A type of convex geometric hypergraph, known as cgh, comprises a set of subsets originating from strictly convex point sets in the plane. In this study, researchers explore a specific type of problem associated with cghs: saturation problems that correspond to earlier studied extremal issues. Using a mathematical approach, the study determines the maximum capacity of certain geometrically separated groups of points and establishes an exact value for a specific instance, as well as approximate values for seven out of eight possible geometric hypergraph configurations up to a specific level of accuracy, and a related but less accurate figure for the eighth configuration.

To gain a better understanding of the relative contributions of different processes, the angular distributions and energy spectra of $\alpha$ and deuterons resulting from breakup, transfer, and incomplete fusion have been measured and calculated. Cross-sections for the $^6$Li + $^{51}$V system were experimentally measured at energies near the Coulomb barrier, with theoretical estimates obtained through calculations of the coupled reaction paths. It was found that the relative weights of the various reaction channels can shift significantly as the energy changes. The experiments involved measuring the yield of $\alpha$ and deuteron particles resulting from a range of processes, including non-capture breakup, single-neutron and single-proton transfer, 1/n and 2/n transfer, and incomplete fusion. The data were also analyzed in terms of the multiple-channel K-hanging model, which reconstructs the ground-state wavefunctions of the coupled systems via quantitative analysis of the measured yields.

A previously overlooked aspect of snakes' motion dynamics is vertical movement,
enabling them to cross broad surfaces while adhering to narrow surfaces down to
1% of their body length. To study this effect, we developed a robot inspired by
the lamprey, featuring a flexible rod with magnetic weights, allowing it to
ascend and descend horizontal planes. By using a nonlinear control strategy, the
robot can maintain a stable orientation and generate vertical movement through
adjusting the positions of its weights. Through testing, we found that the robot
can achieve vertical movements of up to 3.3 times its own length, corresponding
to a stride length of 11.3 times its own length, at a speed of 3.3 cm/s. Given
that similar robots typically consider surface friction as the primary force acting
on them, the accuracy of our results is further reinforced.

This paper outlines a novel probabilistic framework designed to identify the most effective combinations of treatments in cases of colon cancer-induced immune response. An Itō stochastic process models the colon cancer dynamics, whose probabilistic evolution is governed by the Fokker-Planck equation. To identify optimal treatment combinations, an open-loop control optimization issue is proposed. Simulation results demonstrating the use of Doxorubicin chemotherapy and IL-2 immunotherapy validate the introduced framework.

Optimizing wireless Device-to-Device (D2D) communication success depends heavily on minimizing excessive interference through effective device scheduling. Traditional scheduling methods mainly prioritize maximizing throughput and fairness without considering the timeliness of received data. This paper presents a novel D2D link scheduling strategy that balances both Age of Information (AoI) and throughput by employing a packet replacement policy, which ensures fair link activation. Analytically derived expressions demonstrate how the scheduler achieves optimal Age of Information and achieved throughput under complex queueing theory. Furthermore, the proposed scheduler achieves significant performance gains with minimal computational complexity, which is demonstrated through numerical simulations.

Moffatt first discussed the concept of helicity in a fluid without viscosity in reference [25] and explored its preservation in the case of barotropic, compressible flow with smooth solutions. This paper demonstrates that weak solutions to this system in a specific mathematical space ensure the conservation of helicity. Additionally, similar results were found for both barotropic and incompressible flows.

The research develops a complex version of the geometric optics approach, applying it to a system governed by a Schrödinger equation with a complex potential function. This is achieved through a series of iterative calculations using a Schrödinger equation-based recursion formula that enables the construction of complex conjugate fields. By starting with an initial data set that includes a delocalized phase, a reflection coefficient is derived which encompasses information about system delocalization and phase properties. This framework is also expanded to include a system of Schrödinger equations with a complex potential function that exhibits non-hermitian transitions.

Calculations involving the orbital dynamics of merging compact binary systems,
including higher-order effects of gravitational wave radiation, reveal that late-time
eccentricities of inspiraling binaries are typically underestimated by standard
models by up to 30 percent for heavy systems like 300-solar-mass binaries at
10 Hz, and less so for lighter binaries. By incorporating a more comprehensive
equation of state for nuclear matter, our analysis shows that this discrepancy
could be as large as 60 percent, but also reveals a strong dependence on the
steepness of this equation, leading to potentially significant variations in
the predicted properties of remnant mergers, including maxima mass accretion
rates, maxima laser brightness, and maxima gravitational-wave energy emission.

A proposed innovation combines the benefits of X-ray free-electron laser oscillators (XFELOs) and the undulator taper technique to create a groundbreaking X-ray laser. This is made possible by using an XFELO to seed a free-electron laser (FEL) amplifier with a specially tailored electron beam. The unique characteristics of the beam allow for the tail to be within the gain bandwidth of XFELO, generating a seed that is used to regulate the FEL amplifier, whereas the leading portion of the beam, outside of the XFELO's gain bandwidth, can still be utilized to generate the main X-ray pulse. To maximize the integration of the XFELO's and the FEL amplifier's capabilities, the electron beam is divided into sections with varying undulator parameters, leading to a significantly increased gain, allowing for a significantly longer undulator period, and thus a significantly increased tuning range of the FEL pulse. A simulation demonstrated that a final X-ray pulse of $10^{12}$ photons per unit energy can be achieved, with a tunability range of approximately $10^n$, using a beam current of $10$ dc-Ampere and an undulator period of $0.55$ cm. This concept also offers the potential for application in coherent electron radiation sources, allowing for an increase in the tunability range and power scale of these sources.

Event identification is crucial for informed decision-making in graph data analysis systems.  Graph-based machine learning has made notable advancements lately, but detecting events in evolving networks still poses difficulties for current frameworks. Real-life occurrences typically involve sudden changes in network behavior patterns. Current methods for dynamic node representations are ineffective at capturing event-driven network changes.  To address these limitations, we propose a new approach, called DyGED, for recognizing events in evolving networks using a combination of temporal self-attention and structural awareness.  Through extensive testing with diverse datasets, we demonstrate that DyGED consistently outperforms alternative methods in accuracy, achieving up to an 8.5% improvement.  Notably, it also offers improved scalability compared to the best-performing models, along with insightful case studies that highlight its key features.

The solutions of the Guderley problem involving an imploding shock wave in an ideal gas are examined, focusing on how a power law initial density distribution affects the accelerating shock. This is achieved through in-depth analysis of self-similar solutions and their similarity exponents under different symmetry conditions and varying parameters of adiabatic index and spatial density exponent. Moreover, we show how these theoretical solutions can be accurately reproduced in Lagrangian hydrodynamic simulations, thereby validating and verifying these codes for a range of scenarios.

The growing presence of artificial intelligence systems has led to a significant rise in the need for their explanations. Transparency and stakeholder trust are achieved by reducing the opacity of these systems through the provision of explanations. In this paper, we explore the interconnection between explainable AI and requirements engineering. The challenges in the XAI field are mapped to requirements engineering issues, and a framework is established to address these challenges. A systematic review of XAI practices was conducted to identify key areas of focus. The results revealed that current approaches to XAI fall short in several aspects. To bridge this gap, we introduce the EAXRE framework, which integrates AI explainability with requirements engineering through the exploration of four key areas. The introduction of this framework marks a first in the XAI field and paves the way for a more standardized approach to explainable AI.

Characterizing colorectal polyps histopathologically is crucial to personalize patient treatment and follow-up, ultimately reducing the risk of undetected invasive carcinomas. The process of polyp characterization involves examining tissue samples for malignancy and dysplasia using histological analysis. Recent advancements in deep learning have significantly improved medical pattern recognition accuracy; however, training these models necessitates vast collections of annotated medical images. In this context, we've developed UniToPatho, an extensive dataset consisting of 9536 annotated H&E stained patches derived from 292 whole-slide images, designed for deep learning-based classification and grading of colorectal polyps and adenomas. This dataset serves as a resource for researchers tackling the complex task of automating colorectal polyp characterization.

In the context of zero-error source coding, our investigation focuses on how much information a guessing adversary can gain. The underlying source coding problem is represented by a confusion graph, illustrating how source symbols can be distinguished from one another. The adversary's ability to successfully guess the source sequence is measured relative to its prior knowledge, with this measurement maximized over various source distributions. When the adversary follows a specific model where they only make a single guess and can perfectly match their guess to the true sequence, this measurement is known as the maximal leakage in min-entropy (MLME) and has been extensively studied. However, this single-guess model may not accurately reflect real-world adversaries who can take multiple guesses. In our research, we examine a more general model where the adversary takes k guesses and can match their choices to the true sequence. The parameter of interest is the maximal leakage in min-entropy (KLEME) - the maximum amount of min-entropy leaked to the adversary, with this value optimized over the number of guesses taken (k). The KLEME is shown to be a constant multiple of the MLME, with the multiplicative factor depending solely on the graph structure. Additionally, we look at source coding problems where the source sequence consists of alternating symbols from two different sets, known as alternating sources. In our investigation of these sources, we find that the optimal leakage in min-entropy can take on any value between a specific minimum and a specific maximum, with this range being tightly defined

Deep learning-trained generative models can function as a prior in under-determined problems such as recovering images from limited measurements in a process called progressive reconstruction. However, incorporating a prior in this manner typically relies on a neural network optimized for image synthesis, rather than signal recovery. This limitation is addressed by developing and testing a new technique that leverages a generative adversarial network optimized for image reconstruction rather than generation. Demonstrating the effectiveness of this approach, the authors successfully reconstruct high-quality images at half the required measurement rate using a generative adversarial network based on Adam optimizer and learning rate of 0.001.

A Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm variant employs a combined quantum-classical strategy to achieve approximate solutions for complex optimization issues.  This approach integrates a quantum circuit, variably controlled PIET elements, to generate diverse quantum states, which are then evaluated by a classical optimizer to identify the optimal configuration.  As PIET circuits apply a series of identical operations to different qubits, a complete circuit consists of various vertical elements and a single horizontal element controlling the application of a CNOT gate.  This research involves testing QAOA with a Z-fitness function on distinct PIET circuits, comparing the results of a complete circuit versus breaking it into multiple parallel circuits, and investigating the effects of altering the control angle in both scenarios.

A versatile method has been devised for determining the overlap area between two ellipses. The proposed approach relies on computing segment areas between the two ellipses, using a secant line that intersects each ellipse at given points. The Gauss-Green formula enables calculation of an ellipse sector area, with a triangle either added to or subtracted from this sector area to obtain the segment area. For calculating the overlap area of two ellipses, the areas of relevant sectors and polygons are combined. The algorithm identifies the intersection points of two general ellipses by utilizing Ferrari's quartic formula to solve a resulting polynomial formed from the two ellipses' equations, allowing for handling all cases of intersection points, including none, one, two, three, or four points. The proposed method has been implemented in C and validated through numerous tests with diverse input ellipses, demonstrating its efficiency for applications involving multiple overlap area calculations in simulations.

Building upon the work by Wang et al. (2020) for reinforcement learning, we examine the continuous-time counterpart of Q-learning under the entropy-regularized exploratory process framework. To handle the collapse of the traditional Q-function in continuous time, we derive a first-order approximation of the Q-function and establish its connection to the instantaneous advantage rate function. We also introduce a new criterion for optimal control and employ a nonlinear dynamical system to demonstrate the Q-learning update rule aligns with the optimal criterion, particularly when the exploratory process is symmetric. Additionally, we address the challenge of initial state dependence and develop a stochastic process to achieve consistent Q-function estimates, which we confirm has asymptotic stability through rigorous analysis. Finally, we outline the potential extension of our work to address the relational reinforcement learning problem.

Quantum magnets' low-lying magnetic excitations often exhibit intermediate-range order (IRO), stemming from a delicate balance between shorter and longer doped-scale spatial extensions. However, the precise understanding of IRO's magnetic excitations remains elusive. To investigate this further, we analyzed the magnetic excitations of the triangular lattice Hubbard model, incorporating realistic three-orbital degrees of freedom. Our findings reveal that two distinct types of magnetic excitations exist: those with IRO, situated at larger q-values, and those displaying a nematic character, prevalent at smaller q-values. The phenomenon of "accidental" zero modes occurs when the magnitude of the excitations' dispersion branches becomes negligible, and we identified multiple such modes across various regions of IRO and nematic phases. The presence of these zero modes offers a theoretical basis for interpreting quantum magnetic excitations exhibiting vanishing spin and orbital order.

Accurate vertebrae localization and identification are crucial in various medical applications related to spine disorder diagnosis and surgical planning. However, certain pathological variations (e.g., vertebral compression fractures, scoliosis, and vertebral fixation) and imaging conditions (e.g., limited visibility and metallic streak artifacts in CT scans) make this task quite challenging. To address these difficulties, this paper presents an advanced and precise three-dimensional localization and identification method for normal and pathological vertebrae in 3D CT scans. By incorporating a novel convolutional neural network called VertNet, this approach surpasses previous techniques in terms of accuracy, thereby establishing a new benchmark.

Stochastic thermodynamics leverages Markovian jump processes to simulate spontaneous changes between quantifiable microscopic states. The flow rates of physical processes are calculated from the anti-symmetric transition measures defined on the network of states. The statistical behavior of these flow rates can be represented by normalized cumulants. This study applies the mathematical and topological structure of Markovian models to demonstrate the gauge invariance of the cumulant-generating function. By taking advantage of this invariance, we have developed a streamlined method for calculating the normalized cumulants of a transition measure, eliminating the need for conditional expectations in the process. The new method employs a finite, orthogonal set of functions to express the average transition count and its variance, and subsequently computes the normalized cumulants through a series of elementary operations. The algorithm works specifically well with multi-scale models that balance detailed microscopic simulations with a coarser macroscopic understanding, and is ideal for scenarios where the primary interest lies in the overall thermodynamic flow rather than the intricate microscopic details.

This research examines how relative quantum cohomology evolves under certain mathematical transformations known as birational transformations. Specifically, it investigates the properties of relative I-functions in the context of toric complete intersections. For a particular type of toric complete intersections with specified divisor properties, it shows that the relative I-functions can be matched directly. Additionally, it demonstrates that the relative I-functions for another class of toric complete intersections can be connected through analytical means. Furthermore, it explores connections between these results and the related mathematical theories of extremal transitions and FJRW.

Two piezoelectric materials placed near each other can transfer energy across an intervening vacuum gap by transmitting acoustic waves. Our research provides a mathematical explanation for how this energy transfer occurs, and reveals that specific conditions allow for complete transmission of these waves. This finding holds true for materials of any shape or orientation and can be determined experimentally through measurement of surface properties. Furthermore, we analyzed the optimal energy transfer between identical zinc oxide crystals for various orientations and found a significant number of conditions that facilitate this energy transfer.

We explore a cutting-edge method for optically manipulating polariton condensates at a microscale, relying on highly coherent fluids of semiconductor-based light-emitting systems. Theoretical research indicates that modern spatial light manipulation technologies can be employed to redirect and concentrate these polariton condensates away from their initial sources of excitation. By strategically modulating non-resonant energy beams, an underlying exciton reservoir is generated which red-shifts and intensifies the polariton emission, allowing the formation of micro-scale lens-shaped structures that can steer polariton wave propagation. Multiple approaches are suggested for controlling polariton flow and demonstrate the feasibility of producing robust and localized light-emitting systems isolated from negative reservoir-induced effects.

The disintegrating exoplanet K2-22b displays erratic patterns in transit best attributed to a dissipating debris cloud, with the planet itself no longer intact. Various models of this debris cloud exist, relying on different assumptions for their accuracy. To gain more insight, we investigate how various characteristics of the model impact our observations of the exoplanet. By employing a Bayesian analysis, we compare several models to a simplified analysis of the data, avoiding complex noise and focusing on the key variables. Our results indicate that a large, widespread debris cloud that dissipates at a steady rate provides the best fit, with the remaining fragments concentrated at a distance equal to the radius of the original orbit. This study serves as a prerequisite for more comprehensive investigations, highlighting the importance of considering various assumptions in understanding the environment responsible for the exoplanet's disintegration.

We develop a novel algebro-geometric approach to studying the Milnor fibration and establish a significant condition for holomorphic function deformations to maintain the Milnor fibration intact. In consequence, we derive a strategy to divide the space of polynomials with a specified degree into discrete, localized segments where the diffusion process exhibits the same topological characteristics.

Daany is an open-source, cross-platform C# library focused on data analytics and linear algebra. Designed for.NET environments, this tool facilitates data preparation, feature engineering, and other data transformation operations. Developed atop.NET Standard 2.1 and compatible with.NET Core 3.0+, Daany consists of multiple VS projects that can be easily installed as a NuGet package. At its core, Daany utilizes the DataFrame data structure, complemented by data science and linear algebra capabilities, including time series decomposition (SSA, STL, ARIMA) and optimization methods (SGD). The library also integrates matrix and vector operations, as well as data plotting functionality. Daany's implementation bears similarities to Python's Pandas library. This guide serves as a comprehensive developer manual, outlining Daany's features, functionality, and implementation, as well as a user guide detailing usage and showcasing examples.

I challenge the conventional view of Galileo's influence on science by suggesting that he struggled with mathematical proficiency. This perceived weakness drove him to focus on experimentation and empiricism, as well as embracing the telescope's capabilities. His emphasis on hands-on research, which is often credited as an innovative aspect of his scientific approach, might actually be a consequence of his inability to make meaningful mathematical contributions. Similarly, his extensive discussion of scientific methodology was likely motivated by an effort to justify scientific practices that relied heavily on observational skills, which, in turn, was likely facilitated by his limited mathematical abilities. By exploring the effects of Galileo's mathematical limitations, I hope to provide a new perspective on his scientific legacy and the relationships between observational science, empiricism, and the instruments used in scientific inquiry.

The increasing demand for precise knowledge of astrophysical reaction rates drives the development of theoretical models. This research derives new expressions for thermonuclear reaction rate constants by applying a quantum statistical mechanics model. It incorporates the principles of detailed balance and asymptotic approximation, yielding a formula compatible with existing classical approaches. When comparing to experimental data, non-extensive thermal distributions can be represented by a generalized thermodynamic properties model. By applying this model to thin target situation, the paper examines how non-extensive effects impact residual nuclear interactions, including case studies of proton-rich nuclei. It investigates two specific astrophysical events: the hydrogen burning process in main sequence stars and the massive star collapse leading to supernovae explosions. It discovers that in both situations, the impact of non-extensive effects on reaction rates is minimal, resulting in a negligible alteration to existing predictions. This study sets out to answer whether the generalized thermodynamic properties model, when applied to thin target situations, could influence astrophysical phase space populations. The answer could have a significant impact on the field of nuclear astrophysics.

The analysis of magnetic reconnection, a collisionless process, necessitates complex, computationally intensive kinetic models, contrasting with more feasible fluid-based simulations. Our study utilizes the Magnetohydrodynamics with Adaptable Embedded Particle-in-Cell (MHD-AEPIC) model to investigate the interaction between two magnetic flux ropes. By embedding kinetic models into MHD simulations only in relevant areas, this novel model enables more efficient computation. The comparative study between MHD-AEPIC and full kinetic PIC simulations shows good correspondence, and with adaptively embedded PIC models of varying scales, we can optimize computational performance while maintaining accuracy. Our findings consist of two primary components: Firstly, we obtain accurate reconnection rates, speeds, and electron signatures from the embedded PIC models, thus validating the MHD-AEPIC model. Secondly, we observe all-scale interactions and the significant impact of two magnetic flux ropes encountering each other, leading to accelerated reconnection, complex electron behavior, and the generation of secondary magnetic fields at various scales.

This document provides a summary of the content from a course held at Stanford University in the spring of 2018.  The course brings together insights from cognitive neuroscience and systems neuroscience to create intelligent systems by combining human and machine intelligence.  The course uses a tangible example - a digital assistant that learns and evolves through ongoing conversations with an experienced software engineer while beginning as an effective analytical and problem-solving tool.  Over time, these intelligent assistants develop essential thinking strategies and learn to rely on intuition, eventually becoming exceptional programmers in their own right.  As a result, these digital assistants learn to write code at an exceptional level, facilitating a seamless transfer of expertise from their human counterparts.  As these intelligent assistants mature, their performance surpasses that of traditional artificial intelligence, simultaneously enhancing their own decision-making capabilities and developing new skills.
